subject: maths
stem:
Ira writes four claims about the number list 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, …

Which claim treats the list as a mathematical pattern?

options.A: The list looks neat, so it is a pattern even with no rule stated.
options.B: The list is a pattern of adding 1, because whole numbers always grow by 1.
options.C: Each term is 2 more than the one before, because we keep adding 2.
options.D: The same list also proves a new theorem about all infinite sequences.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Esha lists bead counts 3, 6, 9, 12, …

parts.text: Which claim treats the list as a mathematical pattern?

options.text: Each term is 3 more than the one before, because we keep adding 3.
The list looks tidy, so it is a pattern with no rule needed.
Saying the rule is what creates the multiples of 3.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Zubin stacks cups in rows: 1, 2, 4, 8, …

parts.text: Which claim treats the list as a mathematical pattern?

options.text: Each term is double the one before, because we keep multiplying by 2.
The list looks neat, so it is a pattern with no rule needed.
Saying the doubling rule is what creates the cup counts.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anya studies the whole-number list 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, …

Which claim correctly continues the list?

options.A: The next term is 10, because whole numbers always grow by 1.
options.B: The next term is 13, because each term is 4 more than the one before.
options.C: The next term is 11, because each term is 2 more than the one before.
options.D: The next term is 25, because 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 25.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Karan writes the whole-number list 4, 7, 10, 13, …

parts.text: Which claim correctly continues the list?

options.text: Each term is 3 more than the one before, so the next term is 16.
Each term is 4 more than the one before, so the next term is 17.
The next term is 14, because 14 comes after 13 when counting.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Esha studies the whole-number list $1$, $4$, $9$, $16$, $\ldots$

Which claim correctly continues the list?

options.A: Each term is the square of $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, $\ldots$, so the next term is $25$.
options.B: Each term is $4$ more than the one before, so the next term is $20$.
options.C: Each term is double the one before, so the next term is $32$.
options.D: The last term repeats, so the next term is $16$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Rina studies the three pictures in the figure. Each picture is a square grid of dots: a 1-by-1 square, then a 2-by-2 square, then a 3-by-3 square.

Which claim correctly describes how to draw the next picture?

options.A: Any larger cluster of dots works, without keeping the square-grid construction from picture to picture.
options.B: Drawing the next square grid is what creates the square numbers in the first place.
options.C: The next picture is a 4-by-4 square of 16 dots, because each picture is an n-by-n square for n = 1, 2, 3, …
options.D: The next picture needs the full chapter shape-sequence table before it can be drawn.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Veer draws three square-dot pictures in order: a $1$-by-$1$ square of $1$ dot, a $2$-by-$2$ square of $4$ dots, then a $3$-by-$3$ square of $9$ dots.

parts.text: Which claim correctly names how the next picture should be drawn?

options.text: The next picture is a $4$-by-$4$ square of $16$ dots, continuing the $n$-by-$n$ square pattern.
Any larger cloud of dots works, because greater size alone continues the pictures.
Drawing the next picture is what creates the square-number list in the first place.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Naveen studies the three pictures in the figure. Each picture is a triangular array of dots: $1$ dot, then a triangle of $3$ dots, then a triangle of $6$ dots.

Which claim correctly describes how to draw the next picture?

options.A: The next picture is a triangular array of $10$ dots, because the pictures show $1$, $1+2$, $1+2+3$, then $1+2+3+4$ dots.
options.B: Any larger cluster of dots works, so the triangular row-by-row construction need not continue.
options.C: Drawing the next triangular array is what creates the earlier counts $1$, $3$ and $6$.
options.D: The next picture needs the full chapter shape-sequence table before it can be drawn.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Isha builds an $n$-by-$n$ square of unit tiles. She peels it into $n$ nested L-shaped layers: the outermost L uses $2n-1$ tiles, then $2n-3$, and so on down to $1$.

Why does the sum of the first $n$ odd numbers equal $n^{2}$?

options.A: Any collection of odd numbers sums to a square, even if the odds are not the first $n$ consecutive odds starting at $1$.
options.B: The same L-layer story also explains the up-and-down sum of ordinary counting numbers, so that sum must equal $n^{2}$ too.
options.C: The $n$-by-$n$ square can be partitioned into those $n$ nested odd L-layers, so $1+3+\cdots+(2n-1)=n^{2}$.
options.D: The answer is "odd numbers", because that phrase is printed most often in the problem.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Reyansh builds an $n$-by-$n$ square of unit tiles. He peels it into $n$ nested L-shaped layers: the outermost L uses $2n-1$ tiles, then $2n-3$, and so on down to $1$.

parts.text: Which claim correctly explains why the sum of the first $n$ odd numbers equals $n^{2}$?

options.text: The $n$-by-$n$ square partitions into those $n$ nested odd L-layers, so $1+3+\cdots+(2n-1)=n^{2}$.
Any collection of odd numbers sums to a square, even when the odds are not the first $n$ consecutive odds from $1$.
The same L-layer story also forces the up-and-down sum of ordinary counting numbers to equal $n^{2}$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The figure shows Esha's $5$-by-$5$ square of unit tiles. She paints it in nested L-shaped borders: the outermost border uses $9$ tiles, the next uses $7$, then $5$, then $3$, and the centre tile is $1$.

Why does the sum of the first $5$ odd numbers equal $5^{2}$?

options.A: The $5$-by-$5$ square partitions into those five nested odd L-borders, so $1+3+5+7+9=25$.
options.B: Any set of odd numbers sums to a square, even when the odds are not the first five consecutive odds from $1$.
options.C: The same L-border story also forces the sum of the first five counting numbers to equal $25$.
options.D: The answer is $25$, because $5$ is the largest number printed on the figure.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anya writes the up-and-down sum $1+2+\cdots+n+\cdots+2+1$ with consecutive counting numbers that climb from $1$ to $n$ and then fall back to $1$.

Why does that sum equal $n^{2}$?

options.A: The sum equals $n^{2}$ for any climb-and-fall of whole numbers, even if the steps are not the consecutive counting numbers from $1$ to $n$ and back.
options.B: Say that $n^{2}$ is what produces the up-and-down counting sum, instead of arranging the sum to fill an $n$-by-$n$ square.
options.C: The climb from $1$ to $n$ and the fall back to $1$ can be paired to fill an $n$-by-$n$ square of unit tiles, so the sum is $n^{2}$.
options.D: The same story also forces triangular and hexagonal number identities, so those must equal $n^{2}$ too.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Ishaan writes the up-and-down sum $1+2+3+4+3+2+1$ with consecutive counting numbers that climb from $1$ to $4$ and then fall back to $1$.

parts.text: Why does this sum equal $4^{2}$?

options.text: The climb from $1$ to $4$ and the fall back to $1$ can be paired to fill a $4$-by-$4$ square of unit tiles.
Any climb-and-fall of whole numbers equals a square, even when the steps are not consecutive counting numbers.
$4^{2}$ is what produces the up-and-down counting sum.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Esha writes the up-and-down sum $1+2+3+4+5+6+5+4+3+2+1$ with consecutive counting numbers that climb from $1$ to $6$ and then fall back to $1$. The figure shows those counts filling a $6$-by-$6$ square of unit tiles. She is checking why this sum equals $6^{2}$, not a triangular or hexagonal number sum.

Why does that sum equal $6^{2}$?

options.A: The consecutive climb and fall from $1$ to $6$ fill the $6$-by-$6$ square of unit tiles, so the sum is $36$.
options.B: Any climb-and-fall list of numbers fills a $6$-by-$6$ square, even when the numbers are not consecutive counting numbers from $1$.
options.C: Filling the $6$-by-$6$ square of unit tiles is what produces the consecutive counting numbers from $1$ to $6$.
options.D: The same filling also makes a triangular or hexagonal number sum equal $36$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Rina builds a row of squares with matchsticks. Shape $1$ uses $4$ sticks, shape $2$ uses $7$ sticks, and shape $3$ uses $10$ sticks.

Which countable feature produces the related number sequence $4$, $7$, $10$, $\ldots$?

options.A: Count sticks on shape $1$ only, then reuse that same count for every later shape.
options.B: Count every interior angle in any polygon from the chapter, as if that also made this sequence.
options.C: Count the matchsticks in each whole shape; repeating that same count gives $4$, $7$, $10$, $\ldots$.
options.D: Pick the printed numeral $10$ alone because it is the largest number shown.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Aryan builds a growing triangle pattern with toothpicks. Shape $1$ uses $3$ toothpicks, Shape $2$ uses $5$ toothpicks, and Shape $3$ uses $7$ toothpicks.

Which countable feature produces the related number sequence $3$, $5$, $7$, $\ldots$?

options.A: Count the toothpicks in Shape $1$ only, then reuse that same count for every later shape.
options.B: Count every interior angle in any polygon from the chapter, as if that also made this sequence.
options.C: Count the toothpicks that make up each whole shape; repeating that same count gives $3$, $5$, $7$, $\ldots$.
options.D: Pick the printed numeral $7$ alone because it is the largest number shown.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Esha builds a row of hexagon houses with drinking straws. Shape $1$ uses $6$ straws, Shape $2$ uses $11$ straws, and Shape $3$ uses $16$ straws.

Which countable feature produces the related number sequence $6$, $11$, $16$, $\ldots$?

options.A: Count the straws that make up each whole shape; repeating that same count gives $6$, $11$, $16$, $\ldots$.
options.B: Count the straws in Shape $1$ only, then reuse that same count for every later shape.
options.C: Count every interior angle from any polygon in the chapter, as if that also made this sequence.
options.D: Pick the printed numeral $16$ alone because it is the largest number shown.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Omkar makes a tiny pencil mark on his notebook page and labels it P.

In geometry, what does this mark stand for?

options.A: A point: a precise location with no length, breadth, or thickness, named by the letter P.
options.B: A short line segment that starts at P and has a measurable length.
options.C: The black disk of graphite itself, which has a real size on the page.
options.D: Any decorative blot on the page, even when it does not name a location.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Raghav makes a chalk mark on the board and labels it R.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: The chalk disk itself is the geometric object, so its size on the board is the point.
options.B: The mark stands for a point: a precise location with no length, breadth, or thickness.
options.C: The point is identified by the letter R.
options.D: Any decorative smudge is a point, even when it does not name a location.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Mini presses a thumb-tack into a notice board and labels it M.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: The metal head itself is the geometric object, so its size on the board is the point.
options.B: The mark stands for a point: a precise location with no length, breadth, or thickness.
options.C: The point is identified by the letter M.
options.D: Any decorative scratch is a point, even when it does not name a location.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit draws a straight path that starts at point A, ends at point B, and does not continue past either point.

What has he drawn?

options.A: A line, because it is straight.
options.B: A ray starting at A and passing through B without ending.
options.C: A line segment AB, because it has two endpoints A and B.
options.D: A line segment even if he erases endpoint B and lets the path run on.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Inaya draws a straight path that starts at point $P$, passes through point $Q$, and continues forever only past $Q$.

Which two claims correctly name that path?

options.A: The path is a line segment $PQ$, because it stops at both $P$ and $Q$.
options.B: The path is a ray that starts at $P$ and goes through $Q$ forever.
options.C: The path has one endpoint at $P$ and no endpoint past $Q$.
options.D: The path is a full line, because any straight mark through $P$ and $Q$ must extend both ways forever.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Alok's straight path through points $R$ and $S$. Arrowheads mark both ends, so the path continues forever past $R$ and forever past $S$.

What has he drawn?

options.A: A line segment $RS$, because $R$ and $S$ are the only points named.
options.B: A ray that starts at $R$ and stops at $S$.
options.C: A line through $R$ and $S$ that extends forever in both directions.
options.D: A ray, because any straight path with two named points must be a ray.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Esha marks three distinct points P, Q, and R on her paper that do not lie on one straight path.

How many distinct lines are determined by these points?

options.A: One line, because any set of points always lies on a single line.
options.B: Infinitely many lines, because one point alone already fixes infinitely many lines.
options.C: Three lines: PQ, QR, and RP, because each pair of distinct points determines exactly one line.
options.D: Nine lines, by multiplying three points by three possible directions.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anvi marks three distinct points $P$, $Q$, and $R$ on her paper that do not lie on one straight path.

Which two claims correctly count the distinct lines fixed by those points?

options.A: One line, because any three points always share a single line.
options.B: Three lines $PQ$, $QR$, and $RP$, because each pair of distinct points fixes exactly one line.
options.C: Each pair among $P$, $Q$, and $R$ determines one unique line, giving three lines in all.
options.D: Nine lines, by multiplying three points by three possible directions.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Oditi marks four distinct points $S$, $T$, $U$ and $V$ on her paper. No three of the points lie on one straight path. The diagram shows the points.

Which claim correctly counts the distinct lines fixed by those points?

options.A: Six lines: each pair among $S$, $T$, $U$ and $V$ determines exactly one line.
options.B: One line, because any set of points always lies on a single line.
options.C: Infinitely many lines, because one point alone already fixes infinitely many lines.
options.D: Sixteen lines, by multiplying four points by four possible directions.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Dev draws the ray shown in the figure. It starts at point A and passes through points B and C in that order.

Which label correctly names the ray?

options.A: Ray BA, because B and A both lie on the path.
options.B: Point A is produced by the ray, so any letter order is fine.
options.C: Ray AB or ray AC, because the starting point A comes first, then a point on the path.
options.D: Line ABC, treating the figure as a two-way line with no starting point.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Aarna's ray. It starts at point $A$ and passes through points $B$ and $C$ in that order.

Which two claims correctly name the ray?

options.A: Ray $BA$ is a correct name, because $B$ and $A$ both lie on the path.
options.B: Ray $AB$ is a correct name, because the starting point $A$ comes first, then a point on the path.
options.C: Ray $AC$ is a correct name, because the starting point $A$ comes first, then another point on the path.
options.D: Line $ABC$ is a correct name, treating the figure as a two-way line with no starting point.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Alok's ray. It starts at point $D$ and passes through points $E$ and $F$ in that order.

Which label correctly names the ray?

options.A: Ray $DE$ or ray $DF$, because the starting point $D$ comes first, then a point on the path.
options.B: Ray $ED$, because $E$ and $D$ both lie on the path.
options.C: Point $D$ is produced by the ray, so any letter order is fine.
options.D: Line $DEF$, treating the path as a two-way line with no starting point.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Veena draws two rays from a common point O on her slate: ray OA and ray OB.

Which statement correctly describes the angle they form?

options.A: The vertex of the angle is arm OA.
options.B: OA and OB form this angle even if they start at two different points.
options.C: The rays share starting point O (the vertex); the arms are OA and OB; the angle may be named ∠AOB.
options.D: The angle is named ∠O because O is the first letter printed on the slate.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows two rays drawn from a common point O on Tara's slate: ray OA and ray OB.

Which statement correctly describes the angle they form?

options.A: The vertex of the angle is arm OA.
options.B: OA and OB form this angle even if they start at two different points.
options.C: The rays share starting point O (the vertex); the arms are OA and OB; the angle may be named $\angle AOB$.
options.D: The angle is named $\angle O$ because O is the first letter printed on the slate.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Alok draws two rays from a common point $P$ on his notebook: ray $PM$ and ray $PN$.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims correctly describe the angle they form?

options.A: Ray $PM$ and ray $PN$ form an angle whose vertex is $P$ and whose arms are $PM$ and $PN$.
options.B: The vertex of the angle is arm $PM$.
options.C: The angle may be named $\angle MPN$, with the vertex letter $P$ written in the middle.
options.D: Ray $PM$ and another ray that does not start at $P$ still form this angle.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tara compares the two angles in the figure. Angle P has short arms and a wide turn. Angle Q has long arms and a narrow turn.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Angle Q is larger, because its arms are drawn longer.
options.B: The drawn arm lengths are what produce the amount of turn.
options.C: Angle P is larger, because it has the greater amount of turn about the vertex.
options.D: Compare decorative arrowheads on the rays before measuring the turn.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Nitya draws two angles on her slate. Angle $R$ has short arms and a wide turn about its vertex. Angle $S$ has long arms and a narrow turn about its vertex.

parts.text: Which claim correctly decides which angle is larger?

options.text: Angle $S$ is larger, because its arms are drawn longer.
Angle $R$ is larger, because it has the greater amount of turn about the vertex.
The drawn arm lengths are what produce the amount of turn.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Alok draws two angles on paper. Angle $M$ has short arms and a wide turn about its vertex. Angle $N$ has long arms and a narrow turn about its vertex.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims correctly decide which angle is larger?

options.A: Angle $M$ is larger, because it has the greater amount of turn about the vertex.
options.B: Angle $N$ is larger, because its arms are drawn longer.
options.C: Arm length does not decide size when the amount of turn is what is compared.
options.D: Angle $M$ and angle $N$ have the same size on Alok's paper.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Mona has two card angles. She wants to know which is larger by overlaying them.

Which method decides correctly?

options.A: Lay them so the vertices miss each other, and still claim the overlay compares the angles.
options.B: Say that the larger angle is what produces a successful overlay, instead of using overlay to compare.
options.C: Place both vertices together and match one arm; the angle whose other arm lies outside is larger (they match if equal).
options.D: Use the same overlay test to decide which decorative colour on the card is brighter.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Veer traces two angles on tracing paper. The diagram shows angle $P$ and angle $Q$ sharing vertex $O$.

Which claim correctly decides which angle is larger?

options.A: Angle $P$ and angle $Q$ are equal, because both rays start at $O$.
options.B: Angle $Q$ is larger than angle $P$, because overlaying with matching vertices shows $Q$ sticks out past $P$.
options.C: Angle $P$ is larger than angle $Q$, because overlaying with matching vertices shows $P$ sticks out past $Q$.
options.D: The sizes cannot be compared, because the angles use different letter names.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Esha holds two cardboard corner pieces. The diagram shows angle $R$ and angle $S$ drawn from those corners.

Which claim correctly decides which angle is larger by overlaying?

options.A: Match the vertices and align one arm of each; the free arm of angle $R$ opens farther, so angle $R$ is larger.
options.B: Leave the vertices apart on the desk and judge the openings from separate places.
options.C: Knowing that angle $R$ is larger is what creates the overlay of the cardboard corners.
options.D: Any two cardboard corner pieces must be equal angles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit looks at the figure: line AOB is straight through O, and ray OC meets AOB so that angle $1$ equals angle $2$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Angle $1$ is a right angle for any split of AOB, even when angle $1$ is not half of the straight angle.
options.B: He should first study the decorative history of the diagram before classifying any angle.
options.C: AOB is a straight angle (a half turn); because angle $1$ equals angle $2$, each is a right angle, so OC is perpendicular to AOB.
options.D: The answer is "straight angle", because those words are printed beside AOB, without using the equal split.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Aarav looks at the diagram. Points $B$, $O$ and $A$ lie on one straight line, and ray $OC$ meets line $BA$ at $O$. The marked angle at $O$ between $OC$ and $OA$ is $90^{\circ}$.

Which claim about the figure is correct?

options.A: Ray $OC$ is perpendicular to line $BA$, and $\angle COA$ is a right angle.
options.B: $\angle BOA$ is a right angle because ray $OC$ is drawn.
options.C: Every angle drawn on line $BA$ must be a straight angle.
options.D: Angle $\angle COA$ is right because the letter $C$ is printed highest on the page.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Esha looks at the figure. Segments $AB$ and $CD$ meet at $M$, and a square mark sits at $\angle AMC$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: $\angle AMC$ is a right angle, so $AB$ and $CD$ are perpendicular at $M$.
options.B: $AB$ and $CD$ are perpendicular at $M$ for any crossing of the two segments, even without a right angle at $M$.
options.C: Every pair of segments drawn through $M$ must form a straight angle at $M$.
options.D: The answer is "right angle" only because the square mark is the darkest print near $M$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Esha measures an angle of $120^\circ$.

Which claim about its type is correct?

options.A: Call it acute even though $120^\circ$ is not less than $90^\circ$.
options.B: First study the decorative history of angle names before classifying $120^\circ$.
options.C: It is obtuse, because $90^\circ < 120^\circ < 180^\circ$.
options.D: It is "$120$", because that numeral is printed largest, without using the size classes.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Adil measures $\angle AOB$ in the diagram. The marked size is $135^{\circ}$.

options.A: Call it acute, treating $135^{\circ}$ as less than $90^{\circ}$.
options.B: First study the decorative history of angle names before classifying $135^{\circ}$.
options.C: It is obtuse, because $90^{\circ} < 135^{\circ} < 180^{\circ}$.
options.D: It is "$135$", because that numeral is printed largest in the diagram.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Dev asks how a numerical degree measure is assigned to an angle formed by two rays from a point.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Answer "one-degree unit", naming that phrase instead of saying how many such units lie between the arms.
options.B: Count any collection of parts of a turn as degrees, even when those parts are not equal parts of a full turn.
options.C: A full turn is split into $360$ equal one-degree parts; the angle's measure is how many of those equal parts lie between its arms.
options.D: Say that the degree reading is what creates the equal one-degree parts, instead of counting those parts between the arms.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kabir looks at the diagram. Ray $OA$ and ray $OB$ meet at $O$ and form $\angle AOB$. A full turn around $O$ is split into $360$ equal parts.

Which claim correctly assigns a degree measure to $\angle AOB$?

options.A: The measure is the count of those equal one-degree parts that lie between ray $OA$ and ray $OB$.
options.B: The measure is the printed letter $O$ at the vertex, read as the degree number.
options.C: Any count of parts between the rays is a degree measure, even if the parts of the full turn are unequal.
options.D: Counting one-degree parts between the rays is what creates the full $360$-part turn.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Veena must measure $\angle PQR$ with a protractor.

Which plan measures the angle correctly?

options.A: Place the protractor on ray $PQ$ and read a scale mark, without putting the center on vertex $Q$.
options.B: Say that reading a degree number is what creates $\angle PQR$, instead of aligning the protractor to the arms.
options.C: Place the center on $Q$, align one arm with the zero-degree line, and read the scale reached by the other arm.
options.D: After reading $\angle PQR$, treat that same reading as also fixing every other unmarked angle at $Q$, beyond measuring these two arms.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yash looks at the diagram of $\angle PQR$. He will measure $\theta$ with a protractor.

Which claim correctly states how he must place the protractor?

options.A: Put the protractor center on vertex $Q$, align ray $QP$ with the zero-degree line, and read the scale reached by ray $QR$.
options.B: Rest the protractor anywhere on ray $QP$ and read a scale mark for $\theta$.
options.C: Say that reading a degree number is what creates $\angle PQR$ on the page.
options.D: After reading $\theta$, treat that same reading as also fixing every unmarked angle at $Q$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tara must construct a $65^\circ$ angle with ruler and protractor.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Call the finished drawing protractor angle only, without placing the protractor and marking $65^\circ$.
options.B: Place the protractor center on the vertex but skip aligning the base arm with the zero mark before reading $65^\circ$.
options.C: Choose a vertex and one base arm, seat the protractor center on the vertex, align the base arm with $0^\circ$, mark $65^\circ$ on the correct scale, and draw the second arm through that mark.
options.D: Mark $65$ only because that number is printed in the stem, without using the protractor steps.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Diya must construct a $70^{\circ}$ angle with ruler and protractor, as suggested by the diagram.

Which plan correctly builds that angle?

options.A: Call the finished drawing the vertex and stop there.
options.B: Seat the protractor centre on the vertex but leave the base arm off the $0^{\circ}$ mark before marking $70^{\circ}$.
options.C: Choose a vertex and one base arm, seat the protractor centre on the vertex, align the base arm with $0^{\circ}$, mark $70^{\circ}$, and draw the second arm through that mark.
options.D: Mark $70$ only because that number is printed largest in the stem.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Isha draws ray $OC$ from the vertex of $\angle AOB$ in the figure.

When does $OC$ bisect $\angle AOB$?

options.A: Call the answer "crease" only, without checking that the two angles at $O$ are equal.
options.B: Treat $OC$ as a bisector after checking only that it starts at $O$, skipping that $\angle AOC$ must equal $\angle COB$.
options.C: When $\angle AOC = \angle COB$, so ray $OC$ from $O$ splits $\angle AOB$ into two equal angles.
options.D: Say that equal angles $\angle AOC$ and $\angle COB$ are what create ray $OC$, instead of ray $OC$ from $O$ making those two angles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Aarav draws ray OC from the vertex of angle AOB.

When does ray OC bisect angle AOB?

options.A: The word ray on OC is what shows that OC bisects angle AOB.
options.B: OC bisects angle AOB whenever OC lies somewhere between OA and OB.
options.C: OC bisects angle AOB when angle AOC equals angle COB.
options.D: Angle AOB produces the equal halves, so the halves create ray OC.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Uma knows a straight angle at point $O$ is $180^\circ$. Ray $OP$ cuts it into adjacent angles $\angle AOP$ and $\angle POB$, and $\angle AOP=70^\circ$.

Which claim finds $\angle POB$?

options.A: Call the answer the "whole angle" $180^\circ$, without subtracting the known adjacent part.
options.B: Say that finding $\angle POB$ is what creates the straight $180^\circ$ angle at $O$, instead of using the whole to find the unknown part.
options.C: The adjacent parts add to the whole: $\angle POB=180^\circ-70^\circ=110^\circ$.
options.D: Report $70^\circ$ as $\angle POB$ only because $70$ is the printed degree number in the stem.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Farhan looks at the diagram. Straight line $AOB$ meets at $O$, and ray $OP$ cuts the straight angle into adjacent angles $\angle AOP$ and $\angle POB$. The marked angle $\angle POB$ is $65^{\circ}$.

Which claim correctly finds $\angle AOP$?

options.A: Call the answer the ray $OP$, and stop.
options.B: Finding $\angle AOP$ is what creates the straight line $AOB$.
options.C: $\angle AOP=180^{\circ}-65^{\circ}=115^{\circ}$, because adjacent angles on a straight line make $180^{\circ}$.
options.D: $\angle AOP=65^{\circ}$, matching the largest printed degree mark in the diagram.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qadir stands in a height line with other children. The rule is: each child says the count of taller children standing immediately next to that child. Qadir says "1".

What does Qadir's "1" report?

options.A: The count of taller children standing immediately next to him.
options.B: His own height in centimetres.
options.C: The total number of children in the whole line.
options.D: How many children in the line are shorter than him.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Mini's class uses this rule: each child says how many storybooks that child brought today. Mini says "4".

What does Mini's "4" report?

options.A: Mini's roll number in the class register.
options.B: The total storybooks brought by the whole class.
options.C: The count of storybooks Mini brought today.
options.D: How many storybooks Mini still needs to bring.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Raghav's class uses this rule: each child says how many erasers that child brought today. Raghav says "3".

What does Raghav's "3" report?

options.A: The count of erasers Raghav brought today.
options.B: Raghav's age in years.
options.C: The total erasers brought by the whole class.
options.D: How many erasers Raghav still needs to bring.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Parul writes this number grid (neighbours are left, right, top, and bottom only):

4  7  3
6  9  5
2  8  1

A supercell is greater than every immediate neighbour.

Which cell is a supercell?

options.A: The cell with 9
options.B: The cell with 8
options.C: The cell with 7
options.D: The cell with 6

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Boman writes this number grid. Immediate neighbours are only left, right, top, and bottom.

$5\quad 8\quad 2$
$7\quad 9\quad 4$
$3\quad 6\quad 1$

A supercell is greater than every immediate neighbour.

Which cell is a supercell?

options.A: The cell $9$
options.B: The cell $8$
options.C: The cell $7$
options.D: Calling $9$ a supercell is what makes its neighbours smaller.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: The diagram shows Imran's number grid. Immediate neighbours are only left, right, top, and bottom. A supercell is greater than every immediate neighbour.

parts.text: Which claim correctly names a supercell in the grid?

options.text: The cell $8$ is a supercell, because it is greater than $6$, $5$, $4$, and $7$.
The cell $6$ is a supercell, because it is the largest number in the top row.
Calling a cell a supercell is what makes its neighbours smaller.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Indira fills three cells in a row with numbers. A cell is a supercell when its number is greater than each immediate neighbour. She wants only the middle cell to be a supercell.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The filling 9, 4, 2 works, because only the left cell is a supercell.
options.B: The filling 4, 9, 2 works, because only the middle cell is greater than each immediate neighbour.
options.C: Any filling where 9 appears is enough, because 9 is the largest number she wrote.
options.D: The filling 2, 4, 9 works, because only the right cell is a supercell.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Shaan fills three cells in a row with numbers. A cell is a supercell when its number is greater than each immediate neighbour. He wants only the middle cell to be a supercell.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The filling $9$, $4$, $2$ works, because only the left cell is a supercell.
options.B: The filling $2$, $4$, $9$ works, because only the right cell is a supercell.
options.C: The filling $4$, $9$, $2$ works, because only the middle cell is greater than each immediate neighbour.
options.D: Any filling where $9$ appears is enough, because $9$ is the largest number he wrote.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Parth fills the three cells in the figure with the numbers shown. A cell is a supercell when its number is greater than each immediate neighbour.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims correctly identify supercells in this row?

options.A: The middle cell $8$ is a supercell, because $8$ is greater than $3$ and greater than $5$.
options.B: The left cell $3$ is a supercell, because $3$ is the intended leftmost number.
options.C: The right cell $5$ is not a supercell, because $5$ is smaller than its neighbour $8$.
options.D: Calling a cell a supercell is what makes its neighbours smaller.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri looks at a number line from 3000 to 4000. The interval is divided into five equal parts with marks at equal spacing.

What number does the first mark after 3000 show?

options.A: 3001, treating each mark as one unit.
options.B: 3500, splitting the interval into two equal halves only.
options.D: 4000, jumping straight to the right endpoint.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Dhruvil looks at a number line from $2000$ to $3000$. The interval is divided into five equal parts with marks at equal spacing.

What number does the first mark after $2000$ show?

options.A: $2001$, treating each mark as one unit.
options.B: $2500$, splitting the interval into two equal halves only.
options.D: $3000$, jumping straight to the right endpoint.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: The diagram shows Imran's number line from $4000$ to $6000$. The interval is divided into four equal parts with marks at equal spacing.

parts.text: Which claim correctly reads the second mark after $4000$?

options.text: The second mark after $4000$ shows $5000$, because each equal part is $500$.
The second mark after $4000$ shows $4002$, treating each mark as one unit.
Reading $5000$ on the mark is what creates the equal spacing on the number line.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Asha asks how many 1-digit counting numbers there are.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: There is 1 such number, because a 1-digit number is itself called a digit.
options.B: There are 10 such numbers, counting 0 through 9 without the chapter start at 1.
options.C: There are 9 such numbers: 1 through 9 each have digit length 1.
options.D: The same count also settles how many 2-digit numbers there are, with no further check.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Dev asks how many 2-digit counting numbers there are.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: There are $2$ such numbers, because a 2-digit number is itself called a digit pair.
options.B: There are $90$ such numbers: $10$ through $99$ each have digit length $2$.
options.C: The smallest 2-digit counting number is $10$ and the largest is $99$.
options.D: The same count also settles how many 3-digit numbers there are, with no further work.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Imran asks how many $3$-digit counting numbers there are.

parts.text: Which claim is correct?

options.text: There are $900$ three-digit counting numbers, from $100$ to $999$.
There are $999$ three-digit counting numbers, counting every whole number from $1$ to $999$.
A $3$-digit number has digit length $3$, so there are exactly $3$ such numbers.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yamini wants a 3-digit number whose digits add to 9.

Which number has digit sum 9?

options.A: 900, reading only the leading digit 9 as the digit sum.
options.B: 123, because 123 looks like the smallest neat 3-digit print.
options.D: 306, because 306 is greater than all its neighbouring cells in a grid.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kabir wants 3-digit numbers whose digits add to $12$.

Which two claims correctly use digit sums for that target?

options.A: Reading only the leading digit $9$ in $903$ gives digit sum $12$.
options.B: $453$ works, because $4+5+3=12$.
options.C: $390$ also works, because $3+9+0=12$.
options.D: $453$ works because $453$ looks neat and large on the page.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Imran wants a $3$-digit number whose digits add to $15$.

parts.text: Which claim correctly uses digit sums for that target?

options.text: $573$ has digit sum $15$, because $5+7+3=15$.
The digit sum is the three-digit number $573$ itself.
$15$ alone is the $3$-digit number he wants, because $15$ is printed as the target.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qadir lists every whole number from $10$ to $19$. He wants the number of times the digit $1$ is written in that list.

Which count is correct?

options.A: Count $10$, $11$, $12$, $13$, $14$, $15$, $16$, $17$, $18$, and $19$ as ten hits, treating each number that contains a $1$ as a single hit.
options.B: Say that writing the digit $1$ is what creates the list from $10$ to $19$.
options.C: Count every written $1$: one in $10$, two in $11$, and one each in $12$ through $19$, for $11$ written ones.
options.D: Use the same $11$ also as the count of how many times $1$ appears from $1$ to $100$, with no further check.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anvi lists every whole number from $20$ to $29$. She wants how many times the digit $2$ is written in that list.

Which two claims are both correct?

options.A: The digit $2$ appears $10$ times, once for each number in the list.
options.B: In the tens place, $2$ appears in every number from $20$ to $29$, so that is $10$ writings.
options.C: In the ones place, $2$ appears once more in $22$, so the total is $11$ writings of the digit $2$.
options.D: Counting only the ones digits from $20$ to $29$ already gives the full answer $10$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Alok lists every whole number from $30$ to $39$. He wants the number of times the digit $3$ is written in that list.

Which count is correct?

options.A: The digit $3$ is written $10$ times, once for each number from $30$ to $39$.
options.B: Writing the digit $3$ eleven times is what produces the list from $30$ to $39$.
options.C: The digit $3$ is written $11$ times, because $33$ contributes two written $3$s.
options.D: The count $11$ also covers every digit written in $30$ to $39$, not only the digit $3$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Omkar wants a $3$-digit palindrome using digits from $1$ to $9$ only.

Which number is a $3$-digit palindrome?

options.A: $123$, claiming it is a palindrome even though the hundreds digit $1$ and the units digit $3$ differ.
options.B: Say that digits are what the palindrome label produces, so any $3$-digit number he likes counts.
options.C: $454$, because it reads the same forwards and backwards (hundreds digit equals units digit).
options.D: Treat $45$ as a $3$-digit palindrome by the same rule.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Diya may use only the digits $2$, $5$ and $7$. She wants 3-digit numbers that read the same forwards and backwards.

Which two claims correctly describe such palindromes?

options.A: Any arrangement of $2$, $5$ and $7$ is a palindrome.
options.B: A 3-digit palindrome must have the same hundreds digit and ones digit.
options.C: $252$ and $575$ are palindromes Diya can make from the allowed digits.
options.D: The middle digit alone decides whether the number is a palindrome.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Alok may use only the digits $1$, $4$ and $8$. He wants a $3$-digit palindrome for a locker code.

Which number is a $3$-digit palindrome he can make?

options.A: $148$, claiming it is a palindrome even though the hundreds digit $1$ and the units digit $8$ differ.
options.B: $414$, because it reads the same forwards and backwards and uses only allowed digits.
options.C: Saying a number is a palindrome is what creates matching hundreds and units digits.
options.D: $41$, treated as a $3$-digit palindrome by the same rule.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Indira starts with the $2$-digit number $23$. She reverses the digits and adds, then repeats reverse-and-add until she should stop.

Which claim applies the process correctly?

options.A: Form $23 + 32 = 55$, notice $55$ reads the same both ways, and keep reverse-and-adding anyway.
options.B: Say that reaching a palindrome is what creates the starting number $23$.
options.C: Form $23 + 32 = 55$; $55$ is a palindrome, so stop at $55$.
options.D: Repeat the chapter word palindrome alone, without reverse-and-adding $23$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Meher starts with the $2$-digit number $47$. She reverses the digits and adds, then repeats reverse-and-add until she should stop.

Which two claims apply the process correctly?

options.A: Form $47+74=121$, notice $121$ reads the same both ways, and keep reverse-and-adding past $121$.
options.B: Form $47+74=121$; $121$ is a palindrome, so stop at $121$.
options.C: The process stops as soon as the current result is a palindrome.
options.D: Say that reaching a palindrome is what creates the starting number $47$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri builds a $5$-digit palindrome. Its ten-thousands digit is $6$ and its hundreds digit is $2$. The thousands digit is half the ten-thousands digit.

Which number is it?

options.A: Call the answer the "thousands digit" label, without building the full palindrome.
options.B: Say the thousands digit is what produces the ten-thousands digit, reversing the given half-relation.
options.C: $63236$, because ten-thousands $=$ units $= 6$, thousands $=$ tens $= 3$ (half of $6$), and hundreds $= 2$.
options.D: Report $2$ alone, because that digit is printed as the hundreds clue.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sia builds a $5$-digit palindrome. Its ten-thousands digit is $8$ and its hundreds digit is $3$. The thousands digit is $2$ more than the hundreds digit.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: The units digit must be $8$ to match the ten-thousands digit.
options.B: The tens digit must be $5$ to match the thousands digit $5$.
options.C: The units digit must be $3$ because $3$ is the hundreds digit printed in the middle.
options.D: Matching the units digit to $8$ is what creates the ten-thousands digit $8$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Asha starts Kaprekar's $4$-digit routine with $6174$ (not all digits equal). She forms the largest and smallest arrangements of its digits and subtracts.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Form $7641 - 1467 = 6174$, then keep rearranging and subtracting as if the constant had not been reached.
options.B: Say that reaching $6174$ is what creates the digit arrangements of the starting number.
options.C: Form $7641 - 1467 = 6174$; the result is again $6174$, so the routine has reached Kaprekar's constant.
options.D: Repeat only the chapter word constant, without forming largest and smallest arrangements from the digits of $6174$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ira starts Kaprekar's routine with the 4-digit number $3524$, which has at least two different digits. She forms the largest and smallest numbers from those digits, subtracts, and repeats.

Which two claims correctly describe the routine?

options.A: Any single rearrangement of $3524$ is already the finished Kaprekar result.
options.B: From $3524$ she computes $5432 - 2345 = 3087$, then continues the same largest-minus-smallest step on $3087$.
options.C: When a step reaches $6174$, the next largest-minus-smallest step stays at $6174$.
options.D: The routine also settles every 3-digit starter by the same $6174$ stop.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yamini searches a list of 12-hour clock times for a digit pattern: the four digits read the same forward and backward (a palindrome), and the time must be valid.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Accept $15$:$51$ as a palindrome time even though $15$ is not a valid hour on a 12-hour clock.
options.B: Say that calling a time a palindrome is what creates the written digits $1$, $2$, $2$, $1$, instead of reading those digits in order.
options.C: Keep $12$:$21$ — the digits $1,2,2,1$ read the same both ways, and $12$:$21$ is a valid 12-hour clock time.
options.D: Also require every calendar date in the same list to be a perfect square, beyond testing digit patterns in the clock times.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Imran searches 12-hour clock times for a digit pattern: the four digits read the same forward and backward, and the time must be valid on a 12-hour clock.

Which two claims correctly identify a time that fits?

options.A: Accept $15$:$51$ as a palindrome time even though $15$ is not a valid hour on a 12-hour clock.
options.B: $12$:$21$ has digits $1$, $2$, $2$, $1$ reading the same both ways.
options.C: $12$:$21$ is a valid 12-hour clock time.
options.D: Also require every calendar date in the same list to be a perfect square.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Mona compares the calendar for year $Y$ with the calendar for year $Z$. She wants to know when year $Y$'s calendar can be reused for year $Z$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Reuse year $Y$'s calendar for year $Z$ after checking that only one special date (such as $1$ January) falls on the same weekday, without checking every date in the year.
options.B: Also treat a match of weekdays alone as settling whether two different month-name lists are the same calendar, beyond comparing dates and weekdays for years $Y$ and $Z$.
options.C: Reuse year $Y$'s calendar for year $Z$ only when every date in year $Z$ falls on the same weekday as that date in year $Y$.
options.D: Say the calendars match only because the printed year numbers $Y$ and $Z$ look alike, without comparing dates and weekdays.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Diya compares the calendar for year Y with the calendar for year Z. She wants to reuse year Y's calendar in year Z.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: Matching only one date's weekday is enough to reuse the whole calendar.
options.B: Year Y's calendar can be reused when every date falls on the same weekday in year Z.
options.C: Year Y's calendar can be reused when all dates and days match exactly across the year.
options.D: The calendar can be reused because year Z is written with larger digits than year Y.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Jatin's addition-only number-box activity allows the middle numbers $2$, $5$, and $5$ to be used as many times as needed. The side target is $12$.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Use subtraction such as $5-2$ as well, skipping that this activity allows addition only.
options.B: Say that writing $12$ is what creates the middle numbers $2$ and $5$, instead of combining those middles to make $12$.
options.C: Add middle numbers as needed, for example $2+5+5=12$, using only addition.
options.D: Use the same reuse-and-add plan for a target that must be built by multiplication of the box numbers, beyond addition.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Tara's addition-only number-box activity allows the middle numbers $3$, $4$, and $7$ to be used as many times as needed. The side target is $14$.

parts.text: Which plan correctly builds the target $14$?

options.text: Add $3$ and $4$ only, then stop at $7$.
Add $7$ and $7$, using the allowed middle number $7$ twice.
Treat the target $14$ as already giving the middle numbers, so no adding is needed.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Naveen adds two 3-digit numbers.

Which claim about the number of digits in the sum is correct?

options.A: The sum is always a 4-digit number.
options.B: The sum is never a 3-digit number.
options.C: The sum is sometimes a 4-digit number.
options.D: The sum is always a 3-digit number.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sameer adds two 3-digit numbers.

Which two claims about the number of digits in the sum are correct?

options.A: The sum is always a 4-digit number.
options.B: The sum is sometimes a 4-digit number.
options.C: The sum is sometimes a 3-digit number.
options.D: The sum is a 3-digit number because each addend shows the digit count 3.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Pooja's board shows this pattern of scores:

3  3  3  3
5  5  5  5
5  5  5  5

Which claim finds the total most quickly and correctly?

options.A: Add the distinct values 3 and 5 to get 8.
options.B: Finding the total is what produces the rows of 3s and 5s.
options.C: $4 \times 3 + 8 \times 5 = 52$.
options.D: Use the same grouping to find a total for an empty board with no scores shown.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Krish's number pattern on a board.

Which claim finds the total most quickly by grouping?

options.A: Four $2$s and six $5$s give $4\times2+6\times5=38$.
options.B: Add only the four $2$s and ignore the $5$s.
options.C: The total $38$ is what creates the displayed pattern of $2$s and $5$s.
options.D: Say the pattern name "board" as the total.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kabir starts at 6 and applies the Collatz rule: if the current number is even, take half of it; if it is odd, multiply by 3 and add 1. He writes 6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: After 5 the next term is 15, using only the multiply-by-3 step.
options.B: Reaching 1 from 6 proves that every whole-number start reaches 1.
options.C: The chain is one Collatz example that reaches 1; it does not prove the rule for every start.
options.D: The Collatz rule applies only to even starts, so the odd terms 3 and 5 are mistakes.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Aarav starts at $7$ and applies the Collatz rule: if the current term is even, halve it; if it is odd, take $3n+1$. He writes $7$, $22$, $11$, $34$, $17$, $52$, $26$, $13$, $40$, $20$, $10$, $5$, $16$, $8$, $4$, $2$, $1$.

parts.text: Which claim correctly separates this chain from the Collatz conjecture?

options.text: The chain is one Collatz example that reaches $1$; it does not prove the rule for every whole-number start.
Reaching $1$ from $7$ proves that every whole-number start reaches $1$.
The Collatz rule applies only to even starts, so the odd terms such as $7$ and $11$ are mistakes.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Rohan needs a sense of how many seats are in the school hall so he can order refreshments. There are about 20 rows with about 15 seats in each row. An exact seat count is not needed.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: An estimate near 300 seats is enough for this purpose.
options.B: Estimation means treating $20 \times 15$ as an exact census of every seat.
options.C: Exact counting is what produces estimates, so he must finish a full seat tally first.
options.D: Refreshment planning requires the perimeter of the hall, not a seat count.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Rohan packs about $25$ boxes with about $12$ notebooks in each box for a school sale. An exact notebook count is not needed to order labels.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: Estimation means treating $25\times12$ as a finished notebook-by-notebook census of every notebook.
options.B: An estimate near $300$ notebooks is enough for ordering labels.
options.C: A reasonable estimate suits this purpose because an exact count is unnecessary here.
options.D: Exact counting is what produces estimates, so he must finish a full tally first.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Neel and Asha take turns adding 1, 2, or 3 to a running total that starts at 0. The player who makes the total exactly 21 wins.

Which claim about the winning totals is correct?

options.A: The winning totals are every total from 18 to 21.
options.B: The only winning total is 21; earlier totals do not form a pattern.
options.C: The winning totals are 1, 5, 9, 13, 17, and 21.
options.D: The winning totals are the multiples of 3 up to 21.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Farhan and Tara take turns adding $1$, $2$, or $3$ to a running total that starts at $0$. The player who makes the total exactly $21$ wins.

Which two claims correctly describe the winning pattern?

options.A: Any running total can be a winning move, because the printed target is $21$.
options.B: If Farhan makes the total $17$, then whatever Tara adds ($1$, $2$, or $3$), Farhan can reach $21$ on the next turn.
options.C: Safe totals to leave for the other player are $4$, $8$, $12$, and $16$.
options.D: Count how many times the digit $2$ is written from $1$ to $21$, and treat that count as the winning pattern.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Uma wants to answer this question: which fruit do the students in Class 6A like most for the mid-day snack?

Which plan correctly sets up the inquiry?

options.A: Treat the words Class 6A as the answer, and collect no fruit choices.

options.A: Call the vertical axis the whole bar graph, without placing the three game categories or their bars.

options.C: Put the game categories on one axis, choose one uniform number scale on the other, and draw equal-width bars whose heights match $8$, $6$, and $4$ on that scale.

options.C: Categories sit on one axis, one uniform number scale sits on the other, and equal-width bars reach heights $6$, $4$, and $2$ on that scale.

Which statement is correct?

options.B: 2 is such a number, because 2 divides both 4 and 6.
options.C: 12 is such a number, because 12 is a multiple of 4 and of 6.
options.D: Any multiple of 4 alone is enough, even if it is not a multiple of 6.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:

Which two claims correctly decide that question?

options.A: $24$ is a multiple of $4$ alone, and that is enough to call it a common multiple.
options.B: $24$ is a multiple of both $4$ and $6$, so $24$ is a common multiple of the pair.
options.C: Because $24 \div 4 = 6$ and $24 \div 6 = 4$ with no remainders, both conditions hold.
options.D: Any multiple of $4$ from a single-number list is automatically a common multiple of $4$ and $6$.

options.D: Any multiple of 4 from a single-number list is automatically a common multiple of 4 and 9.

stem:
Jatin lists the factors of three whole numbers: $1$ has only $\{1\}$; $7$ has $\{1,7\}$; $12$ has $\{1,2,3,4,6,12\}$.

How should he classify $1$, $7$, and $12$?

options.A: Call $1$ a composite number, using the label composite instead of reading its factor count.
options.B: Say the prime/composite labels are what produce the factor lists, instead of reading the lists to decide the labels.
options.C: $1$ is neither (one factor); $7$ is prime (exactly two factors); $12$ is composite (more than two factors).
options.D: Treat the question as a jump-size treasure hunt on a number line, and classify from landing spots instead of factor counts.

stem: Aryan lists the factors of three whole numbers: $1$ has only $\{1\}$; $11$ has $\{1,11\}$; $15$ has $\{1,3,5,15\}$.

parts.text: How should he classify $1$, $11$, and $15$?

options.text: Call $1$ a composite number from the label composite alone.
$1$ is neither (one factor); $11$ is prime (exactly two factors); $15$ is composite (more than two factors).

stem:

stem:
Gauri runs the Sieve of Eratosthenes on the whole numbers from $1$ to $20$.

Which statement is correct when the sieve is finished?

options.A: Call every uncrossed number the sieve method itself, without separating primes from composites.
options.B: Say the final circled primes are what produce the earlier crossing out of multiples.
options.C: $1$ is crossed out; each next uncrossed number is circled as prime and its later multiples are crossed out; circled numbers are primes and other crossed-out numbers are composites.
options.D: Find common factors of pairs such as $12$ and $18$, and treat that factor check as the sieve.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Diya runs the Sieve of Eratosthenes on the whole numbers from $1$ to $15$.

parts.text: Which claim is correct after the sieve is finished?

options.text: $9$ stays unmarked as prime, because it is odd.

options.A: $23$ stays circled as prime, while $1$ is crossed out and $25$ is crossed out as composite.
options.B: $1$ is circled as a prime because it is the first uncrossed label on the list.
options.C: Circling the primes is what produces the earlier crossing out of their multiples.
options.D: $25$ is found by dividing values in the sieve instead of crossing out multiples of $5$.

subject: maths
stem:

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call them a safe pair as a name only, without checking common factors of $8$ and $9$.
options.B: Say the co-prime decision is what creates the absence of a common factor greater than $1$, instead of checking factors first.
options.C: They are co-prime, because their only common factor is $1$.
options.D: Decide from the final digit alone, as in a divisibility-by-$2$ or $5$ check, without listing common factors of $8$ and $9$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nitya checks whether $14$ and $15$ form a co-prime pair before calling them a safe treasure pair.

options.A: They are co-prime because both numbers are even.
options.B: They fail the co-prime test because $14$ is larger than $15$.
options.C: They are co-prime because their only common factor is $1$.
options.D: They are co-prime because the printed digit $1$ appears in $15$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sonia checks whether $15$ and $28$ are co-prime by looking at their common factors before calling them a safe treasure pair.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Safe treasure pair is another name for the larger number $28$.
options.B: Calling them a safe treasure pair is what creates the absence of a common factor greater than $1$.
options.C: $15$ and $28$ are co-prime, because their only common factor is $1$.
options.D: $15$ and $28$ are co-prime, because $28$ ends with the digit $8$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bharat ties thread on a circular board with $12$ pegs, stepping a fixed gap of $5$ pegs each time. He asks whether the thread will eventually reach every peg.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Answer "thread-gap", naming that phrase instead of checking whether $12$ and $5$ share a common factor.
options.B: Say that reaching every peg is what creates the co-primality of $12$ and $5$, instead of using co-primality to predict the reach.
options.C: Yes: $12$ and $5$ are co-prime, so stepping by $5$ visits every peg before repeating.
options.D: Treat the question as a treasure-pair hunt that only asks whether two numbers are co-prime, without linking that fact to the cyclic peg walk.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Ira ties thread on a circular board with $8$ pegs, stepping a fixed gap of $3$ pegs each time. She asks whether the thread will eventually reach every peg.

parts.text: Which claim is correct?

options.text: Answer with the phrase thread-gap alone, instead of checking $8$ and $3$.
Yes: $8$ and $3$ share no common factor greater than $1$, so stepping by $3$ visits every peg before repeating.
Say that reaching every peg is what creates the co-primality of $8$ and $3$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sonia ties thread on a circular board with $10$ pegs, stepping a fixed gap of $4$ pegs each time. She asks whether the thread will eventually reach every peg.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Answer with the phrase thread-gap alone, instead of checking whether $10$ and $4$ share a common factor.
options.B: Say that reaching every peg is what creates the co-primality of $10$ and $4$.
options.C: No: $10$ and $4$ share common factor $2$, so stepping by $4$ repeats a smaller cycle and misses some pegs.
options.D: Treat the question as only asking whether $10$ and $4$ are co-prime, without linking that fact to the cyclic peg walk.

subject: maths
stem:
Padma writes $56=14\times 4$ and $63=21\times 3$. She asks whether that single pair of factorisations proves $56$ and $63$ have no common factor greater than $1$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Conclude they are co-prime from those two products alone, without checking whether another common factor was missed.
options.B: Say that calling them co-prime is what creates the incomplete factor listing, instead of testing all possible common factors.
options.C: No: one chosen factorisation of each number can miss a common factor; the search must account for every possible common factor.
options.D: Require a full prime-factorisation write-up of every integer as the only allowed method for this decision.
