subject: maths
stem:
Aarav writes $48 = 12 \times 4$ and $90 = 15 \times 6$. He asks whether that single pair of factorisations proves that $48$ and $90$ have no common factor other than $1$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Yes, because those written factor pairs show no matching factor on the page.
options.B: No, because another factorisation can still reveal a common factor such as $6$.
options.C: An incomplete factor listing is what creates the claim that the numbers share a factor.
options.D: The same single-pair check also settles every later prime-factorisation question about these numbers.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ekta writes $60 = 6 \times 10$ and wants the prime factorisation of $60$ by breaking composite factors until only primes remain.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Call the finished answer "prime factor" only, without writing the full product of primes for $60$.
options.B: Say that writing $2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 5$ is what creates the breaking of $6$ and $10$, instead of breaking those composites first.
options.C: Replace $6$ by $2 \times 3$ and $10$ by $2 \times 5$, so $60 = 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 5$ with only primes left.
options.D: Fill a different prime product-grid puzzle for every row and column, and treat that puzzle as this factor-breaking of $60$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Adil wants the prime factorisation of $84$. He keeps replacing composite factors until only primes remain.

parts.text: Which claim correctly gives that prime factorisation?

options.text: $84 = 2^{2} \times 3 \times 7$

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Chitra writes $60 = 2\times 2\times 3\times 5$ and also $60 = 2^{2}\times 3\times 5$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the answer order of factors, without deciding whether the two prime factorisations are the same.
options.B: Say that having the same product $60$ is what creates the matching primes with the same repetitions.
options.C: $2\times 2\times 3\times 5$ and $2^{2}\times 3\times 5$ are the same prime factorisation; order and grouping do not change it.
options.D: Decide they differ only because one printed form uses an exponent and the other writes two $2$s.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Krish writes $84 = 2\times 2\times 3\times 7$ and also $84 = 2^{2}\times 3\times 7$.

parts.text: Which claim correctly compares those two prime factorisations?

options.text: Call the answer order of factors and stop there.
Having the same product $84$ is what creates the matching primes with the same repetitions.
$2\times 2\times 3\times 7$ and $2^{2}\times 3\times 7$ are the same prime factorisation; order and grouping do not change it.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qadir first writes $60 = 6 \times 10$, then $6 = 2 \times 3$ and $10 = 2 \times 5$.

Which claim builds the prime factorisation of $60$ correctly?

options.A: Call the answer prime factorisation only, without combining the prime factors of $6$ and $10$.
options.B: Write $60 = 6 \times 10$ and stop, without replacing $6$ and $10$ by their prime factorisations.
options.C: Combine the factorisations: $60 = (2 \times 3) \times (2 \times 5) = 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 5$.
options.D: Also treat $60 = 6 + 10$ by combining prime factorisations of $6$ and $10$ the same way, beyond a product of factors.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Kabir first writes $84 = 12 \times 7$, then $12 = 2 \times 2 \times 3$ and $7 = 7$.

parts.text: Which claim builds the prime factorisation of $84$ correctly?

options.text: The prime factorisation of $84$ is $12 \times 7$.
The prime factorisation of $84$ is $2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 7$.
The prime factorisation of $84$ is $2 \times 2 \times 3$ from $12$ alone.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nitin has $14=2\times7$ and $15=3\times5$. He wants to decide whether $14$ and $15$ are co-prime from those prime factorisations.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call them co-prime after looking at the products $14$ and $15$ alone, without checking whether any prime appears in both factorisations.
options.B: Also use the same co-prime test to decide whether two fractions are in lowest terms without comparing prime factors, beyond this two-number prime-factor check.
options.C: They are co-prime: the primes $2,7$ and $3,5$ share no common prime factor.
options.D: Call them co-prime only because $14$ and $15$ are consecutive printed integers, without using the prime factorisations.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ishaan has $21=3\times 7$ and $22=2\times 11$. He wants to decide whether $21$ and $22$ are co-prime from those prime factorisations.

Which two claims correctly settle that decision?

options.A: The factorisations share no common prime factor, so $21$ and $22$ are co-prime.
options.B: Co-prime status also covers every pair that merely ends with different digits.
options.C: Because the listed primes $3$, $7$, $2$, and $11$ are all distinct across the two factorisations, the numbers are co-prime.
options.D: Call them co-prime only because $22$ is the larger printed number.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Soham writes the prime factorisations $180=2\times2\times3\times3\times5$ and $12=2\times2\times3$.

Which claim about divisibility is correct?

options.A: $180$ is divisible by $12$ because both factorisations include the prime $2$.
options.B: $180$ is not divisible by $12$ because $180$ has prime factors that $12$ does not have.
options.C: $180$ is divisible by $12$ because $2\times2\times3$ from $12$ is included in the factorisation of $180$.
options.D: Whether $180$ and $12$ are co-prime settles whether $180$ is divisible by $12$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Ritu writes the prime factorisations $168=2\times2\times2\times3\times7$ and $12=2\times2\times3$.

parts.text: Which claim about divisibility is correct?

options.text: $168$ is divisible by $12$ because both factorisations include the prime $2$.
$168$ is divisible by $12$ because $2\times2\times3$ from $12$ is included in the factorisation of $168$.
$168$ is not divisible by $12$ because $168$ has prime factors that $12$ does not have.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Rina looks at the number $340$ and checks divisibility using only its final digit.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: $340$ is even, so it is divisible by $10$.
options.B: $340$ is divisible by $10$ because it ends in $0$.
options.C: $340$ is divisible by $5$ because it ends in $0$.
options.D: $340$ is divisible by $4$ by the same final-digit rules used for $2$, $5$ and $10$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Imran looks at the number $250$ and checks divisibility using only its final digit.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: Divisibility by $10$ is the only rule that applies, so skip checks for $5$ and $2$.
options.B: $250$ is divisible by $10$, by $5$, and by $2$, because it ends in $0$.
options.C: A number ending in $0$ meets the final-digit tests for $10$, for $5$, and for $2$.
options.D: Use the divisibility rules for $4$ and $8$ on the last digit alone for this check.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Dev checks whether $3816$ is divisible by $4$ by testing one digit block of $3816$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Test whether $38$, formed by the first two digits, is divisible by $4$.
options.B: Test whether $4$ is divisible by $16$, the number formed by the last two digits.
options.C: Test whether $16$, formed by the last two digits, is divisible by $4$.
options.D: Test whether $816$, formed by the last three digits, is divisible by $4$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Diya checks whether $3\,572$ is divisible by $4$. She knows the test uses the number formed by the last two digits.

Which two claims correctly apply that test?

options.A: Call the answer "divisibility by $4$" as a label only, and stop.
options.B: Form the two-digit number $72$ from the last two digits of $3\,572$.
options.C: Decide yes or no by checking whether $72$ itself is divisible by $4$.
options.D: Decide only from the leading digit $3$, because $3$ is the largest printed digit.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Naina checks whether $59216$ is divisible by $8$ by testing one digit block of $59216$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Test whether $59$, formed by the first two digits, is divisible by $8$.
options.B: Test whether $16$, formed by the last two digits, is divisible by $8$.
options.C: Test whether $216$, formed by the last three digits, is divisible by $8$.
options.D: Test whether the digit sum $5+9+2+1+6$ is divisible by $8$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Sia checks whether $73824$ is divisible by $8$ by testing one digit block of $73824$.

parts.text: Which claim correctly names the block to test?

options.text: Test whether $73$, formed by the first two digits, is divisible by $8$.
Test whether $824$, formed by the last three digits, is divisible by $8$.
Test whether the digit sum $7+3+8+2+4$ is divisible by $8$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Vimal's prime product grid. Each blank must be a prime. Each row multiplies to the number on its right. Each column multiplies to the number below it.

Which pair fills the two blanks?

options.A: The blanks are $2$ and $7$.
options.B: The blanks are $6$ and $35$.
options.C: The blanks are $4$ and $7$.
options.D: The blanks are $3$ and $5$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Raghav fills a 2-by-2 prime product grid. Top-right is 2 and bottom-left is 3. Top-left and bottom-right are blanks. The top row multiplies to 10. The bottom row multiplies to 21. The left column multiplies to 15. The right column multiplies to 14. Each blank must be a prime.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: The blanks may be 4 and 7.
options.B: The blanks are 5 and 7.
options.C: Each blank must be a prime so every row and column product matches its margin.
options.D: The blanks are 10 and 21, the row margin numbers.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Mona's rectangular garden is 8 m long and 5 m wide. She wants the distance around the garden once, along the boundary.

What is that distance?
author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Mini's rectangular garden as a closed figure. Side lengths are marked in metres.

What is the perimeter of the garden?
author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Raghav's rectangular courtyard as a closed figure. Side lengths are marked in metres.

What is the perimeter of the courtyard?
author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Farhan's rectangular playground has perimeter 30 m. One side is 9 m long.

What is the length of the adjacent side?

options.C: 6 m

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Sia's rectangular garden. Opposite sides are equal. The marked length is $8\,\mathrm{m}$ and the marked breadth is $3\,\mathrm{m}$.

Which claim correctly gives the perimeter of the garden?

options.A: Perimeter $= 2 \times (8 + 3) = 22\,\mathrm{m}$.
options.B: Perimeter $= 8 \times 3 = 24\,\mathrm{m}$.
options.C: Perimeter $= 8 + 3 = 11\,\mathrm{m}$.
options.D: The perimeter number is what creates the $8\,\mathrm{m}$ length and $3\,\mathrm{m}$ breadth.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Bhavna's rectangular classroom floor. Opposite sides are equal. The marked length is $9\,\mathrm{m}$ and the marked breadth is $4\,\mathrm{m}$.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims correctly give the perimeter of the floor?

options.A: Perimeter $= 2 \times (9 + 4) = 26\,\mathrm{m}$.
options.B: Perimeter $= 9 \times 4 = 36\,\mathrm{m}$.
options.C: Perimeter $= 9 + 4 + 9 + 4 = 26\,\mathrm{m}$.
options.D: Perimeter $= 9 + 4 = 13\,\mathrm{m}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Wasim's triangular flower bed has side lengths 5 m, 7 m, and 9 m.

What is its perimeter?

options.A: 7 m, taking the middle side length as the perimeter.
options.B: Each side equals 21 m, because the perimeter produces each side.
options.C: 21 m, by adding the three side lengths.
options.D: 3 m, because a triangle is named by having three sides.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Anvi's triangular plot. The side lengths are $6\,\mathrm{m}$, $8\,\mathrm{m}$, and $10\,\mathrm{m}$.

Which claim correctly gives the perimeter of the plot?

options.A: Perimeter $= 6 + 8 + 10 = 24\,\mathrm{m}$.
options.B: Perimeter $= 10\,\mathrm{m}$, taking the longest side length as the perimeter.
options.C: Each side equals $24\,\mathrm{m}$, because the perimeter produces each side.
options.D: Perimeter $= 3\,\mathrm{m}$, because a triangle is named by having three sides.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Tanvi's triangular garden plot. The side lengths are $4\,\mathrm{m}$, $9\,\mathrm{m}$, and $11\,\mathrm{m}$.

Which claim correctly gives the perimeter of the plot?

options.A: Perimeter $= 4 + 9 + 11 = 24\,\mathrm{m}$.
options.B: Perimeter $= 11\,\mathrm{m}$, taking the longest side length as the perimeter.
options.C: Each side equals $24\,\mathrm{m}$, because the perimeter produces each side.
options.D: Perimeter $= 3\,\mathrm{m}$, because a triangle is named by having three sides.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nitin's square courtyard has each side $6$ m long.

Which calculation gives its perimeter?

options.A: Call the shape an equilateral triangle, and use $3 \times 6$.
options.B: Use $4 \times 6$ even if two sides were a different length.
options.C: $4 \times 6 = 24$ m, because all four sides are equal.
options.D: $6$ m, taking the printed side length on the plan as the perimeter.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Aarna's square courtyard. Each side is marked $5\,\mathrm{m}$.

Which calculation gives its perimeter?

options.A: $4 \times 5 = 20\,\mathrm{m}$, because all four sides are equal.
options.B: Call the shape an equilateral triangle, and use $3 \times 5$.
options.C: Use $4 \times 5$ even if two sides were a different length.
options.D: $5\,\mathrm{m}$, taking the printed side length on the plan as the perimeter.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bhavna's equilateral triangular garden has each side $8\,\mathrm{m}$ long.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims correctly give the perimeter of the garden?

options.A: Perimeter $= 3 \times 8 = 24\,\mathrm{m}$, because all three sides are equal.
options.B: Perimeter $= 4 \times 8 = 32\,\mathrm{m}$, treating the garden as a square.
options.C: Perimeter $= 8 + 8 + 8 = 24\,\mathrm{m}$.
options.D: Perimeter $= 8\,\mathrm{m}$, taking the printed side length as the perimeter.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Farhan runs on a rectangular track whose perimeter is $400$ m. He runs $950$ m from a start mark.

Which claim about full rounds and leftover distance is correct?

options.A: Call "one round" the leftover distance, without using the perimeter.
options.B: Convert using $400$ m even if the actual track perimeter were a different length.
options.C: Full rounds $= 2$ and leftover $= 150$ m along the track, because $950 = 2 \times 400 + 150$.
options.D: Report $950$ alone, because that numeral is printed largest.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Dev runs on a square track whose perimeter is $200$ m. He runs $650$ m from a start mark that is also the finish line.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: Call "one round" the leftover distance alone.
options.B: Full rounds $= 3$ because $650 = 3 \times 200 + 50$.
options.C: The leftover distance is $50$ m along the track from the finish line.
options.D: Report $650$ alone, because that numeral is printed largest.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bhavna runs on a square track whose perimeter is $300$ m. She runs $1000$ m from a start mark that is also the finish line.

Which claim about full rounds and leftover distance is correct?

options.A: She completes $3$ full rounds with $100$ m left over.
options.B: She completes $1000$ full rounds, reading the run distance as the round count.
options.C: Full rounds can be counted without using the $300$ m perimeter of the track.
options.D: She completes $300$ full rounds, matching the perimeter number alone.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Soham traces a path on square-grid paper. One segment runs $3$ straight grid units along the lines; the next segment cuts diagonally across one square.

Which claim about the path length is correct?

options.A: Call the answer grid path only, without separating straight and diagonal lengths.
options.B: Count the diagonal cut as $1$ grid unit, the same as a straight side, with no separate estimate.
options.C: Measure the straight parts in grid units and treat the diagonal as longer than one straight grid unit, then add the lengths.
options.D: Say that calling the diagonal longer is what creates the grid path itself.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nitya looks at the diagram of polygon $PQRS$ on square-grid paper. Sides $PQ$ and $QR$ run along the grid lines. Side $PS$ cuts diagonally across grid squares.

Which claim about the boundary length is correct?

options.A: Call the answer grid path only, with one shared length label for every side.
options.B: Count the diagonal side $PS$ as $1$ grid unit, the same as a straight grid side.
options.C: Measure the straight sides in grid units and treat diagonal side $PS$ as longer than one straight grid unit, then add those lengths.
options.D: Say that calling the diagonal longer is what creates polygon $PQRS$ on the grid.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bhavna traces a path on square-grid paper. One segment runs $4$ straight grid units along the lines; the next segment cuts diagonally across one square.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims about the path length are correct?

options.A: The straight segment measures $4$ straight grid units along the lines.
options.B: The diagonal segment has the same unit length as one straight grid step.
options.C: The diagonal segment must be measured or estimated as its own length, not counted as one straight grid unit.
options.D: The path length is the printed label "square-grid paper".

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ekta has two $3$ cm by $2$ cm rectangles. She joins them along a shared $2$ cm edge and asks how the perimeter changes.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the answer "joined arrangement" only, without measuring the new outside boundary.
options.B: Add the two separate perimeters in full, counting the touching $2$ cm edges as if they were still outside.
options.C: After the join, the touching $2$ cm edges are inside, so the new perimeter is $16$ cm (a $6$ cm by $2$ cm rectangle), not $20$ cm.
options.D: Say that the new $16$ cm perimeter is what creates the joining along the $2$ cm edge, instead of joining first and then reading the outside boundary.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Veer has one $5$ cm by $3$ cm rectangle. He cuts it into two pieces along a mid-line parallel to the $3$ cm side and then rejoins the pieces along a different edge.

parts.text: Which claim about perimeter is correct?

options.text: The perimeter must stay $16$ cm, because the same pieces are used.
The new outline can have a different perimeter even though the pieces are the same.
The perimeter always becomes half of $16$ cm after any cut.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice that compares the outer edges before and after rejoining.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tushar has two $5$ cm by $1$ cm rectangles. He joins them along a shared $1$ cm edge and asks how the perimeter changes.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The joined perimeter is the area $10$ square centimetres of the joined strip.
options.B: The joined perimeter is $12+12=24$ cm, the sum of the separate perimeters.
options.C: The joined perimeter is $22$ cm, because the two touching $1$ cm edges are inside and not on the outside boundary.
options.D: The new outside boundary is what creates the two separate $5$ cm by $1$ cm rectangles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Uma must cover a $5$ cm by $4$ cm rectangular floor tile with paint. The problem asks how much surface the paint covers.

Which plan matches the request?

options.A: Multiply $5 \times 4$ but report the answer in centimetres, skipping that covered surface needs square units.
options.B: Say that writing $20\ \mathrm{cm}^{2}$ is what creates the $5$ cm by $4$ cm rectangle, instead of computing area from those sides.
options.C: Compute area as $5 \times 4 = 20\ \mathrm{cm}^{2}$, because covered surface is the enclosed region in square units.
options.D: Use the same length$\times$width product to find how far a bug walks around the tile's boundary, beyond this covered-surface request.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Aarav must cover a rectangular desk top that is $6$ units long and $4$ units wide with square tiles of side $1$ unit. He also has a square tray of side $5$ units.

Which two claims correctly use area in square units?

options.A: The desk needs $6+4=10$ square tiles, counting length and width as the covered region.
options.B: The desk area is $6\times4=24$ square units.
options.C: The square tray area is $5\times5=25$ square units.
options.D: Area is the distance around the desk edge, so the tray and desk share one perimeter rule for covering.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tushar must cover a rectangular garden bed that is $7$ m long and $3$ m wide with grass. The problem asks how much ground the grass covers.

Which plan matches the request?

options.A: Add $7+3$ and report $10$ m for the ground covered.
options.B: Saying the grass covers the bed is what creates the product $7\times3$.
options.C: Compute area as $7\times3=21$ square metres.
options.D: Use the same area rule to find only the length of one diagonal of the bed.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ritu's rectangular courtyard is $12$ m by $8$ m. A rectangular carpet $5$ m by $3$ m is placed on it.

Which plan finds the uncovered area correctly?

options.A: Find only the courtyard area $12\times8$, without subtracting the carpet area.
options.B: Say that the uncovered area is what creates the courtyard and carpet rectangles, instead of subtracting carpet area from courtyard area.
options.C: Uncovered area $=12\times8-5\times3=96-15=81$ square metres.
options.D: Also subtract the carpet area from the courtyard perimeter, as if the same remaining-area step settled a length around the edge.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Adil's rectangular courtyard is $10$ m by $6$ m. A rectangular flower bed $4$ m by $2$ m lies inside it.

Which two claims find the uncovered area correctly?

options.A: Find only the courtyard area $10\times 6$, and stop there.
options.B: Uncovered area $=10\times 6-4\times 2=60-8=52$ square metres.
options.C: Subtract the flower-bed area from the courtyard area because the bed lies inside and is not part of the uncovered region.
options.D: Say that the uncovered area is what creates the courtyard and flower-bed rectangles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nalini draws the irregular closed shape shown in the diagram on 1 cm² squared paper.

How should she estimate its area in square centimetres?

options.A: Count every whole square fully inside the shape and estimate each partly covered square as a fraction of one square centimetre.
options.B: Answer with the words squared paper; that label is the estimate.
options.C: The squared paper produces the shape, so the area equals the area of the whole grid.
options.D: Measure the perimeter of the shape in centimetres and take that number as the area.
