author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sia looks at the diagram of an irregular closed shape drawn on $1\,\mathrm{cm}^{2}$ squared paper.

Which claim correctly estimates the area of the shape?

options.A: Read the printed label "squared paper" beside the grid as the area value.
options.B: Count square units covered by the shape, including reasonable fractions of partly covered squares.
options.C: The squared paper is what draws the closed shape, so the grid lines alone are the area.
options.D: Add only the length and breadth of a surrounding rectangle and report that sum as the area.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Padma cuts a paper rectangle into two triangles and rearranges those same pieces into a parallelogram with no gaps and no overlaps.

Which claims are correct? One or more options may be correct.

options.A: Same area is only a label for the activity, not a conclusion about the pieces.
options.B: The rearranged parallelogram has the same total area as the original rectangle.
options.C: Matching the two triangles on top of each other shows that the two pieces have equal areas.
options.D: The question asks for perimeter, so add the outer lengths of the parallelogram.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Meher looks at the diagram. Pieces $A$ and $B$ cover a region in Arrangement 1. The same pieces $A$ and $B$ are moved to Arrangement 2 with no overlaps and no gaps left between them.

Which claim correctly compares the total areas?

options.A: The total area of $A$ and $B$ in Arrangement 2 equals the total area in Arrangement 1.
options.B: Call the answer the label Arrangement 2 alone.
options.C: Say that equal total area is what creates the two arrangements on the grid.
options.D: Find the area of Arrangement 1 by treating only the outer rectangle perimeter as the area measure.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Omkar draws rectangle $ABCD$ with diagonal $AC$, as in the diagram.

Which claim about the areas is correct?

options.A: Triangle $ABC$ has half the area of rectangle $ABCD$.
options.B: The area of triangle $ABC$ equals the length of diagonal $AC$.
options.C: Rectangle $ABCD$ has half the area of triangle $ABC$.
options.D: Triangle $ABC$ and rectangle $ABCD$ have the same area.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anvi draws rectangle $ABCD$ with diagonal $AC$, as in the diagram. Triangle $ABC$ uses three corners of the rectangle.

Which claim about the areas is correct?

options.A: Triangle $ABC$ has half the area of rectangle $ABCD$.
options.B: The area of triangle $ABC$ equals the length of diagonal $AC$.
options.C: Rectangle $ABCD$ has half the area of triangle $ABC$.
options.D: Triangle $ABC$ and rectangle $ABCD$ have the same area.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Diya's garden plot is the irregular figure in the diagram: a rectangle $8\ \mathrm{cm}$ by $4\ \mathrm{cm}$ with a triangle of height $3\ \mathrm{cm}$ on the top side.

Which plan finds the area correctly?

options.A: Add the rectangle area $8\times 4$ to the triangle area $\tfrac{1}{2}\times 8\times 3$ to get $32+12=44$.
options.B: Use only the rectangle area $8\times 4=32$ and ignore the triangle.
options.C: The triangle area is what produces the rectangle, so report $12$ alone.
options.D: Multiply $8\times 4\times 3=96$ as if one product covers the whole figure.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The figure shows Nitya's garden plot: rectangle ABCD is $6\ \mathrm{cm}$ by $4\ \mathrm{cm}$, and right triangle AEB has base $6\ \mathrm{cm}$ and height $3\ \mathrm{cm}$ on top of the rectangle.

How should she find the area of the figure?

options.A: Add the rectangle area $6 \times 4$ and the triangle area $\frac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 3$.
options.B: Use only the rectangle area $6 \times 4$, because the triangle sits on the rectangle.
options.C: The triangle area produces the rectangle area, so multiply those two part areas.
options.D: Any closed garden plot has area $6 \times 4$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Irfan builds two shapes from the same 6 unit squares, side-aligned with no gaps. Shape P is a 2-by-3 rectangle. Shape Q is an L-shape made by moving one square.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Both shapes have area 6 square units; their perimeters can differ.
options.B: Both shapes have the same perimeter because each uses 6 unit squares.
options.C: Moving the square changes the area; the perimeter stays the same.
options.D: Equal area for these 6-square shapes also forces every polygon of any size to share one perimeter.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kavya looks at the diagram of Shape $P$ and Shape $Q$. Both are built from the same $8$ unit squares, side-aligned with no gaps. Shape $P$ is a $2$-by-$4$ rectangle. Shape $Q$ is an L-shape made by moving squares.

Which claim correctly compares area and perimeter?

options.A: Area and perimeter both stay the same for every rearrangement of the $8$ squares.
options.B: Changing the arrangement creates the $8$ unit squares.
options.C: Area stays the same because both shapes use $8$ unit squares, but the perimeter can change.
options.D: Only Shape $P$ has an area, because it is a rectangle.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Pia's classroom floor plan is a large rectangle $10\,\mathrm{m}$ by $6\,\mathrm{m}$. It is split into Room L and Room R that share a straight side parallel to the $6\,\mathrm{m}$ sides. Room L has area $24\,\mathrm{m}^{2}$.

parts.text: Which claim correctly finds the width of Room L along the $10\,\mathrm{m}$ side?

options.text: Width $= 24 \div 6 = 4\,\mathrm{m}$.
Width $= 24\,\mathrm{m}$, taking the printed area as the width.
Width $= 24 \times 6 = 144\,\mathrm{m}$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Neil's classroom floor plan: a large rectangle $12\,\mathrm{m}$ by $8\,\mathrm{m}$, split into Room A and Room B that share a straight side parallel to the $8\,\mathrm{m}$ sides. Room A has area $40\,\mathrm{m}^{2}$.

Which claim correctly finds the width of Room A along the $12\,\mathrm{m}$ side?

options.A: Width $=40\,\mathrm{m}$, taking the printed area as the width.
options.B: Width $=40\,\mathrm{m}$, and that holds even when the shared side length is unknown.
options.C: Width $=40\div8=5\,\mathrm{m}$.
options.D: Width $=12\,\mathrm{m}$, because $12$ is printed on the long side of the plan.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ritu shares the same chapati equally. She compares the unit fractions 1/6 and 1/8 from that whole.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: 1/8 is greater than 1/6 because 8 is greater than 6.
options.B: 1/6 is greater than 1/8 because fewer equal shares make each share larger.
options.C: 1/6 and 1/8 are equal because each numerator is 1.
options.D: 1/8 is greater because the denominator is the size of the share.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Zubin shares one idli equally. He compares the unit fractions $1/5$ and $1/10$ from that whole.

parts.text: Which statement is correct?

options.text: $1/5$ is greater than $1/10$ because fewer equal shares make each share larger.
$1/10$ is greater than $1/5$ because 10 is greater than 5.
$1/5$ and $1/10$ are equal because each numerator is 1.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice that uses the size of a unit fraction.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Mini shares one roti equally. She compares the unit fractions $1/3$ and $1/9$ from that whole.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: $1/9$ is greater than $1/3$ because 9 is greater than 3.
options.B: $1/3$ is greater than $1/9$ because fewer equal shares make each share larger.
options.C: $1/3$ and $1/9$ are equal because each numerator is 1.
options.D: $1/9$ is greater because the denominator is the size of the share.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Mona and Nitin each start with the same whole chapati. Mona cuts hers into 4 equal pieces. Nitin cuts his into 4 pieces of different sizes. Each takes one piece and calls it one-fourth of the chapati.

Whose piece is a valid fractional unit of one-fourth?

options.A: Only Mona's piece, because the parts must be equal in size.
options.B: Both pieces, because each chapati was cut into 4 pieces.
options.C: Only Nitin's piece, because unequal shapes still make fourths.
options.D: Neither piece, because fourths must be triangles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Inaya and Boman each start with the same whole chapati. Inaya cuts hers into $4$ equal pieces. Boman cuts his into $4$ pieces of different sizes. Each takes one piece and calls it one-fourth of the chapati.

parts.text: Which claim correctly decides whose piece is a valid one-fourth?

options.text: Only Inaya's piece is one-fourth, because the whole was split into equal-size parts.
Both pieces are one-fourth, because each person took one of four pieces.
Calling a piece one-fourth is what forces the chapati cuts to be equal.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: The diagram shows Chirag's and Leela's square dosas of the same whole size. Chirag cuts his into $3$ equal pieces. Leela cuts hers into $3$ pieces of different sizes. Each takes one piece and calls it one-third of the dosa.

parts.text: Which claim correctly decides whose piece is a valid one-third?

options.text: Only Chirag's piece is one-third, because the whole was split into equal-size parts.
Both pieces are one-third, because each person took one of three pieces.
Calling a piece one-third is what forces the dosa cuts to be equal.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Javed places the fraction 3/4 on a number line marked from 0 to 1.

Which plan places 3/4 correctly?

options.A: Divide the interval from 0 to 1 into 4 equal lengths and count 3 of those lengths from 0.
options.B: Mark a point near 1 because the printed 4 looks large, without making equal lengths.
options.C: Place 3/4 by comparing only how large 3 looks next to 4 on the page.
options.D: The number-line placement rule also requires changing 3/4 into another kind of number first.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Shaan places the fraction $\dfrac{2}{5}$ on a number line marked from $0$ to $1$.

parts.text: Which claim correctly places $\dfrac{2}{5}$?

options.text: Divide the interval from $0$ to $1$ into $5$ equal lengths and count $2$ of those lengths from $0$.
Mark a point near $1$ because the printed $5$ looks large.
The number-line placement rule also requires changing $\dfrac{2}{5}$ into a decimal first.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Uday places the fraction $\dfrac{5}{6}$ on a number line marked from $0$ to $1$. The diagram shows that number line.

Which plan places $\dfrac{5}{6}$ correctly?

options.A: Divide the interval from $0$ to $1$ into $6$ equal lengths and count $5$ of those lengths from $0$.
options.B: Mark a point near $1$ because the printed $6$ looks large on the page.
options.C: The number-line placement rule also requires changing $\dfrac{5}{6}$ into another kind of number first.
options.D: Place $\dfrac{5}{6}$ by comparing only how large $5$ looks next to $6$ as a unit fraction of a different whole.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Harish has the improper fraction 17/5 and wants it as a mixed number.

Which mixed number is correct?
author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Dhruvil has the improper fraction $\dfrac{23}{6}$ and wants it as a mixed number.

parts.text: Which mixed number is correct?
Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Chirag has the improper fraction $\dfrac{29}{8}$ and wants it as a mixed number.

parts.text: Which mixed number is correct?
Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bharat has the fraction 2/3 of a chapati. He wants another fraction for the same quantity of that chapati.

Which plan gives an equivalent fraction?

options.A: Change only the numerator to 4 and keep the denominator 3.
options.B: Multiply numerator and denominator by the same nonzero number, for example write 4/6.
options.C: Write 4/6 even when the new pair is no longer about the same chapati.
options.D: First convert 2/3 into a decimal; equivalence requires that conversion.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anvi has the fraction $\dfrac{3}{4}$ of a roti. She wants another fraction for the same quantity of that roti.

Which plan gives an equivalent fraction?

options.A: Change only the numerator to $6$ and keep the denominator $4$.
options.B: Write $\dfrac{6}{8}$ even when the new pair is no longer about the same roti.
options.C: Multiply numerator and denominator by the same nonzero number, for example write $\dfrac{6}{8}$.
options.D: First convert $\dfrac{3}{4}$ into a decimal; equivalence requires that conversion.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Chirag has the fraction $\dfrac{2}{5}$ of a chocolate bar. He wants another fraction for the same quantity of that bar.

parts.text: Which plan gives an equivalent fraction?

options.text: Multiply numerator and denominator by $3$ to get $\dfrac{6}{15}$.
Change only the numerator to $6$ to get $\dfrac{6}{5}$.
Keep the numerator $2$ and replace the bar with a different whole to get another fraction equal to $\dfrac{2}{5}$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Zaid reduces the fraction 18/24 to lowest terms.

Which result is correct?

options.A: 6, reporting the common factor as the answer.
options.B: 6/1, because lowest terms are said to produce the common factor.
options.C: 3/4, by dividing numerator and denominator by 6.
options.D: 18, by counting how many 1/24-units make up 18/24.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kabir reduces the fraction $\dfrac{24}{36}$ to lowest terms.

Which two claims correctly describe that reduction?

options.A: Report $12$ alone as the finished reduced fraction.
options.B: Divide numerator and denominator by $12$ to obtain $\dfrac{2}{3}$.
options.C: $\dfrac{2}{3}$ is in lowest terms because $2$ and $3$ share no common factor except $1$.
options.D: Say that writing $\dfrac{2}{3}$ is what creates the common factor $12$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Chirag reduces the fraction $\dfrac{30}{45}$ to lowest terms.

parts.text: Which claim correctly describes that reduction?

options.text: Divide numerator and denominator by $15$ to get $\dfrac{2}{3}$.
Multiply numerator and denominator by $15$ to get $\dfrac{450}{675}$.
Lowest terms is what produces the common factor $15$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ritu must decide which is larger, $\dfrac{3}{4}$ or $\dfrac{5}{6}$.

Which plan compares them correctly?

options.A: Call the answer equivalent fractions, without comparing the two given fractions.
options.B: First invent which fraction is larger, and say that choice is what creates a common denominator.
options.C: Rewrite both with denominator $12$ as $\dfrac{9}{12}$ and $\dfrac{10}{12}$, then compare the numerators $9$ and $10$.
options.D: Convert each fraction to a percent first, and compare only after that conversion.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anvi must decide which is larger, $\dfrac{2}{5}$ or $\dfrac{3}{7}$.

Which two claims correctly describe a sound comparison?

options.A: $\dfrac{2}{5}$ is larger because $5$ is smaller than $7$.
options.B: Rewrite as $\dfrac{14}{35}$ and $\dfrac{15}{35}$, then compare the numerators $14$ and $15$.
options.C: With the same denominator $35$, the larger numerator marks the larger fraction, so $\dfrac{3}{7}$ is larger.
options.D: Cross-multiplying and then swapping the fractions reverses which one is larger.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bhavna must decide which is larger, $\dfrac{3}{5}$ or $\dfrac{4}{7}$.

Which plan compares them correctly?

options.A: Equivalent fractions means the denominators $5$ and $7$ alone.
options.B: A common denominator is produced by already knowing that $\dfrac{3}{5}$ is larger.
options.C: Rewrite as $\dfrac{21}{35}$ and $\dfrac{20}{35}$; then $21>20$, so $\dfrac{3}{5}$ is larger.
options.D: Compare them by checking only whether each fraction is a unit fraction $\dfrac{1}{n}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Parul adds $\frac{2}{7}$ and $\frac{3}{7}$.

How should she find the sum?

options.A: Call the shared denominator the sum, without adding the numerator counts.
options.B: Say that adding the fractions is what creates the common denominator after the fact.
options.C: Keep the denominator $7$ and add the numerators: $\frac{2}{7} + \frac{3}{7} = \frac{5}{7}$.
options.D: Report $3$ alone because that numeral is printed largest in the second fraction.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Diya adds $\dfrac{1}{4}$ and $\dfrac{3}{8}$ of a chocolate bar she shares with Kabir.

parts.text: Which claim correctly states how to add the fractions?

options.text: Add the numerators and add the denominators to get $\dfrac{4}{12}$.
Rewrite $\dfrac{1}{4}$ as $\dfrac{2}{8}$, then add numerators over $8$ to get $\dfrac{5}{8}$.
Keep the larger denominator $8$ and write $\dfrac{1+3}{8}=\dfrac{4}{8}$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bhavna adds $\dfrac{3}{10}$ and $\dfrac{2}{5}$ of a juice bottle she shares with her brother.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims correctly describe the sum?

options.A: Same denominator means writing the sum as $\dfrac{3+2}{10+5}=\dfrac{5}{15}$.
options.B: Rewrite $\dfrac{2}{5}$ as $\dfrac{4}{10}$, then add numerators over $10$ to get $\dfrac{7}{10}$.
options.C: Both fractions must be expressed with denominator $10$ before the numerators are added.
options.D: A common denominator is produced by already knowing that the sum equals $\dfrac{7}{10}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Javed must compute $\dfrac{5}{6} - \dfrac{1}{4}$.

Which plan subtracts the fractions correctly?

options.A: Call the answer same denominator, without finding the value of the difference.
options.B: Subtract as $\dfrac{5-1}{6-4} = \dfrac{4}{2}$, skipping common-denominator alignment.
options.C: Rewrite as $\dfrac{10}{12} - \dfrac{3}{12} = \dfrac{7}{12}$.
options.D: Say that the difference $\dfrac{7}{12}$ is what creates the common denominator $12$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Meher must compute $\dfrac{7}{8}-\dfrac{1}{3}$.

options.A: Call the answer same denominator, and stop with that label.
options.B: Subtract as $\dfrac{7-1}{8-3}=\dfrac{6}{5}$.
options.C: Rewrite as $\dfrac{21}{24}-\dfrac{8}{24}=\dfrac{13}{24}$.
options.D: Say that the difference $\dfrac{13}{24}$ is what creates the common denominator $24$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Harish rewrites $\frac{2}{3}$ with denominator $12$ so he can add it to $\frac{5}{12}$.

Why must the numerator change along with the denominator?

options.A: Call the result an "equivalent fraction" label while keeping numerator $2$ and only writing denominator $12$.
options.B: Change the denominator to $12$ without multiplying the numerator by the same factor.
options.C: Multiply numerator and denominator by the same factor $4$: $\frac{2}{3} = \frac{8}{12}$, so the value is unchanged for the common-denominator sum.
options.D: Say the equivalent fraction is what produces the common denominator after the fact.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kabir rewrites $\dfrac{3}{4}$ so that its denominator is $12$, in order to add it to $\dfrac{5}{12}$.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: Multiply numerator and denominator by the same factor $3$, giving $\dfrac{9}{12}$.
options.B: Once both fractions use denominator $12$, their numerators can be added.
options.C: Change only the denominator to $12$ and leave the numerator as $3$.
options.D: Writing $\dfrac{9}{12}$ is what creates the original fraction $\dfrac{3}{4}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Wasim chooses the unit $\dfrac{1}{5}$ metre and finds that a ribbon is covered by exactly $7$ such units.

Which claim measures the ribbon correctly?

options.A: Report the length as $\dfrac{7}{5}$ metre even if the unit length changes mid-count, without keeping one fixed metre as the whole.
options.B: Say that writing $\dfrac{7}{5}$ metre is what creates the seven copies of $\dfrac{1}{5}$ metre.
options.C: Count $7$ copies of the unit $\dfrac{1}{5}$ metre, so the ribbon length is $\dfrac{7}{5}$ metre.
options.D: Also treat the same $7$ copies as settling the ribbon's area in square metres, beyond this length count.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yash measures a ribbon using the fractional unit $\dfrac{1}{8}$ metre. Exactly $5$ of those units cover the ribbon end to end.

Which claim correctly writes the ribbon length?

options.A: The length is $5$ metres, taking only the count of units.
options.B: Say that writing $\dfrac{5}{8}$ is what creates the unit size $\dfrac{1}{8}$.
options.C: The length is $\dfrac{5}{8}$ metre, because $5$ copies of $\dfrac{1}{8}$ make $\dfrac{5}{8}$.
options.D: The same reading $\dfrac{5}{8}$ also fixes the length when a different unit such as $\dfrac{1}{10}$ is chosen instead.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Vivek opens a compass to a fixed length, keeps the metal point fixed at P, and moves only the pencil.

What path does the pencil draw?

options.A: A circle whose radius is the point P.
options.B: A circle with centre at the moving pencil tip, and with P on the rim.
options.C: A circle with centre P, and with every pencil point at the same fixed distance from P.
options.D: A square that has one corner fixed at P.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Zubin keeping the metal point fixed at P with the compass open to a fixed length, and moving only the pencil.

What path does the pencil draw?

options.A: A circle with centre P, and with every pencil point at the same fixed distance from P.
options.B: A circle whose radius is the point P.
options.C: A circle with centre at the moving pencil tip, and with P on the rim.
options.D: A straight line through P.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Esha keeping the metal point fixed at E with the compass open to a fixed length, and moving only the pencil.

What path does the pencil draw?

options.A: A circle with centre E, and with every pencil point at the same fixed distance from E.
options.B: A circle whose radius is the point E.
options.C: A circle with centre at the moving pencil tip, and with E on the rim.
options.D: A triangle that has one vertex fixed at E.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tanya wants a circular hole of radius 2 cm at the centre of a square card of side 10 cm. She will use a compass.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Place the compass tip at a corner of the square and set the radius to 2 cm.
options.B: Place the tip anywhere on the card; only setting the radius to 2 cm matters.
options.C: Place the tip at the centre of the square and set the radius to 2 cm.
options.D: Draw the curve freehand without a fixed centre, because neat artwork is enough.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Karan's square card of side $8\,\mathrm{cm}$ with centre marked $O$. He wants a circular hole of radius $2\,\mathrm{cm}$ at that centre, drawn with a compass.

Which claim correctly states where the compass point must sit and what radius to use?

options.A: Place the compass point at $O$ and set the radius to $2\,\mathrm{cm}$.
options.B: Place the compass point anywhere on the card; only the $2\,\mathrm{cm}$ opening matters.
options.C: Place the compass point on the dashed circle and set the radius from there to $O$.
options.D: Draw the hole freehand, because neat artwork on the square card is enough.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Falguni's square sheet of side $12\,\mathrm{cm}$ with centre marked $O$. She wants a circular arc of radius $3\,\mathrm{cm}$ with centre $O$, drawn with a compass.

Which claim correctly states where the compass point must be placed and what radius is needed?

options.A: Place the compass point at $O$ and open the compass to radius $3\,\mathrm{cm}$.
options.B: Place the compass point at a corner of the square and open it to $12\,\mathrm{cm}$.
options.C: Opening the compass to $3\,\mathrm{cm}$ is what creates the centre $O$.
options.D: Freehand sketch quality settles the arc, so the compass point may be anywhere.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Omkar studies the four-sided figure drawn below. It is tilted on the page. Every side is $3$ cm, and every corner is $90^\circ$.

What is the figure?

options.A: A rectangle only, because any four-sided shape with right angles is called a rectangle and not a square.
options.B: A square, from the equal sides alone, without using the right-angle marks.
options.C: A square, because all sides are equal and all angles are $90^\circ$, even though it is rotated.
options.D: Not a square, because rotating the shape is what changes its side lengths and angles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Rumi's four-sided card, tilted on the page. Every side is $4\,\mathrm{cm}$, and every corner is $90^\circ$.

Which claim correctly names the figure?

options.A: A square, because all sides are equal and all angles are $90^\circ$, even though the card is tilted.
options.B: A rectangle only, because any four-sided shape with right angles is called a rectangle.
options.C: A square, because the four sides are equal.
options.D: Not a square, because tilting the card is what changes its side lengths and angles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: The diagram shows Vedika's four-sided card, tilted on the page. Opposite sides are $5\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $3\,\mathrm{cm}$, and every corner is $90^\circ$.

parts.text: Which claim correctly names the figure?

options.text: A rectangle, because opposite sides are equal and all angles are $90^\circ$, even though the card is tilted.
A square, because any four-sided shape with right angles is called a square.
A rectangle, because the opposite sides are equal.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit labels the corners of a rectangle A, B, C, D in order going around the boundary. A valid name may start at any corner and then follow that travel order.

Which name is valid for that rectangle?

options.A: Rectangle ACDB, listing corners by jumping across instead of travelling the boundary.
options.B: Only rectangle ABCD is allowed; starting at any other corner makes the name invalid.
options.C: Rectangle ABCD is valid only after renaming the corners in alphabetical order first.
options.D: Rectangle BCDA is valid: it lists corners in boundary travel order, starting at B.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Sana's rectangle with corners labelled $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ in order going around the boundary. A valid name may start at any corner and then follow that travel order.

Which name is valid for that rectangle?

options.A: Rectangle $QRSP$ is valid: it lists corners in boundary travel order, starting at $Q$.
options.B: Rectangle $PRSQ$, listing corners by jumping across instead of travelling the boundary.
options.C: Only rectangle $PQRS$ is allowed; starting at any other corner makes the name invalid.
options.D: Rectangle $PQRS$ is valid only after renaming the corners in alphabetical order first.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Falguni labels the corners of a square $W$, $X$, $Y$, $Z$ in order going around the boundary. A valid name may start at any corner and then follow that travel order.

Which name is valid for that square?

options.A: Square $XYZW$ is valid: it lists corners in boundary travel order, starting at $X$.
options.B: Square $WYZX$, listing corners by jumping across instead of travelling the boundary.
options.C: Only square $WXYZ$ is allowed; starting at any other corner makes the name invalid.
options.D: Square $WXYZ$ is valid only after renaming the corners in alphabetical order first.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Farid must construct a square of side $5$ cm with ruler and compass.

Which plan forces the square?

options.A: Draw a base of $5$ cm and raise perpendiculars at both ends, but mark any new lengths on those perpendiculars.
options.B: First draw the upright sides, and say those upright sides are what create the $5$ cm base.
options.C: Draw base AB of $5$ cm, construct a perpendicular at A and at B, mark $5$ cm on each perpendicular to get D and C, then join DC.
options.D: Find the area $25$ cm$^{2}$ first, and treat that area calculation as the construction of the square.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Ishaan must construct a square of side $6$ cm with ruler and compass.

parts.text: Which plan forces the square?

options.text: Draw base AB of $6$ cm, construct a perpendicular at A and at B, mark $6$ cm on each perpendicular, and join the new ends.
Draw a base of $6$ cm and raise perpendiculars at both ends, but mark any new lengths on those uprights.
Find the area $36$ cm$^{2}$ first, and treat that area calculation as the construction.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Falguni must construct a rectangle of length $5$ cm and breadth $3$ cm with ruler and compass. She does not need the area of the rectangle to finish the construction.

Which plan forces the rectangle?

options.A: Draw a base of $5$ cm, erect perpendiculars of length $3$ cm at both ends, then join the top points.
options.B: Draw a base of $5$ cm and mark $3$ cm along that same base only.
options.C: Erecting the perpendiculars is what creates the $5$ cm base.
options.D: The construction is finished once the area $15$ cm$^{2}$ is written beside the rectangle.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Deepak draws rectangle ABCD. Point X moves on side AD and point Y moves on side BC. He wants to track how near or far X and Y are.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Track only the position of Y; the position of X is not needed.
options.B: Nearness can be decided without placing X on AD and Y on BC.
options.C: Measure the length of segment XY; that length changes as X and Y move.
options.D: X and Y are near when the printed letters look close on the page.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sara looks at the diagram of rectangle $ABCD$. Point $X$ moves on side $AD$ and point $Y$ moves on side $BC$. She wants to track how near or far $X$ and $Y$ are.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Track only the position of $Y$; the position of $X$ is not needed.
options.B: Nearness can be decided before $X$ is placed on $AD$ and $Y$ on $BC$.
options.C: Measure the length of segment $XY$; that length changes as $X$ and $Y$ move.
options.D: $X$ and $Y$ are near when the printed letters look close on the page.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Falguni draws rectangle $WXYZ$. Point $P$ moves on side $WX$ and point $Q$ moves on side $ZY$. She wants to track how near or far $P$ and $Q$ are.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Measure the length of segment $PQ$; that length changes as $P$ and $Q$ move.
options.B: Track only the position of $Q$; the position of $P$ is not needed.
options.C: Nearness can be decided without placing $P$ on $WX$ and $Q$ on $ZY$.
options.D: $P$ and $Q$ are near when the printed letters look close on the page.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Vivek must divide a $6$ cm by $4$ cm rectangle into identical squares that fill the rectangle with no gaps.

Which claim correctly plans the equal segments?

options.A: Mark any set of cuts across the $6$ cm side alone, and skip making every square side equal.
options.B: First draw the finished identical squares, and say those squares are what create the $6$ cm and $4$ cm sides.
options.C: Choose a common side length that divides both $6$ cm and $4$ cm, then cut so every square has all four sides equal to that length.
options.D: First find the rectangle's area $24$ cm$^{2}$, and treat that area formula as the tiling into identical squares.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Sameer must tile a $8$ cm by $6$ cm rectangle with identical squares that fill it with no gaps and no overlaps.

parts.text: Which claim plans the tiling correctly?

options.text: Any square side works if the area $48$ is divisible by that side.
The square side must be a common divisor of $8$ and $6$, so sides such as $2$ cm work because both lengths split into equal segments.
Only a $8$ cm square can be used, matching the longer side alone.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice that names which segments must be equal.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Chirag must divide the $12$ cm by $9$ cm rectangle in the diagram into identical squares that fill it with no gaps and no overlaps.

parts.text: Which claim correctly plans the equal segments?

options.text: Mark equal $3$ cm segments along the $12$ cm and $9$ cm sides so squares of side $3$ cm fill the rectangle.
Mark segments of length $12$ cm only, and ignore making the $9$ cm side match equal square sides.
The rough diagram of the rectangle produces identical squares even when corresponding sides are unequal.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tanya draws rectangle PQRS. She wants to explore its diagonals by length and by the angles they make.

Which plan starts the comparison correctly?

options.A: Compare side PQ with side QR only, without joining any opposite corners.
options.B: Say that drawing the diagonals is what creates rectangle PQRS.
options.C: Join opposite corners to form diagonals PR and QS, then compare those lengths and the angles they form.
options.D: Also prove the general diagonal laws for every parallelogram, as if that proof were required for this exploration.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nitya explores the diagram of rectangle $PQRS$. She wants to study its diagonals.

Which claim correctly says which corners to join and what to compare?

options.A: Join opposite corners $P$ to $R$ and $Q$ to $S$, then compare those diagonal lengths and the angles they form.
options.B: Join adjacent corners $P$ to $Q$ only, because a diagonal is any side of the rectangle.
options.C: Join $P$ to $S$ and call that the only diagonal, reversing which corners count as opposite.
options.D: Compare only the labels $P$ and $R$ printed on the page as if they were the diagonals.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Chirag explores the diagram of rectangle $WXYZ$. He wants to study its diagonals by length and by the angles they make.

parts.text: Which claim correctly says which corners to join and what to compare?

options.text: Join opposite corners $W$ to $Y$ and $X$ to $Z$, then compare those diagonal lengths and the angles they form.
Join adjacent corners $W$ to $X$ only, because a diagonal is any side of the rectangle.
Join $W$ to $Z$ alone and call that the only diagonal, reversing which corners count as opposite.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Omkar must construct rectangle $ABCD$ so that diagonal $AC$ divides $\angle DAB$ into $60^\circ$ and $30^\circ$.

Which plan locates the next sides and vertex $D$ correctly?

options.A: Call the finished figure diagonal $AC$ only, without using the right angle at $A$ or the $60^\circ$ and $30^\circ$ parts.
options.B: Say that drawing diagonal $AC$ is what creates rectangle $ABCD$, instead of building the rectangle from right angles and equal opposite sides.
options.C: Use $\angle DAB=90^\circ$, so the $60^\circ$ part leaves $30^\circ$; then place $D$ with right angles (or equal opposite sides) from the known sides.
options.D: Choose the plan only because $60$ is the largest printed angle number among $60$ and $30$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Yash must construct rectangle $ABCD$ so that diagonal $AC$ divides $\angle DAB$ into $60^{\circ}$ and $30^{\circ}$. The diagram shows the right angle at $A$ and those parts along diagonal $AC$.

options.A: Call the finished figure diagonal $AC$ only.
options.B: Say that drawing diagonal $AC$ is what creates rectangle $ABCD$.
options.C: Use $\angle DAB=90^{\circ}$, so the $60^{\circ}$ part leaves $30^{\circ}$; then place sides and vertex $D$ from that split.
options.D: Choose the plan only because $60$ is the largest printed angle number among $60$, $30$, and $90$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit must construct rectangle $ABCD$ given side $DC = 5$ cm and diagonal $DB = 7$ cm.

Which plan locates vertex $B$ correctly?

options.A: Erect a perpendicular at $C$ without first drawing side $DC$ at its given length $5$ cm.
options.B: Locate $B$ by trial-and-error with a ruler only, without using a perpendicular and an arc.
options.C: Draw $DC$; erect a perpendicular to $DC$ at $C$; from $D$ draw an arc of radius $7$ cm; $B$ is their intersection.
options.D: Place $B$ using only the printed length $5$ cm, ignoring the diagonal length $7$ cm.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Anvi must construct rectangle $ABCD$ with side $DC = 6\,\mathrm{cm}$ and diagonal $DB = 8\,\mathrm{cm}$.

parts.text: Which plan locates vertex $B$ correctly?

options.text: Draw $DC = 6\,\mathrm{cm}$. At $C$ draw the line perpendicular to $DC$. With centre $D$ and radius $8\,\mathrm{cm}$, mark where that arc meets the perpendicular; that point is $B$.
Draw $DC = 6\,\mathrm{cm}$ and place $B$ anywhere $8\,\mathrm{cm}$ from $D$, with no perpendicular through $C$.
Locate $B$ by reading the printed numeral $8$ alone, with no arc centred at $D$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bharat must locate a point that is $5$ cm from point $B$ and $5$ cm from point $C$.

Which plan finds that point correctly?

options.A: Call the answer point $B$, without locating an intersection of equal-radius arcs.
options.B: Say that the intersection point is what creates the given points $B$ and $C$.
options.C: Draw an arc of radius $5$ cm centred at $B$ and an arc of radius $5$ cm centred at $C$; a required point is their intersection.
options.D: Choose a point only because the printed length $5$ cm stands out, without drawing the equal-radius arcs.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ira looks at the diagram. Points $B$ and $C$ are fixed. She needs every point that is $5\,\mathrm{cm}$ from $B$ and also $5\,\mathrm{cm}$ from $C$.

Which claim correctly locates those points?

options.A: They are the intersection points of the circle of radius $5\,\mathrm{cm}$ centered at $B$ with the circle of radius $5\,\mathrm{cm}$ centered at $C$.
options.B: Call the answer the single label midpoint of $BC$.
options.C: Say that the finished intersection points are what create the equal $5\,\mathrm{cm}$ distances.
options.D: Choose the points only because the printed $5$ is the largest number on the page.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kavya has a paper square with a design on it. She wants to know whether the design has mathematical symmetry.

Which check decides that?

options.A: The design looks attractive, so it is symmetric.
options.B: The design has matching colours, so it is symmetric.
options.C: A fold or a turn maps the design onto itself.
options.D: A definite pattern of matching parts is what creates symmetry by itself.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Esha has a square rangoli tile with a design on it. She wants to know whether the design has mathematical symmetry.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: A fold that maps the design onto itself shows symmetry.
options.B: Matching colours alone settle that the design is symmetric.
options.C: A turn that maps the design onto itself shows symmetry.
options.D: A definite pattern of matching parts is what creates symmetry by itself.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Raghav has a square handkerchief with a painted design. He wants to know whether the design has mathematical symmetry.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: A fold that maps the design onto itself shows symmetry.
options.B: Matching colours alone settle that the design is symmetric.
options.C: A turn that maps the design onto itself shows symmetry.
options.D: A definite pattern of matching parts is what creates symmetry by itself.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Xavier has a paper heart and a possible vertical mid-line drawn on it.

When is that mid-line a line of symmetry?

options.A: Whenever the heart looks roughly balanced, even if it is never folded.
options.B: When folding along the mid-line is treated as a result produced by an already known line of symmetry.
options.C: Only when folding along that mid-line makes the two parts overlap exactly point for point.
options.D: Only when a group-theory symmetry order of 2 is named for the heart.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Boman has a paper heart with a possible mid-line drawn on it.

Which two claims correctly decide whether that mid-line is a line of symmetry?

options.A: The mid-line is a line of symmetry whenever the heart looks balanced, even if the two halves need not be folded onto each other.
options.B: Fold the heart along the mid-line; the mid-line is a line of symmetry only when the two halves overlap exactly.
options.C: Exact fold-overlap of the two halves is the test that decides the mid-line is a line of symmetry.
options.D: A line of symmetry is what creates the fold along the mid-line.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Gopal's paper kite with a possible vertical mid-line drawn as a dashed fold line.

When is that mid-line a line of symmetry?

options.A: When folding along the mid-line makes the two parts overlap exactly point for point.
options.B: When the two halves look roughly similar from a distance.
options.C: Calling the mid-line a line of symmetry is what forces the two parts to match.
options.D: The mid-line is a line of symmetry for any paper kite, even when the fold test is never tried.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Chitra draws the square shown in the figure. She wants to count its lines of symmetry by testing folds.

How many lines of symmetry does the square have?

options.A: Infinitely many, because any line through the centre looks balanced at a glance.
options.B: Four folds are what create the square in the first place.
options.C: Four: two through midpoints of opposite sides and two through opposite corners, each passing the fold test.
options.D: The count needs group-theory language before any fold can be checked.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Veer has a square paper. He wants to count its lines of symmetry by testing folds.

Which two claims correctly count those lines?

options.A: Infinitely many, because any line through the centre looks balanced at a glance.
options.B: Four lines: two through midpoints of opposite sides and two through opposite corners, each passing the fold test.
options.C: Systematic fold checks find exactly four valid fold lines on the square.
options.D: Four folds are what create the square in the first place.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Wasim draws the equilateral triangle shown in the figure. He wants to count its lines of symmetry by testing folds.

How many lines of symmetry does the equilateral triangle have?

options.A: Three: each line from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side passes the fold test.
options.B: Infinitely many, because any line through the centre looks balanced at a glance.
options.C: Three folds are what create the equilateral triangle in the first place.
options.D: The count needs group-theory language before any fold can be checked.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qasim is completing a mirror image across a fixed vertical symmetry line. Point A is $2$ cm to the left of the line, at a marked height.

Where does the reflected point A' belong?

options.A: A' is the name mirror image for the symmetry line itself.
options.B: A' may sit anywhere on the right of the line, at any distance.
options.C: A' is $2$ cm to the right of the line, at the same height as A.
options.D: First place A', and that placement is what creates the symmetry line.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Reyansh is completing a mirror image across a fixed vertical symmetry line. Point $A$ is $3\,\mathrm{cm}$ to the left of the line, at a marked height.

Which two claims correctly place the reflected point $A'$?

options.A: $A'$ is the name mirror image for the symmetry line itself.
options.B: $A'$ is $3\,\mathrm{cm}$ to the right of the line, at the same height as $A$.
options.C: $A'$ and $A$ are the same distance from the symmetry line, on opposite sides.
options.D: First place $A'$, and that placement is what creates the symmetry line.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Gopal completing a mirror image across a fixed horizontal symmetry line. Point $B$ is $4\,\mathrm{cm}$ above the line, at a marked horizontal position.

Where does the reflected point $B'$ belong?

options.A: $B'$ is $4\,\mathrm{cm}$ below the line, at the same horizontal position as $B$.
options.B: $B'$ is the name mirror image for the symmetry line itself.
options.C: $B'$ may sit anywhere below the line, at any distance.
options.D: First place $B'$, and that placement is what creates the symmetry line.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Soham folds the square sheet in the figure once down the middle, punches one hole through both layers, then unfolds the sheet.

Which claim correctly predicts the unfolded design?

options.A: The fold line itself is the punched design.
options.B: One hole appears anywhere on the paper, even where the layers did not meet.
options.C: Two holes appear as mirror images across the fold line, because the fold forced matching positions to coincide.
options.D: The punched holes are what create the fold line.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tara folds a square sheet once down the middle, punches one hole through both layers, then unfolds the sheet.

Which two claims correctly predict the unfolded design?

options.A: The fold line itself is the punched design.
options.B: Two holes appear as mirror images across the fold line.
options.C: The fold forced matching positions on both halves of the sheet.
options.D: The punched holes are what create the fold line.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gopal folds a rectangular sheet once down the middle, presses a paint blot through both layers, then unfolds the sheet. The fold line is a line of symmetry for the action.

Which claim correctly predicts the unfolded design?

options.A: The unfolded sheet shows two blots mirror-symmetric about the fold line.
options.B: The fold line is the paint blot.
options.C: Two mirror blots appear even when the fold line is not treated as a line of symmetry.
options.D: The two blots are what create the fold line after unfolding.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Hassan studies the equilateral triangle in the figure below, with centre O marked.

Does the triangle have rotational symmetry?

options.A: Call O the name rotational symmetry, without testing any turn of the triangle.
options.B: Say the centre O is what the matching turn creates, instead of using O to test a turn.
options.C: Yes, because a turn of $120^\circ$ about O makes the triangle coincide with itself, and $120^\circ$ is less than a full turn.
options.D: Count three equal sides and report the order of rotational symmetry from that count alone, without naming a turn angle less than $360^\circ$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Aryan studies a square with centre $O$ marked at the meeting point of the diagonals.

parts.text: Does the square have rotational symmetry?

options.text: Call $O$ the name rotational symmetry.
Yes, because a turn of $90^{\circ}$ about $O$ makes the square coincide with itself, and $90^{\circ}$ is less than a full turn.
Say the centre $O$ is what the matching turn creates.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gopal studies a regular hexagon with centre $O$ marked at the meeting point of lines joining opposite vertices.

Does the hexagon have rotational symmetry?

options.A: Yes, because a turn of $60^{\circ}$ about $O$ makes the hexagon coincide with itself, and $60^{\circ}$ is less than a full turn.
options.B: Call $O$ the name rotational symmetry.
options.C: Say the centre $O$ is what the matching turn creates.
options.D: Yes, because counting the six vertices of the hexagon decides that it has rotational symmetry.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Komal studies the regular hexagon in the figure. It is divided into $6$ equal triangular parts meeting at the centre O.

What is the smallest angle of rotational symmetry, and what is the order?

options.A: Any turn about O works, even if the six parts are not equal or equally spaced.
options.B: She must use group-theory language about rotation groups before naming an angle or order.
options.C: The smallest angle is $360^\circ/6 = 60^\circ$, and the order is $6$.
options.D: She should test only for a mirror line through O, and treat that line test as the rotational order.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Diya looks at a regular octagon divided into $8$ equal triangular parts that meet at the centre.

Which claim correctly states the smallest rotation angle about the centre that maps the octagon onto itself, and the order of that rotation?

options.A: The smallest angle is $90^{\circ}$ and the order is $4$, using only quarter-turns.
options.B: The smallest angle is $45^{\circ}$ and the order is $8$, because $360^{\circ}\div 8 = 45^{\circ}$.
options.C: The smallest angle is $30^{\circ}$ and the order is $12$, as for a clock face.
options.D: The smallest angle is $180^{\circ}$ and the order is $2$, because a half-turn is enough for every regular polygon.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Falguni studies a regular pentagon divided into $5$ equal triangular parts that meet at the centre.

Which claim correctly states the smallest rotation angle about the centre that maps the pentagon onto itself, and the order of that rotation?

options.A: The smallest angle is $72^{\circ}$ and the order is $5$, even when the five parts are unequal.
options.B: The same $72^{\circ}$ and order $5$ rule also covers triangular parts that are unequal or do not meet at the centre.
options.C: The smallest angle is $72^{\circ}$ and the order is $5$.
options.D: Line symmetry alone gives the smallest rotation angle $72^{\circ}$ and order $5$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Xavier asks why a circle is a special limiting case for line symmetry and rotational symmetry.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Say the circle matches itself after some turn, but skip that the turn is about the centre and that every diameter is a symmetry line.
options.B: Say the centre is what the circle creates, instead of using the centre to test turns and diameters.
options.C: A circle matches itself after a turn by any angle about its centre, and every diameter is a line of symmetry, so it has infinitely many rotational symmetries and infinitely many symmetry lines.
options.D: Require group-theory language about symmetry groups, beyond line and turn matching for the circle.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kabir turns a circular paper disc about its centre and also folds it along diameters.

Which claim correctly explains why the circle is a special limiting case for symmetry?

options.A: The circle has symmetry only for a $180^{\circ}$ turn, like a parallelogram.
options.B: The circle matches itself after any turn about its centre, and every diameter is a line of symmetry.
options.C: Symmetry holds for the circle only when the fold misses the centre.
options.D: The circle has exactly four symmetry lines, matching a square.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Falguni spins a round steel plate about its centre and also folds it along diameters through that centre.

Which claim correctly explains why the circle is a special limiting case for symmetry?

options.A: The plate matches itself after any turn about its centre, and every diameter is a line of symmetry.
options.B: Symmetry holds for the plate only when the fold misses the centre.
options.C: The centre is produced by already knowing the plate has infinitely many symmetries.
options.D: The plate has exactly four symmetry lines, matching a square.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Chitra has a paper cut-out of a capital letter S. She wants to decide whether it has line symmetry and whether it has rotational symmetry.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Answer "rotational symmetry" alone, naming that label instead of running both tests.
options.B: Decide from a single glance that whatever is true of one kind of symmetry is automatically true of the other.
options.C: Apply the fold test for line symmetry and the turn test for rotational symmetry separately; the letter may have one, both, or neither.
options.D: Pick the answer from the printed word "letter" in the stem, without folding or turning the cut-out.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Ira has a paper cut-out of a capital letter $H$. She wants to decide whether it has line symmetry and whether it has rotational symmetry.

parts.text: Which plan is correct?

options.text: Answer rotational symmetry alone, naming that label instead of running both tests.
Apply the fold test for line symmetry and the turn test for rotational symmetry as separate checks.
Decide from a single glance that whatever is true of one kind of symmetry is automatically true of the other.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nitin marks three temperatures on a number line with 0 as the reference: −3 °C, 0 °C, and 4 °C.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: −3 °C is below zero, 4 °C is above zero, and 0 °C is neither positive nor negative.
options.B: 0 °C is a positive temperature because it is written without a minus sign.
options.C: −3 °C is above zero, and 4 °C is below zero.
options.D: −3 °C and 4 °C are the same kind of signed value because both sit away from zero.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Mini marks three floor levels on a number line with ground as 0: $-2$ (basement), $0$, and $3$ (third floor).

Which statement is correct?

options.A: $0$ is a positive level because it is written without a minus sign.
options.B: $-2$ is above zero, and $3$ is below zero.
options.C: $-2$ is below zero, $3$ is above zero, and $0$ is neither positive nor negative.
options.D: $-2$ and $3$ are the same kind of signed value because both sit away from zero.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Zubin marks three depths on a number line with the water surface as 0: $-4$ m (below the surface), $0$, and $2$ m (above the surface on a pier).

parts.text: Which statement is correct?

options.text: $-4$ m is below zero, $2$ m is above zero, and $0$ is neither positive nor negative.
$0$ is a positive depth because it is written without a minus sign.
$-4$ m is above zero, and $2$ m is below zero.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice that uses positions relative to zero.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri places −7, −2, and 3 on a number line with 0 marked.

Which statement about their order is correct?

options.A: −7 is greater than −2 because 7 is greater than 2.
options.B: −2 is farther left than −7, so −2 is smaller.
options.C: −7 is farther left than −2, so −7 is smaller than −2, and both are smaller than 3.
options.D: 3 is smaller than −7 because it is written with fewer digits.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sia places $-6$, $-2$, and $4$ on a number line with $0$ marked.

Which claim correctly orders those integers from least to greatest?

options.A: Call the answer the phrase number line, and stop there.
options.B: $-2$, $-6$, $4$, because $2$ is a smaller digit than $6$.
options.C: $-6$, $-2$, $4$, by their positions from left to right on the number line.
options.D: The order is settled only after comparing products of the integers.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Hema's number line with $0$ marked and the integers $-5$, $-1$, and $2$ placed on it.

Which claim correctly orders those integers from least to greatest?

options.A: Any listing of $-5$, $-1$, and $2$ is correct, because the integers already sit on a number line.
options.B: $-1$, $-5$, $2$, because $1$ is a smaller digit than $5$.
options.C: $-5$, $-1$, $2$, by their positions from left to right on the number line.
options.D: $2$, $-1$, $-5$, because $2$ is farthest right, so it is least.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yamini stands at +3 on a number line and then moves −5.

Where does she finish?

options.A: −5, reporting only the movement.
options.B: +8, by adding 3 and 5 as same-direction jumps on a sparse unmarked line.
options.C: −2, because start + movement = 3 + (−5).
options.D: 28, by computing 3 + 5².

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anvi stands at $+4$ on a number line and then moves $-7$.

Which claim correctly names where she finishes?

options.A: $-7$, reporting only the movement.
options.B: $+11$, by adding $4$ and $7$ as same-direction jumps.
options.C: $-3$, because start plus movement equals $4 + (-7)$.
options.D: $53$, by computing $4 + 7^{2}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yuvraj's floor counter shows $+6$. He then takes a signed movement of $-9$.

Which claim correctly names where the counter finishes?

options.A: The counter finishes at $-9$.
options.B: The counter finishes at $+15$.
options.C: The counter finishes at $-3$.
options.D: The counter finishes at $87$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Omkar stands at $+2$ on a number line. He wants to reach $-4$.

What signed movement does he need?

options.A: Call $-4$ the needed movement, without using the start.
options.B: Say the needed movement is what produces the start $+2$ after he arrives.
options.C: $-6$, because target $-$ start $= -4 - (+2)$.
options.D: Treat the jump as a place-value regrouping of $2$ and $4$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Aarna stands at $+3$ on a number line. She wants to reach $-5$.

What signed movement does she need?

options.A: Call $-5$ the needed movement, ignoring the start $+3$.
options.B: Say the needed movement is what produces the start $+3$ after she arrives.
options.C: $-8$, because target $-$ start $= -5-(+3)$.
options.D: Treat the jump as a place-value regrouping of $3$ and $5$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Hema's game token stands at $-2$ on a number line. She wants to reach $+6$.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims correctly give the signed movement she needs?

options.A: The needed movement is $+8$, because target $-$ start $= 6-(-2)$.
options.B: The needed movement is $+6$, equal to the target alone.
options.C: Adding $+8$ to $-2$ reaches $+6$.
options.D: The needed movement is what produces the start $-2$ after she arrives at $+6$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri needs the additive inverse of $-7$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call "opposite integer" the finished answer, without naming the number that cancels $-7$.
options.B: Say $+7$ even if the two numbers did not have equal distance from zero.
options.C: $+7$, because $(-7)+(+7)=0$ (same distance from zero, opposite sign).
options.D: Report $7$ alone, because that digit is printed in $-7$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Dev needs the additive inverse of $-9$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call "opposite integer" the finished answer, and stop before naming the number that cancels $-9$.
options.B: Say $+9$ even if the two numbers did not have equal distance from zero.
options.C: $+9$, because $(-9)+(+9)=0$ (same distance from zero, opposite sign).
options.D: Report $9$ alone, because that digit is printed in $-9$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Hema needs the additive inverse of $0$. The two integers in an inverse pair have equal distance from zero.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims are correct?

options.A: The additive inverse of $0$ is $0$.
options.B: The opposite integer of $0$ is $+1$.
options.C: $0+0=0$, so $0$ cancels with itself to zero.
options.D: Any integer can be the additive inverse of $0$, even one that is not at equal distance from zero.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qasim must rewrite $6-(-2)$ as addition of an inverse.

Which rewrite is correct?

options.B: $4 \times 15 + 20$ is an arithmetic expression for the total.

options.D: The expression must be the printed 20 alone, because 20 is the last number she sees.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Mini buys 6 bananas at Rs 7 each and writes $6 \times 7$ for the cost she should pay.

parts.text: Which claim is correct?

options.text: $6 \times 7$ is an arithmetic expression for the cost, and its value is 42.
42 is the expression; $6 \times 7$ is only a name for that value.
The expression must be the printed 7 alone, because 7 is the last number she sees.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice that uses expression and value.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Padma writes the two expressions $7 + 5$ and $3 \times 4$.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: 12 is the comparison sign between the two expressions.
options.B: The expressions can be ordered without finding either value.
options.C: $7 + 5 = 3 \times 4$, because both expressions have value 12.
options.D: She should also compare the separate decimals $7.0$ and $5.0$ before deciding.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Karan writes the two expressions $9 + 6$ and $4 \times 4$.

Which two claims correctly compare them?

options.A: Call the answer the phrase expression value, and stop there.
options.C: Evaluating both expressions and comparing the results shows $15$ is less than $16$.
options.D: The comparison sign can be decided from the printed symbols alone, even when the expressions are not evaluated.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Komal writes the two expressions $8 + 7$ and $5 \times 3$.

Which claim correctly compares them?

options.A: $8 + 7$ and $5 \times 3$ cannot be compared, because they use different operation signs.
options.C: The comparison sign can be decided from the printed symbols alone, even when the expressions are not evaluated.
options.D: $8 + 7$ is greater, because addition is written first.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri must evaluate $3 \times (8 - 5) + 2$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the word grouping the answer, without evaluating any part of the expression.
options.B: Ignore the brackets and evaluate as if the expression were unbracketed term by term from left to right only.
options.C: First evaluate $8 - 5$ inside the brackets to get $3$, then compute $3 \times 3 + 2 = 11$.
options.D: Multiply $3 \times 8$ first, then subtract $5$, giving $19$ after adding $2$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Rumi must evaluate $5 \times (6 - 2) + 3$.

Which two claims correctly decide the order of working?

options.A: Call the answer the word grouping, and stop there.
options.B: First evaluate $6 - 2$ inside the brackets to get $4$, then compute $5 \times 4 + 3 = 23$.
options.C: The brackets force $6 - 2$ to be done before the multiplication by $5$.
options.D: Multiply $5 \times 6$ first, then subtract $2$, giving $31$ after adding $3$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Amit must evaluate $4 \times (9 - 6) + 5$.

parts.text: Which value is correct?
Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Walia studies the expression $83 - 14$.

What are its terms?

options.A: Call the plus-sign idea the terms, without naming the parts of $83 - 14$.
options.B: Say the listed terms are what create the expression $83 - 14$, instead of reading terms from the written expression.
options.C: Rewrite as $83 + (-14)$; the terms are $83$ and $-14$.
options.D: Report only the printed digits $8$, $3$, $1$, and $4$ as the terms, ignoring how $83 - 14$ is grouped.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sana studies the expression $57-19$.

Which two claims correctly identify its terms?

options.A: Call the plus-sign idea the terms, with no named parts of $57-19$.
options.B: Rewrite as $57+(-19)$; the terms are $57$ and $-19$.
options.C: The terms are the addends after rewriting the subtraction as addition of the opposite.
options.D: Report only the printed digits $5$, $7$, $1$, and $9$ as the terms, ignoring how $57-19$ is grouped.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Komal studies the expression $91 - 38$.

What are its terms?

options.A: Rewrite as $91 + (-38)$; the terms are $91$ and $-38$.
options.B: The plus-sign idea alone is the terms, with no named parts of $91 - 38$.
options.C: The listed terms are what create the expression $91 - 38$.
options.D: The printed digits $9$, $1$, $3$, and $8$ are the terms.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Padma must evaluate the unbracketed expression $7 + 3 \times 4 - 2$.

Which order is correct?

options.A: Call the answer multiplication only, without evaluating each term and then combining the terms.
options.B: Work strictly left to right as $((7+3)\times 4)-2$, as if brackets already fixed that order.
options.C: First form the terms: compute $3\times 4=12$, then evaluate $7+12-2=17$.
options.D: Also treat an exponent such as $2^{3}$ under the same left-to-right walk, as if this hinge settled powers.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ishaan must evaluate the unbracketed expression $8 + 2 \times 5 - 3$.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: Call the answer multiplication only, and stop before combining the remaining terms.
options.B: First form the product: compute $2\times 5=10$.
options.C: Then evaluate $8+10-3=15$.
options.D: Work strictly left to right as $((8+2)\times 5)-3$, as if brackets already fixed the order.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Komal must evaluate the unbracketed expression $9 + 4 \times 3 - 6$. The expression has no exponents.

Which order is correct?

options.A: Multiply $4 \times 3$ first to get $12$, then compute $9 + 12 - 6 = 15$.
options.B: Add and subtract left to right first: $(9 + 4) \times 3 - 6$.
options.C: The word multiplication is the value of the expression.
options.D: The same order also requires evaluating exponents before the terms in this expression.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yamini has rewritten an expression as the sum of terms $5 + (-3) + 8$.

Which claim about rearranging is correct?

options.A: Swap and group the terms freely even while a subtraction sign still sits between unsigned parts, without first writing signed terms.
options.B: Also claim that regrouping $(5+(-3))+8$ changes products such as $5\times(-3)\times 8$ the same way, as if products followed this sum rule.
options.C: Once the expression is a sum of terms, any order or grouping of $5$, $-3$, and $8$ keeps the same value, such as $5+8+(-3)$ or $(5+8)+(-3)$.
options.D: Decide only because $8$ is the largest printed number among $5$, $-3$, and $8$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sara has rewritten an expression as the sum of terms $7+(-2)+9$.

Which claim about rearranging is correct?

options.A: Swap and group freely while a subtraction sign still sits between unsigned parts.
options.B: Also claim that regrouping $(7+(-2))+9$ changes products such as $7\times(-2)\times 9$ the same way.
options.C: Once the expression is a sum of terms, any order or grouping of $7$, $-2$, and $9$ keeps the same value, such as $(-2)+9+7$.
options.D: Decide only because $9$ is the largest printed number among $7$, $-2$, and $9$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Komal has rewritten an expression as the sum of terms $4+(-6)+11$.

Which claim about rearranging is correct?

options.A: She may rewrite the sum as $4+11+(-6)$ without changing its value.
options.B: She may rearrange only after leaving the subtraction unconverted into signed terms.
options.C: The same rearranging rule also covers multiplying grouped sums in this item.
options.D: The printed numeral $11$ alone is the rearranged value of the expression.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Uday must remove the brackets in $8-(3-5)$.

Which rewrite is correct?

options.A: Call the step remove brackets only, without changing any signs inside.
options.B: Write $8-(3-5)=8-3-5$, keeping the inner signs as if no minus preceded the brackets.
options.C: Write $8-(3-5)=8-3+5$, because a minus before the brackets flips each inner sign.
options.D: Apply the same sign flip when removing brackets in $8+(3-5)$, where a plus precedes the brackets.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sameer must remove the brackets in $9-(4-6)$.

Which two claims are both correct?

options.A: The expression becomes $9-4-6$ with both inner signs unchanged.
options.B: Subtracting $(4-6)$ flips each inner sign, so the rewrite is $9-4+6$.
options.C: After removing brackets, $9-4+6$ equals $11$.
options.D: Removing brackets always deletes the inner minus and leaves only $9-4$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Jatin must remove the brackets in $12-(7-3)$.

parts.text: Which rewrite is correct?

options.text: Negative sign before brackets means the word "brackets" alone.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ritu starts with the sum of terms $7 + 4 + (-2)$ and then increases the term $4$ by $3$.

Which claim about the new value is correct?

options.A: Call the answer expression value only, without saying how the change in one term moves the total.
options.B: Increase the term $4$ by $3$, but leave the total unchanged as if the sum ignored that term change.
options.C: The new sum is $7 + 7 + (-2)$; increasing the term $4$ by $3$ increases the expression value by $3$.
options.D: Choose $+3$ as the new total only because $3$ is the largest printed change among the given numbers.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nitya evaluates the expression $8+5+3$. She then increases the term $5$ by $2$.

Which claim correctly states how the expression's value changes?

options.A: The value becomes $8$ only, because increase is just a label on the page.
options.B: The value stays $16$, because changing one term never changes a sum.
options.C: The value increases by $2$ to $18$, matching the increase in that term.
options.D: The value becomes $2$, because the printed increase $2$ replaces the whole sum.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Jatin starts with the sum of terms $9+6+(-1)$ and then decreases the term $6$ by $4$.

parts.text: Which claim correctly states how the expression's value changes?

options.text: The value becomes $9$ only, because decrease is just a label on the page.
The value stays $14$, because changing one term never changes a sum.
The value decreases by $4$ to $10$, matching the decrease in that term.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Omkar has the expression $6(n+4)$ and wants to know whether he may expand or factor a multiplication over a sum.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the step "multiple of a sum" only, without writing an expanded or factored form.
options.B: Say that writing $6n+24$ is what creates the factor $6$ outside $(n+4)$, instead of expanding from $6(n+4)$.
options.C: Yes: $6(n+4)=6n+24$, and factoring $6n+24$ returns $6(n+4)$, because a multiple of a sum equals the sum of the multiples.
options.D: Decide the rewrite by left-to-right order for an unbracketed mix of operations, instead of using the multiply-over-sum rule.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Neil must rewrite $4 \times (7 + 5)$ as a sum of products that keeps the same value.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the answer a multiple of a sum, and stop there.
options.B: Write $4 \times 7 + 5$, so only $7$ is multiplied by $4$.
options.C: Write $4 \times 7 + 4 \times 5$, multiplying each part of the sum by $4$.
options.D: Say the expanded sum $4 \times 7 + 4 \times 5$ is what creates the factored form $4 \times (7 + 5)$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Rina wants to find $63\times48$ by rewriting one factor and using the distributive property.

Which rewrite keeps the product unchanged and makes the calculation easier?

options.A: The product is already settled by naming $63\times48$ a product.
options.C: $63\times48=(60+3)\times48=60\times48+3\times48$.
options.D: Long multiplication of $63$ by $48$ is the same move as this factor decomposition.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Kabir wants to compute $47 \times 36$ by rewriting one factor and using the distributive property.

parts.text: Which rewrite keeps the product unchanged?

options.text: Write $47$ as $50 - 3$, then compute $50 \times 36 - 3 \times 36$.
Write $47$ as $50 + 3$, then compute $50 \times 36 + 3 \times 36$.
Treat the word product alone as the answer, with no rewrite of $47$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit measures a pencil on a ruler marked in centimetres. The tip ends between the 7 cm and 8 cm marks.

What should he do to report the length more accurately?

options.A: Report 7 cm, because the tip has not reached 8 cm.
options.B: Split the gap into unequal marks of any sizes he likes.
options.C: Split the 1 cm gap into equal smaller parts and count how many the tip passes.
options.D: Ignore the ruler marks and use only the printed number 7 on the pencil.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Chitra measures a ribbon on a ruler marked only in centimetres. The cut end sits between the $11\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $12\,\mathrm{cm}$ marks.

parts.text: Which claim correctly states how she should report the length more accurately?

options.text: Report $11\,\mathrm{cm}$, because the cut end has not reached $12\,\mathrm{cm}$.
Split the $1\,\mathrm{cm}$ gap into equal smaller parts and count how many the cut end passes.
Treat the printed $11$ on the ribbon spool as the measured length.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lila measures a crayon on a ruler marked only in centimetres. The tip sits between the $9\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $10\,\mathrm{cm}$ marks.

Which two claims correctly state how she should report the length more accurately?

options.A: Report $9\,\mathrm{cm}$, because the tip has not reached $10\,\mathrm{cm}$.
options.B: Split the $1\,\mathrm{cm}$ gap into equal smaller parts and count how many the tip passes.
options.C: Those equal smaller parts of the same centimetre interval let her name a length between $9\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $10\,\mathrm{cm}$.
options.D: Treat the printed $9$ on the crayon wrapper as the measured length.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Dev has a length of 3 tenths of a metre on a measuring strip marked in tenths and hundredths.

Which statement describes the same length?

options.A: The length is 3 hundredths of a metre.
options.B: The length is 3 thousandths of a metre, ignoring regrouping by tens.
options.C: The length is 30 hundredths of a metre, because ten hundredths make one tenth.
options.D: The length is 3 metres, because the strip shows the digit 3 most clearly.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Jatin measures a strip of tape as $4$ tenths of a metre on a scale marked in tenths and hundredths.

parts.text: Which claim correctly renames that length using hundredths?

options.text: The length is $4$ hundredths of a metre.
The length is $40$ hundredths of a metre.
The length is $4$ metres, because the digit $4$ is the clearest mark on the scale.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit pours $5$ tenths of a litre of oil into a bottle marked in tenths and hundredths.

Which statement describes the same amount of oil?

options.A: $5$ tenths of a litre is the same as $5$ hundredths of a litre.
options.B: $5$ tenths of a litre is the same as $50$ hundredths of a litre.
options.C: $5$ tenths of a litre is the same as $5$ thousandths of a litre.
options.D: $5$ tenths of a litre is the same as the printed $5$ on the bottle cap.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tara reads the length 3.142 m on a measuring strip marked with a decimal point.

Which statement correctly names the place of each digit?

options.A: The digit 3 is a tenth, because it sits next to the decimal point.
options.B: The length is 3142 m, because those digits are the largest printed string on the strip.
options.C: 3 is ones; 1 is tenths; 4 is hundredths; 2 is thousandths, with the decimal point separating whole-number places from fractional places.
options.D: Add the digits 3 + 1 + 4 + 2 by combining like place values to read the number.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Darsh writes the decimal $5.307$ on the board. He wants to name each digit by its place value around the decimal point.

parts.text: Which claim correctly names the places?

options.text: Call $5.307$ a whole-number label only, and stop naming places.
$5$ is ones; $3$ is tenths; $0$ is hundredths; $7$ is thousandths, with the decimal point separating whole-number places from fractional places.
Read $5307$ as the number, because those digits form the longest printed string.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice that uses the decimal point and place value.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bharti reads the mass $4.268\,\mathrm{kg}$ on a digital scale marked with a decimal point.

Which claim correctly names the place of each digit?

options.A: $4$ is ones, $2$ is tenths, $6$ is hundredths, and $8$ is thousandths.
options.B: $4$ is tenths, $2$ is hundredths, $6$ is thousandths, and $8$ is ones.
options.C: The answer is the decimal point, because that mark is the most obvious symbol on the scale.
options.D: $4$, $2$, $6$, and $8$ are combined by adding like place values as if the reading were a sum to find.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit measures a ribbon as $45$ millimetres long. He needs the length in centimetres. There are $10$ millimetres in $1$ centimetre.

Which conversion is correct?

options.A: Report the answer as "centimetre", naming the unit instead of writing the decimal length.
options.B: Say that centimetres are what produce millimetres, so he must invent $45$ mm from a finished centimetre reading.
options.C: $45$ mm $= 4.5$ cm, because each millimetre is $0.1$ of a centimetre.
options.D: Write $45$ cm, copying the printed digits $45$ without shifting by the $10$-to-$1$ place relation.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Tanya counts $280$ paise in a coin pouch. She needs the same amount written in rupees. There are $100$ paise in $1$ rupee.

parts.text: Which claim correctly converts the money?

options.text: Report the answer as the word paise, naming the smaller unit instead of writing a rupee amount.
Say that rupees are what produce paise, so she must invent $280$ paise from a finished rupee reading.
$280$ paise $= 2.80$ rupees, because each paise is $0.01$ of a rupee.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit weighs a bag of flour as $650$ grams. He needs the same mass in kilograms. There are $1000$ grams in $1$ kilogram.

Which conversion is correct?

options.A: The converted reading is the word kilogram.
options.C: $650\,\mathrm{g} = 0.65\,\mathrm{kg}$.
options.D: $650\,\mathrm{g} = 650\,\mathrm{kg}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Dev must mark $2.7$ on a number line that already shows the whole numbers $2$ and $3$.

How should he place $2.7$?

options.A: Answer "endpoint", naming that word instead of placing a mark between $2$ and $3$.
options.B: Say the finished mark is what creates the equal tenths between $2$ and $3$, instead of using those tenths to locate $2.7$.
options.C: Split the segment from $2$ to $3$ into $10$ equal tenths and count $7$ tenths from $2$ toward $3$.
options.D: Copy the printed digit $7$ and put the mark at $7$ on the number line, ignoring the interval from $2$ to $3$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows a number line from $3.0$ to $4.0$ with equal tenth marks. Yash must place point $P$ at $3.4$.

Which claim correctly places $P$?

options.A: $P$ is the left endpoint $3.0$, so rename the target as that endpoint.
options.B: Marking $P$ at $3.4$ is what creates the equal tenths between $3.0$ and $4.0$.
