Pihu multiplies $\frac{3}{4} \times \frac{5}{7}$.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: The product is the word denominator, with no multiplications done.
options.B: The new numerator is $3 \times 5 = 15$.
options.C: The new denominator is $4 \times 7 = 28$, so the product is $\frac{15}{28}$.
options.D: Report $7$ alone, because that numeral is printed last.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qasim multiplies $\frac{5}{6} \times \frac{2}{7}$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The product is the word denominator.
options.B: The new numerator is $5 \times 2 = 10$, and the denominator stays $6$.
options.C: $\frac{5 \times 2}{6 \times 7} = \frac{10}{42}$.
options.D: The product is the printed $7$ alone.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Hassan multiplies $\dfrac{4}{9} \times \dfrac{3}{8}$ and wants to cancel common factors before multiplying.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Cancel the two numerators $4$ and $3$ with each other, skipping that cancellation pairs a numerator with a denominator.
options.B: Say that writing the cancelled product is what creates the common factors in $\frac{4}{9}$ and $\frac{3}{8}$, instead of cancelling factors that are already there.
options.C: Cancel $4$ with $8$ and $3$ with $9$ first: $\dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{6}$.
options.D: Use the same cancellation steps when adding $\frac{4}{9}$ and $\frac{3}{8}$, beyond this fraction-product hinge.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Rudra multiplies $\dfrac{6}{35} \times \dfrac{14}{9}$ and wants to cancel common factors before multiplying.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: Multiply $6 \times 14$ and $35 \times 9$ first, and leave every common factor uncancelled.
options.B: Cancel a common factor $7$ between $14$ and $35$, leaving $\dfrac{6}{5} \times \dfrac{2}{9}$.
options.C: Cancel a common factor $3$ between $6$ and $9$, leaving $\dfrac{2}{5} \times \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{4}{15}$.
options.D: Treat the product as a sum of the two fractions instead of a product.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qasim multiplies $\dfrac{8}{15} \times \dfrac{5}{12}$ and wants to cancel common factors before multiplying.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Multiply $8 \times 5$ and $15 \times 12$ first, leaving every common factor uncancelled.
options.B: Cancelling is what creates the common factors $5$ and $4$ in the product.
options.C: Cancel $5$ between $5$ and $15$, and cancel $4$ between $8$ and $12$, then multiply to get $\dfrac{2}{9}$.
options.D: Cancel a common factor between the two numerators $8$ and $5$ before multiplying.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit multiplies $8 \times 0.25$ and wants to predict the size of the product before finishing the calculation.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Say the product is less than $8$ after looking only at $8$, skipping whether the other factor is between $0$ and $1$ or greater than $1$.
options.B: Use the same greater-than / less-than rule for a product that includes a negative factor, beyond positive factors.
options.C: Because $0.25$ is between $0$ and $1$, the product is less than $8$ (and greater than $0$).
options.D: Choose "greater than $8$" only because $8$ is the larger printed factor in $8 \times 0.25$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Ishan multiplies $6 \times 0.4$ and wants to predict the size of the product before finishing.

parts.text: Which claim correctly predicts how $6 \times 0.4$ compares with $6$?

options.text: The product is greater than $6$, because both factors are positive.
The product is less than $6$, because one factor is between $0$ and $1$.
The product equals $6$, because the printed digits $6$ and $4$ look close on the page.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Pallavi multiplies $9 \times 0.3$ and wants to predict the size of the product before finishing the calculation.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Because $0.3$ is between $0$ and $1$, the product is less than $9$.
options.B: The product is greater than both $9$ and $0.3$.
options.C: The product is less than $9$ even when one factor is negative.
options.D: The product is $9$, because $9$ is the larger printed factor in $9 \times 0.3$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Xavier multiplies $\dfrac{2}{5}\times\dfrac{3}{7}$ and then $\dfrac{3}{7}\times\dfrac{2}{5}$. He asks whether the products differ.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call both products "fraction factors" only, without comparing the effect of changing factor order.
options.B: Say that writing the same product is what creates the two factor orders, instead of the order change leaving the product unchanged.
options.C: The products are equal: $\dfrac{2}{5}\times\dfrac{3}{7}=\dfrac{3}{7}\times\dfrac{2}{5}=\dfrac{6}{35}$.
options.D: Report $\dfrac{2}{5}$ as the product only because $\dfrac{2}{5}$ is the first printed fraction in the stem.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sia multiplies $\dfrac{2}{3}$ by $\dfrac{5}{7}$.

Which claim about the product is correct?

options.A: Call the answer fraction factors, and stop with no product written.
options.B: Writing $\dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{5}{7}$ is what creates the order of the factors.
options.C: $\dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{5}{7} = \dfrac{5}{7} \times \dfrac{2}{3}$, because the order of the factors does not change the product.
options.D: The product equals $\dfrac{2}{3}$, because $2$ and $3$ are the first numerals printed.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Pallavi multiplies $\dfrac{3}{8}\times\dfrac{4}{5}$ and then $\dfrac{4}{5}\times\dfrac{3}{8}$. She asks whether the products differ.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: $\dfrac{3}{8}\times\dfrac{4}{5}=\dfrac{4}{5}\times\dfrac{3}{8}$, because the order of the factors does not change the product.
options.B: The answer is the phrase fraction factors, with no product compared.
options.C: Writing the products is what creates the order of the two factors.
options.D: The product equals $\dfrac{3}{8}$, because $3$ and $8$ are the first numerals printed.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Padma works out \(\dfrac{3}{4} \div \dfrac{2}{5}\).

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Multiply \(\dfrac{3}{4}\) by \(\dfrac{2}{5}\).
options.B: The divisor is what the dividend produces, so write \(\dfrac{2}{5} \div \dfrac{3}{4}\).
options.C: Multiply \(\dfrac{3}{4}\) by the reciprocal \(\dfrac{5}{2}\).
options.D: Treat division of fractions like commutative multiplication, so \(\dfrac{2}{5} \div \dfrac{3}{4}\) equals the original.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sameer must compute $\dfrac{3}{4} \div \dfrac{2}{5}$.

Which two claims correctly carry out the division?

options.A: Keep $\dfrac{3}{4}$ and multiply by $\dfrac{2}{5}$ directly, with no reciprocal of the divisor.
options.B: Replace the divisor $\dfrac{2}{5}$ by its reciprocal $\dfrac{5}{2}$, then multiply $\dfrac{3}{4} \times \dfrac{5}{2}$.
options.C: The product is $\dfrac{15}{8}$, which equals $\dfrac{3}{4} \div \dfrac{2}{5}$.
options.D: Say the reciprocal $\dfrac{5}{2}$ is what creates the original divisor $\dfrac{2}{5}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Divya writes division for two milk problems.
Problem 1: Share $\frac{3}{4}$ litre equally among 3 cups.
Problem 2: How many $\frac{1}{8}$ litre servings are in $\frac{3}{4}$ litre?

Which expressions are correct? Two options are correct.

options.A: Problem 1 is $\frac{3}{4} \div 3$.
options.B: Problem 1 is $3 \div \frac{3}{4}$.
options.C: Problem 2 is $\frac{3}{4} \div \frac{1}{8}$.
options.D: Problem 2 is $\frac{3}{4} \times \frac{1}{8}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Vihaan writes division for two juice problems.
Problem 1: Share $\frac{2}{3}$ litre equally among 4 cups.
Problem 2: How many $\frac{1}{6}$ litre servings are in $\frac{2}{3}$ litre?

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: Problem 1 is answered by the phrase total amount, not by a division expression.
options.B: Problem 1 is $\frac{2}{3} \div 4$.
options.C: Problem 2 is $\frac{2}{3} \div \frac{1}{6}$.
options.D: The division expressions are what create the sharing and serving stories.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Poonam will compute $18 \div 0.6$. Before calculating, she wants to predict how the quotient compares with the dividend $18$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The quotient is less than $18$ whenever a division is written, even for divisor $0.6$.
options.B: The divisor $0.6$ is produced by the dividend $18$, so the size comparison runs from quotient back to $0.6$.
options.C: Because the divisor $0.6$ is between $0$ and $1$, the quotient is greater than the dividend $18$.
options.D: The same size rule also settles the comparison when the divisor is negative.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Meher divides the positive length $12$ by a positive divisor. She wants to know whether the quotient is greater or less than $12$ from the size of the divisor alone.

parts.text: Which claim correctly predicts the quotient compared with $12$?

options.text: If the divisor is $4$, the quotient is less than $12$; if the divisor is $\dfrac{1}{2}$, the quotient is greater than $12$.
Every positive divisor makes the quotient less than $12$.
Every positive divisor makes the quotient greater than $12$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Farhan starts with a full bottle. He pours out $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of the bottle, then pours out $\dfrac{1}{3}$ of what remains.

Which claim correctly tracks the amounts?

options.A: After the first pour, $\dfrac{3}{4}$ remains; $\dfrac{1}{3}$ of that remaining is $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of the bottle, so $\dfrac{1}{2}$ of the bottle is left.
options.B: He pours $\dfrac{1}{4}$ and then $\dfrac{1}{3}$ of the original bottle, so $\dfrac{7}{12}$ is poured in total.
options.C: The second pour uses $\dfrac{1}{3}$ of the original, and that step creates the remaining $\dfrac{3}{4}$.
options.D: The two pour fractions multiply to make the remaining amount, so the bottle ends with $\dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{1}{12}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Aarav starts with a full bottle. He pours out $\dfrac{1}{5}$ of the bottle, then pours out $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of what remains.

parts.text: Which claim correctly tracks the amount poured the second time?

options.text: The second pour is $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of the original full bottle.
After the first pour, $\dfrac{4}{5}$ remains; the second pour is $\dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{4}{5} = \dfrac{1}{5}$ of the original.
The remaining part produces the original whole, so the second pour is $\dfrac{1}{4} \div \dfrac{4}{5}$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Rehan's school has two taps on the same tank. Tap A alone fills the tank in $4$ days. Tap B alone fills the tank in $12$ days. Both taps run together on that tank.

Which claim correctly finds how long they take together?

options.A: The answer is the one-day rate itself, reported as the filling time.
options.B: Add the filling times to get $4 + 12 = 16$ days.
options.C: The one-day rates are $\dfrac{1}{4}$ and $\dfrac{1}{12}$; together $\dfrac{1}{3}$ of the tank fills per day, so the tank fills in $3$ days.
options.D: Adding the one-day rates also gives the fill time when Tap A runs alone for some days and then Tap B runs alone afterward.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Ishaan's school has two taps on the same tank. Tap A alone fills the tank in $6$ days. Tap B alone fills the tank in $3$ days. Both taps run together on that tank.

parts.text: Which claim correctly finds how long they take together?

options.text: Add the days: $6+3=9$ days together.
Convert to one-day rates $\dfrac{1}{6}$ and $\dfrac{1}{3}$, add the rates, then convert the combined rate back to days.
Use only Tap B's $3$ days, because $3$ is smaller.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qadir has two paper triangles of the same shape and size. One fits exactly over the other after he flips it.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: They are congruent only if he does not flip or rotate either triangle.
options.B: They are congruent: exact copies under superimposition, and flipping is allowed.
options.C: Same shape alone is enough for congruence even when the sizes differ.
options.D: Congruence here requires a right angle, hypotenuse, and one matching side before he can decide.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Feroz studies the diagram of figures $F$ and $G$. Figure $G$ is the same shape and size as figure $F$, and $G$ is shown after a flip.

Which claim correctly decides whether $F$ and $G$ are congruent?

options.A: $F$ and $G$ are congruent: same shape and size under exact superimposition, and flipping is allowed.
options.B: $F$ and $G$ are congruent because they are both called figures on the page.
options.C: Exact fit under superimposition is needed only after congruence is already known.
options.D: Congruence here requires a right angle, hypotenuse, and one matching side before the flip can be used.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lila studies the diagram of figures $R$ and $S$. Figure $S$ is the same shape and size as figure $R$, and $S$ is shown after a turn.

Which two claims correctly decide whether $R$ and $S$ are congruent?

options.A: $R$ and $S$ are congruent: same shape and size under exact superimposition, and turning is allowed.
options.B: $R$ and $S$ are congruent because they are both called figures on the page.
options.C: Exact fit under superimposition settles congruence, and a turn does not block that fit.
options.D: Congruence here requires a right angle, hypotenuse, and one matching side before the turn can be used.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Indira has triangles PQR and XYZ. She knows PQ = XY, QR = YZ, and RP = ZX. She asks whether equal corresponding side lengths are enough for congruence.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The triangles are congruent: three corresponding equal side lengths are enough.
options.B: Equal side lengths are produced only after congruence is already known, so sides cannot settle it.
options.C: She also needs a matching angle between two of those sides before she can decide.
options.D: Same shape alone is enough even when the three side lengths do not match.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Pranav studies the diagram of triangles $PQR$ and $XYZ$. Matching tick marks show $PQ=XY$, $QR=YZ$, and $RP=ZX$.

Which claim correctly decides congruence from those side lengths?

options.A: The triangles are congruent: three corresponding equal side lengths are enough.
options.B: Equal side lengths appear only after congruence is already known, so sides cannot settle it.
options.C: An included matching angle between two of those sides is also required before congruence can be decided.
options.D: Same shape alone is enough even when the three side lengths do not match.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Rachna studies the diagram of triangles $DEF$ and $LMN$. Matching tick marks show $DE = LM$, $EF = MN$, and $FD = NL$.

Which claim correctly decides congruence from those side lengths?

options.A: The three matching side lengths are enough: triangles $DEF$ and $LMN$ are congruent by SSS.
options.B: The triangles are congruent because each figure is called a triangle.
options.C: Congruence here also needs a right angle and hypotenuse before the side lengths can be used.
options.D: Matching side lengths are what the congruence statement creates after the triangles are already named congruent.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Asha writes △ABC ≅ △DEF. She needs the side that corresponds to side AB.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Any side that looks the same length as AB corresponds, whatever the vertex order.
options.B: Correspondence still holds even when the vertex order does not make equal sides overlap.
options.C: A non-corresponding angle that looks equal to angle A settles which side matches AB.
options.D: Side DE corresponds to AB, because A matches D and B matches E in the congruence statement.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lochan looks at the diagram. The marking shows $\triangle PQR \cong \triangle XYZ$.

Which claim correctly names the side that corresponds to side $PQ$?

options.A: Side $PQ$ corresponds to side $XY$.
options.B: Side $PQ$ corresponds to side $YZ$.
options.C: Side $PQ$ corresponds to side $PR$.
options.D: Side $PQ$ corresponds to side $XZ$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Hina looks at the diagram. The marking shows $\triangle LMN \cong \triangle RST$.

Which claim correctly names the side that corresponds to side $LM$?

options.A: Side $LM$ corresponds to side $RS$.
options.B: Side $LM$ corresponds to side $ST$.
options.C: Side $LM$ corresponds to side $LN$.
options.D: Side $LM$ corresponds to side $RT$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qadir has two triangles. Each angle of the first equals the matching angle of the second, but one triangle has sides twice as long as the other.

Are the triangles congruent?

options.A: Yes: they are the same shape, and same shape means congruent.
options.B: Yes: the matching equal angles alone settle congruence.
options.C: No: equal angles give the same shape, but different sizes mean the triangles need not be congruent.
options.D: Yes, because the printed word twice is the standout cue in the stem.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gaurav studies the diagram of triangles $PQR$ and $XYZ$. Each angle of $PQR$ equals the matching angle of $XYZ$, but the sides of $XYZ$ are longer.

Which claim correctly decides whether the triangles are congruent?

options.A: Yes: they are the same shape, and same shape means congruent.
options.B: Yes: the matching equal angles alone settle congruence.
options.C: No: equal angles give the same shape, but different sizes mean the triangles need not be congruent.
options.D: Yes, because the printed degree marks are the standout cue in the diagram.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Rachna studies the diagram of triangles $DEF$ and $LMN$. Each angle of $DEF$ equals the matching angle of $LMN$, but the sides of $LMN$ are longer.

Which claim correctly decides whether the triangles are congruent?

options.A: The triangles are not congruent: equal angles give the same shape, but different sizes mean they need not be congruent.
options.B: The triangles are congruent because they have the same shape.
options.C: The triangles are congruent from the equal angles alone.
options.D: The triangles are congruent because the printed angle marks match.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Indira compares $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DEF$. She knows $AB = DE$, $AC = DF$, and $\angle A = \angle D$ with $\angle A$ between sides $AB$ and $AC$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Claim the triangles are congruent from $AB = DE$ and $AC = DF$ alone, skipping that the equal angle must be the included angle.
options.B: Say that congruence is what creates the two equal sides and the equal included angle.
options.C: The triangles are congruent by SAS: two sides and the included angle match.
options.D: Claim congruence from two sides and a non-included angle (SSA) as if that were enough.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows $\triangle PQR$ and $\triangle XYZ$. In both triangles the sides $6\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $4\,\mathrm{cm}$ meet at a $70^{\circ}$ angle.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The triangles are congruent from the two equal side lengths alone.
options.B: Congruence is what creates the two equal sides and the equal included angle.
options.C: The triangles are congruent by SAS: two sides and the included angle match.
options.D: Two sides and a non-included angle are enough for congruence here.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: The diagram shows $\triangle DEF$ and $\triangle GHI$. In both triangles the sides $7\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $5\,\mathrm{cm}$ meet at a $65^{\circ}$ angle.

parts.text: Which claim correctly decides whether the triangles are congruent?

options.text: The triangles are congruent from the two equal side lengths alone.
The triangles are congruent by SAS: two sides and the included angle match.
Two sides and a non-included angle are enough for congruence here.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Rina compares two triangles that share two pairs of equal corresponding sides and one pair of equal corresponding angles that is not between those sides.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Conclude the triangles must be congruent from those matches alone, skipping that the equal angle is not the included angle.
options.B: Treat that side-side-angle match as a congruence test for every polygon, not only as a failed triangle test.
options.C: Those matches do not always guarantee congruence; the same data can fit two non-congruent triangles.
options.D: Claim congruence only because the word equal is repeated often in the stem.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows $\triangle PQR$ and $\triangle XYZ$. Each triangle has sides $7\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $5\,\mathrm{cm}$ and a $40^{\circ}$ angle that is not between those two sides.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The matching sides and non-included angle do not always make the triangles congruent.
options.B: The triangles are congruent from the two equal side lengths alone.
options.C: SSA is a congruence rule that covers every triangle pair with those matching parts.
options.D: The triangles are congruent because $40$ is the standout printed number in the diagram.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: The diagram shows $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DEF$. Each triangle has sides $6\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $4\,\mathrm{cm}$ and a $35^{\circ}$ angle that is not between those two sides.

parts.text: Which claim is correct?

options.text: The matching sides and non-included angle do not always make the triangles congruent.
The triangles are congruent from the two equal side lengths alone.
SSA is a congruence rule that covers every triangle pair with those matching parts.
The triangles are congruent because $35$ is the standout printed number in the diagram.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Parul has $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DEF$. She knows $\angle A=\angle D$, $\angle B=\angle E$, and side $AB=DE$ lies between those equal angles in each triangle.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Conclude congruence from $\angle A=\angle D$ and $\angle B=\angle E$ alone, without using the included side $AB=DE$.
options.B: Say that naming the triangles congruent is what creates the two equal angles and the included equal side, instead of using ASA to conclude congruence.
options.C: The triangles are congruent by ASA: two angles and the included side $AB=DE$ match the corresponding two angles and included side.
options.D: Also conclude congruence from three equal angles with no side given, as if angle-only data were enough.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Meher studies the diagram of $\triangle PQR$ and $\triangle XYZ$. Marked arcs show $\angle P=\angle X$ and $\angle Q=\angle Y$, and the included sides $PQ$ and $XY$ have matching ticks.

Which claim correctly decides congruence from that information?

options.A: The triangles are congruent from the two angle pairs alone, even if the equal sides are not between those angles.
options.B: Congruence of the triangles is what creates the equal angles and the included equal sides.
options.C: The triangles are congruent by ASA: two angles and the included side match.
options.D: The triangles are congruent from any two angles with any third side, including a non-included side.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qasim has $\triangle LMN$ and $\triangle RST$. He knows $\angle L=\angle R$, $\angle M=\angle S$, and side $LM=RS$ lies between those equal angles in each triangle.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims correctly decide congruence from that information?

options.A: The triangles are congruent by ASA: two angles and the included side $LM=RS$ match.
options.B: The triangles are congruent from $\angle L=\angle R$ and $\angle M=\angle S$ alone.
options.C: Side $LM$ lies between $\angle L$ and $\angle M$, matching included side $RS$ between $\angle R$ and $\angle S$.
options.D: Congruence of the triangles is what creates the equal angles and the included equal sides.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri compares triangles DEF and XYZ. Angle D equals angle X, angle E equals angle Y, and side DF equals side XZ. Side DF is not between angles D and E, and side XZ is not between angles X and Y.

Which claim correctly decides whether the triangles are congruent?

options.A: The triangles are congruent because DF equals XZ.
options.B: The equal non-included sides are what produce the two pairs of equal angles.
options.C: The third angles are equal by the angle sum, so the triangles satisfy ASA and are congruent.
options.D: The triangles are congruent because DF and XZ are the longest printed lengths in the list.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows $\triangle PQR$ and $\triangle XYZ$. In both triangles $\angle P = \angle X = 40^{\circ}$ and $\angle Q = \angle Y = 70^{\circ}$, and $QR = YZ = 6\,\mathrm{cm}$ is a corresponding side that does not lie between those two angles.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The triangles are congruent by AAS: the third angles are each $70^{\circ}$ by the angle sum, so two angles and a non-included corresponding side match.
options.B: Call the answer non-included side, and stop with no congruence decision.
options.C: The non-included side $QR = YZ$ is what produces the $40^{\circ}$ and $70^{\circ}$ angles.
options.D: The triangles are congruent because the three corresponding side lengths are equal.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qasim compares $\triangle LMN$ and $\triangle STU$. Angle $L$ equals angle $S$, angle $M$ equals angle $T$, and side $LN$ equals side $SU$. Side $LN$ is not between angles $L$ and $M$, and side $SU$ is not between angles $S$ and $T$.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims correctly decide congruence?

options.A: The third angles are equal by the $180^{\circ}$ angle sum, so the triangles satisfy ASA and are congruent.
options.B: Two equal angles and a matching non-included side are enough to guarantee congruence for these triangles.
options.C: The triangles are congruent because $LN$ equals $SU$ alone.
options.D: The equal non-included sides are what produce the two pairs of equal angles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Triangles $PQR$ and $XYZ$ are right-angled at $Q$ and $Y$. Hypotenuse $PR=XZ$, and leg $PQ=XY$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The triangles are congruent even if one of them is not right-angled.
options.B: The same three matching pieces also guarantee congruence for two non-right triangles under SSA.
options.C: The triangles are congruent by RHS: right angle, hypotenuse, and one corresponding leg.
options.D: The triangles are congruent because the letters $P,Q,R$ and $X,Y,Z$ look alike.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ritu studies the diagram of right-angled triangles $PQR$ and $XYZ$, each with a right angle marked. The hypotenuses $QR$ and $YZ$ are equal, and legs $PQ$ and $XY$ are equal.

Which claim correctly decides congruence?

options.A: Call the triangles congruent even when either triangle need not be right-angled.
options.B: Say the same RHS match also settles congruence for non-right SSA pairs in general.
options.C: The triangles are congruent by RHS: right angle, equal hypotenuses, and one equal corresponding leg.
options.D: Require two equal angles and the included side (ASA) before congruence can be decided here.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Rohan knows $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF$ with correspondence $A \leftrightarrow D$, $B \leftrightarrow E$, $C \leftrightarrow F$. Side $AB$ equals side $DE$, and $\angle BAC$ equals $\angle EDF$.

Which claim correctly uses the congruence?

options.A: $\angle ABC$ equals $\angle DFE$, matching $B$ with $F$.
options.B: Side $BC$ equals side $EF$, as corresponding sides under $A \leftrightarrow D$, $B \leftrightarrow E$, $C \leftrightarrow F$.
options.C: Congruence of the triangles is enough even if the vertex matching is ignored.
options.D: Only sides can be equal from congruence; angles need a separate rule.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: The diagram shows isosceles triangle PQR with $PR = QR$ and midpoint M of base PQ. Rohan has already shown $\triangle PRM \cong \triangle QRM$.

parts.text: Which claim correctly uses that congruence?

options.text: Corresponding parts are equal, so $\angle PRM = \angle QRM$.
Equal angles at R are what create the congruence of $\triangle PRM$ and $\triangle QRM$.
Congruence applies to every triangle pair in the figure, including ones that were not matched.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows lines $PQ$ and $RS$ cut by transversal $AC$. Triangles $PAC$ and $RCA$ are congruent, and that congruence makes a pair of alternate interior angles equal.

Which claim correctly concludes that $PQ \parallel RS$?

options.A: Because the congruent triangles give equal alternate interior angles for transversal $AC$, lines $PQ$ and $RS$ are parallel.
options.B: Report the words alternate interior angles as the names of lines $PQ$ and $RS$.
options.C: The triangles are congruent, so $PQ \parallel RS$ even when no alternate interior angles are used.
options.D: Equal side lengths in the triangles alone prove $PQ \parallel RS$, with no equal alternate interior angles needed.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows lines $PQ$ and $RS$ cut by transversal $AC$. Triangles $PAC$ and $RCA$ are congruent, and that congruence makes one pair of alternate interior angles equal.

Which claim correctly concludes that $PQ \parallel RS$?

options.A: $PQ \parallel RS$, because the congruent triangles make a pair of alternate interior angles equal for transversal $AC$.
options.B: Lines $PQ$ and $RS$ are the alternate interior angles on transversal $AC$.
options.C: $PQ \parallel RS$, because the triangles are congruent, even when those alternate interior angles are unequal.
options.D: $PQ \parallel RS$, because matching sides of the triangles are equal, and equal sides alone settle parallelism.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Uma needs an ordered pair of numbers whose sum is 10 and whose difference (first minus second) is 4.

Which ordered pair is correct?

options.B: The second number 3 alone, without a first number.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Adeel needs an ordered pair of numbers whose sum is $15$ and whose difference (first minus second) is $3$.

parts.text: Which ordered pair satisfies both conditions?
Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Pranav needs an ordered pair of numbers whose sum is $18$ and whose difference (first minus second) is $4$.

Which ordered pair is correct?

options.B: The second number $7$ alone, with no first number.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nalini stands at $0$ on a number line. She first walks $4$ steps to the right, then $6$ steps to the left. She must mark each movement before she computes.

Which marking is correct?

options.A: Mark $0$ as the movement, and ignore direction.
options.B: Write the sizes $4$ and $6$ only, without signs from direction.
options.C: Mark $+4$ for the rightward walk and $-6$ for the leftward walk.
options.D: Find the final position first by an unsigned total, then invent signs afterwards.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Misha stands at $0$ on a number line. She walks $5$ steps to the right, then $3$ steps to the left. She must mark each movement before she computes.

parts.text: Which marking correctly records the signs from direction?

options.text: Mark $0$ as the movement, and ignore direction.
Mark $+5$ for the rightward walk and $-3$ for the leftward walk.
Write the sizes $5$ and $3$ only, with no signs from direction.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sagar stands at $0$ on a number line. He first walks $7$ steps to the right, then $2$ steps to the left. He must mark each movement before he computes.

Which marking is correct?

options.A: Right $7$ as $+7$, then left $2$ as $-2$.
options.B: Right $7$ as the mark $0$, then left $2$ as the mark $0$.
options.C: Both movements as $7$ and $2$ with no signs.
options.D: Both movements as $+7$ and $+2$, because every walk starts from $0$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ekta starts at $0$ on a number line. She moves $5$ steps to the right, then $8$ steps to the left. The movements are already written as $+5$ and $-8$.

What is her final position?

options.A: Add the sizes $5$ and $8$ only, without using the signs that encode direction.
options.B: Treat $-8$ as what produces $+5$, and reverse the order of the two movements as a rule.
options.C: $-3$, because the final position is $(+5) + (-8)$.
options.D: First invent signs from a finished unsigned total, instead of adding the signed movements she already has.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Amaya starts at $0$ on a number line. She moves $4$ steps to the right, then $7$ steps to the left. The movements are written as $+4$ and $-7$.

parts.text: Which claim correctly gives her final position?

options.text: Her final position is $+4$, from the first movement alone.
Her final position is $+11$, from adding $4$ and $7$ as unsigned lengths.
Her final position is $-3$, from $0 + 4 + (-7)$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice that uses the signed movements.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Iqbal starts at $0$ on a number line. He moves $6$ steps to the right, then $9$ steps to the left. The movements are already written as $+6$ and $-9$.

parts.text: What is his final position?
Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Uma models integers with tokens. She has $2$ positive tokens and must subtract $3$ positive tokens.

Which move lets her complete the subtraction?

options.A: Rename her $2$ positive tokens as negative tokens, and remove nothing.
options.B: Try to remove $3$ positive tokens at once, skipping any zero pairs, even though only $2$ positive tokens are present.
options.C: Add one zero pair (one positive and one negative token), then remove $3$ positive tokens; $1$ negative token remains.
options.D: Say the finished difference is what creates the need for zero pairs, instead of adding zero pairs before removal.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Ishita models integers with tokens. She has $3$ positive tokens and must subtract $5$ positive tokens.

parts.text: Which move lets her complete the subtraction?

options.text: Rename her $3$ positive tokens as negative tokens, and remove nothing.
Add two zero pairs (each one positive and one negative token), then remove $5$ positive tokens; $2$ negative tokens remain.
Try to remove $5$ positive tokens at once even though only $3$ positive tokens are present, and add no zero pairs.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sagar models integers with tokens. He has $4$ positive tokens and must subtract $6$ positive tokens.

Which move lets him complete the subtraction?

options.A: The finished difference is the label negative tokens.
options.B: Remove $6$ positive tokens from the $4$ he has.
options.C: Add $2$ zero pairs, then remove $6$ positive tokens; $2$ negative tokens remain.
options.D: The finished difference is what creates the need for zero pairs.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nalini must rewrite $9-(-5)$ by replacing subtraction with addition of an additive inverse.

Which rewrite is correct?

options.A: Call the step addition only, without stating which integer is replaced by its additive inverse.
options.B: Write $9-(-5)=(-9)+(-5)$, applying the inverse to the first integer instead of the subtrahend.
options.C: Write $9-(-5)=9+(+5)$, because subtracting $-5$ is adding the additive inverse of $-5$.
options.D: Say that writing $9+(+5)$ is what creates the original expression $9-(-5)$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Arnav rewrites $8 - (-3)$ by replacing subtraction with addition of an additive inverse.

parts.text: Which rewrite is correct?

options.text: $8 - (-3) = (-8) + (-3)$, applying the inverse to the first integer.
$8 - (-3) = 8 + (+3)$, because subtracting $-3$ is adding the additive inverse of $-3$.
Call the step addition only, with no inverse stated.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sagar must rewrite $12-(-4)$ by replacing subtraction with addition of an additive inverse.

Which rewrite is correct?

options.A: Call the step addition only, with no inverse stated.
options.B: $12-(-4)=(-12)+(-4)$, applying the inverse to the first integer.
options.C: $12-(-4)=12+(+4)$, because subtracting $-4$ is adding the additive inverse of $-4$.
options.D: Writing $12+(+4)$ is what creates the original expression $12-(-4)$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Veena models $(-3)\times(+4)$ with a token bag that starts empty. Positive tokens are $+1$ and negative tokens are $-1$.

Which interpretation is correct?

options.A: Call the answer multiplicand only, without saying whether the multiplier places or removes tokens.
options.B: Remove four groups of three positive tokens even though the multiplier is negative and the multiplicand is $+4$, skipping the signed roles.
options.C: The negative multiplier removes the multiplicand's tokens repeatedly: remove $3$ groups of four $+1$ tokens (using zero pairs as needed), matching $(-3)\times(+4)$.
options.D: Also treat the same bag moves as settling how to add $(-3)+(+4)$ on a number line, beyond this multiplication model.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Avni models $(-3)\times(+4)$ with a token bag that starts empty. Positive tokens are $+1$ and negative tokens are $-1$.

parts.text: Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Call the model the word bag only, with no tokens placed or removed.
Place three negative tokens, and do that placing four times, for twelve negative tokens in all.
Place three negative tokens four times even when the bag is not allowed to hold negative tokens.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sagar models $(+4)\times(-2)$ with a token bag that starts empty. Positive tokens are $+1$ and negative tokens are $-1$.

Which interpretation is correct?

options.A: Treat $-2$ as the repeat count, and place four positive tokens twice.
options.B: Begin with eight negative tokens already in the bag, then multiply.
options.C: Place two negative tokens into the bag, four times.
options.D: The product is $-8$ from the sign rule alone, with no tokens placed or removed.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tanya must find $(-6)\times(+4)$ from signs and magnitudes.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the answer product only, without using the magnitudes $6$ and $4$ and the opposite signs.
options.B: Multiply the magnitudes to get $24$, but omit the opposite-sign rule and leave the product unsigned.
options.C: The magnitude is $6\times4=24$ and the signs differ, so $(-6)\times(+4)=-24$.
options.D: Choose $-6$ as the product only because $-6$ is the first printed factor among $-6$ and $+4$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Rohan must find $(-5)\times(+3)$ from the signs and magnitudes of the two factors.

Which two claims correctly determine the product?

options.A: Call $+3$ the multiplier label alone, and stop before combining signs with magnitudes.
options.B: The magnitude is $5\times 3=15$.
options.C: Different signs give a negative product, so $(-5)\times(+3)=-15$.
options.D: The answer is $-15$ because the printed $-5$ is the largest-looking mark on the page.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Rachna must find $(-7)\times(+5)$ from the signs and magnitudes of the two factors.

parts.text: What is the product?
Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Varun multiplies integers by 1 or by $-1$.

Which claim is always true?

options.D: $1 \times (-7) = -7$ only when a minus sign is printed next to 7.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anaya multiplies any integer $a$ by $1$ or by $-1$.

Which two claims are always true?

options.A: Call the answer $-1$, and stop with no product stated for either factor.
options.B: $1 \times a = a$ for every integer $a$.
options.C: $-1 \times a = -a$, where $-a$ is the additive inverse of $a$.
options.D: $-1 \times a = a$, because the printed numeral $1$ is kept and the minus is dropped.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Rachna multiplies any integer $a$ by $1$ or by $-1$ on her number line practice sheet.

parts.text: Which claim is always true for every integer $a$?

options.text: $1\times a=a$ and $-1\times a=-a$, where $-a$ is the additive inverse of $a$.
The answer is the factor $-1$, with no product stated.
$-1\times a=a$, because the printed numeral $1$ is kept and the minus is dropped.
$-1\times a=-a$ only when $a$ is already positive.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Shreya multiplies \((-3) \times 4 \times (-5)\).

Which claims keep the same product? One or more options may be correct.

options.A: Report the word product as the value of the calculation.
options.B: \((-3) \times 4 \times (-5) = 4 \times (-3) \times (-5)\).
options.C: \((-3) \times \bigl(4 \times (-5)\bigr) = \bigl((-3) \times 4\bigr) \times (-5)\).
options.D: The factors are −3, 4 and −5, so the product equals −3 because that is the first printed number.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Neil multiplies the integers $(-2) \times (-3) \times 4$.

parts.text: Which claim correctly states what regrouping or reordering does to the product?

options.text: Call the answer the product alone, with no check that the factors stay the same integers.
$(-2) \times \bigl((-3) \times 4\bigr)$ and $\bigl((-2) \times (-3)\bigr) \times 4$ both equal $24$, and any order of these factors keeps that product.
Treat the product as unchanged even when the factors are no longer these integers.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Isha's game score starts at $0$. She gains $5$ points on each of $3$ turns and loses $4$ points on each of $2$ turns.

Which expression gives her final score?

options.B: $3 \times (-5) + 2 \times (+4)$
options.C: $3 \times (+5) + 2 \times (-4)$
options.D: $3 \times (+4) + 2 \times (-5)$

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nitya's game score starts at $0$. She gains $8$ points on each of $3$ turns and loses $5$ points on each of $2$ turns.

Which expression gives her final score?

options.A: Write gains and losses as the labels score words, not as signed numbers in a sum.
options.B: Because the final score is known, it produces the signed turn values $3 \times (+8)$ and $2 \times (-5)$.
options.D: Add the turn counts only: $3 + 2$, treating counts as if they already carried the point values.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ananya asks what integer $q$ satisfies $(-4) \times q = -36$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: $q = 9$, and that $q$ is $(-36) \div (-4)$.
options.B: $q = -9$, because the product $(-4) \times q$ must be negative.
options.C: Division asks for $q$ in $q \div (-4) = -36$, so reverse the missing-factor layout.
options.D: $q = 144$, from writing $(-4) \times q$ as adding the absolute values.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Neil asks what integer $q$ satisfies $(-6)\times q = 42$.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: $q = 7$, because the product $42$ is positive so the missing factor must be positive.
options.C: Division finds the missing factor in $(-6)\times q = 42$, so $q = 42\div(-6) = -7$.
options.D: Division asks for $q$ in $q\div(-6) = 42$, reversing the missing-factor layout.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gopal multiplies $(-2)\times 3\times(-5)\times(-1)$.

Which two claims about the sign of this product are correct?

options.A: The product is negative because the factor 3 is odd.
options.B: The product is negative because there are three negative factors.
options.C: The product equals $-30$.
options.D: The product is positive because there are three negative factors.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Diya multiplies $(-3) \times 2 \times (-4) \times (-1)$.

Which claim about the sign of the product is correct?

options.A: The product is called a positive product because a product is being formed.
options.B: Negative signs pair away, so three negative factors still leave a positive product.
options.C: Three negative factors give a negative product.
options.D: The product is negative because $-3$ is the first factor written.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Asha rewrites the product $7\times(12+5)$.

Which claim is correct?

options.C: $7\times(12+5)=7\times12+7\times5$.
options.D: $7\times(12+5)=7\times12\times7\times5$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kavya rewrites the product $6\times(9+4)$.

Which two claims correctly use the distributive property?

options.A: Call the answer the sum $9+4$ alone.
options.B: $6\times(9+4)=6\times 9+6\times 4$.
options.C: Expanding gives $54+24$, which equals $78$, matching $6\times 13$.
options.D: Distribution means $6\times 9+4$, keeping the $4$ outside the product.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Jatin has two ribbons of lengths 18 cm and 24 cm. He wants to cut both into pieces of the same whole-number length, using the largest possible piece length with no ribbon left over.

What should he find?

options.A: A common multiple of 18 and 24.
options.B: Any common factor of 18 and 24, even if a larger one also fits.
options.C: The highest common factor of 18 and 24.
options.D: The sum of 18 and 24.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Pranav has two ropes of lengths $36\,\mathrm{m}$ and $48\,\mathrm{m}$. He wants to cut both into pieces of the same whole-number length, using the largest possible piece length with no rope left over.

Which two claims correctly state what he should find and why?

options.A: Find a common multiple of $36$ and $48$.
options.B: Find the highest common factor of $36$ and $48$.
options.C: The largest equal piece length that divides both $36$ and $48$ with no remainder is that highest common factor.
options.D: Any common factor of $36$ and $48$ is enough, even when a larger one also fits.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Chitra has two sticks of lengths $28\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $42\,\mathrm{cm}$. She wants to cut both into pieces of the same whole-number length, using the largest possible piece length with no stick left over.

parts.text: Which claim correctly states what she should find?

options.text: A common multiple of $28$ and $42$.
The highest common factor of $28$ and $42$.
Any common factor of $28$ and $42$, even when a larger one also fits.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bharat starts factorising 60 as 6 × 10 and wants a complete prime factorisation.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Stop at 6 × 10, because those factors are already named composite factors.
options.B: Rewrite only 6 as 2 × 3 and leave 10 as it is.
options.C: Continue until every factor is prime: 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5.
options.D: Choose 60 itself as the answer, because 60 is the largest number printed in the stem.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Jatin starts factorising $84$ as $6 \times 14$ and wants a complete prime factorisation.

Which two claims correctly finish the work?

options.A: Stop at $6 \times 14$, because those factors are already named composite factors.
options.B: Rewrite $6$ as $2 \times 3$ and rewrite $14$ as $2 \times 7$.
options.C: Continue until every remaining factor is prime: $84 = 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 7$.
options.D: Choose $84$ itself as the answer, because $84$ is the largest number printed in the stem.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tejas starts factorising $90$ as $9 \times 10$ and wants a complete prime factorisation.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: $9 \times 10$ is already complete, because both factors are whole numbers.
options.B: Rewrite $9$ as $3 \times 3$ and $10$ as $2 \times 5$, so $90 = 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 5$.
options.C: Stop at $9 \times 10$, because $90$ is printed as the starting number.
options.D: Keep $9$ as it is and only split $10$, giving $90 = 9 \times 2 \times 5$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Rina writes 60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5. She asks whether 12 is a factor of 60.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Yes, by using three factors of 2, even though 60 shows only 2^2.
options.B: Listing 12 first is what produces the prime factors of 60.
options.C: Yes, because 12 = 2^2 \times 3 uses only primes that appear in 60, each no more times than allowed.
options.D: She must leave this chapter and use a unique-factorisation theorem before deciding.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Darsh writes $84 = 2^{2} \times 3 \times 7$. He asks whether $12$ is a factor of $84$.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: $12$ is a factor only when $12$ appears as a single printed prime in the factorisation.
options.B: $12 = 2^{2} \times 3$, and that product is formed from a subpart of $2^{2} \times 3 \times 7$.
options.C: $12$ is a factor of $84$, because its primes sit inside the prime factorisation of $84$.
options.D: $12$ is not a factor, because $84$ divided by $12$ must be checked by long division alone.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Jaya writes $90 = 2 \times 3^{2} \times 5$. She asks whether $18$ is a factor of $90$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: $18 = 2 \times 3^{2}$ uses only prime factors available in $90$, so $18$ is a factor of $90$.
options.B: $18$ is a factor of $90$ only after first finding the HCF of several other numbers.
options.C: $90$ is a factor of $18$, because the larger prime product produces the smaller one.
options.D: $18$ is not a factor of $90$, because $18$ is not itself one of the primes $2$, $3$, or $5$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Jatin hears the claim: "A larger whole number always has more prime factors, counting multiplicity, than a smaller whole number." He checks $96 = 2^{5}\times 3$ and $121 = 11^{2}$.

Does one verified counterexample overturn that general claim?

options.A: The answer is the word "counterexample", without saying what the example does to the claim.
options.B: The claim still stands for all numbers, even though he never uses an explicit failing example.
options.C: Yes: $96$ is larger than $121$ yet has six prime factors against two, so the universal claim is false.
options.D: Finding a counterexample is what creates the original general claim.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Mihir hears the claim: "A larger whole number always has more prime factors, counting multiplicity, than a smaller whole number." He checks $25 = 5^{2}$ and $16 = 2^{4}$.

Which two claims correctly decide what his check shows?

options.A: The answer is the word counterexample, with no statement of what the example does to the claim.
options.B: Yes: $25$ is larger than $16$ yet has two prime factors against four, so the universal claim is false.
options.C: One verified failing pair is enough to overturn a claim that was meant to hold for every whole number.
options.D: Finding a counterexample is what creates the original general claim.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tejas hears the claim: "A larger whole number always has more prime factors, counting multiplicity, than a smaller whole number." He checks $8 = 2^{3}$ and $49 = 7^{2}$.

Does one verified counterexample overturn that general claim?

options.A: The decision is the word counterexample.
options.B: The claim still stands for other numbers after this check fails.
options.C: Yes: $8 < 49$ but $8$ has three prime factors and $49$ has two, so the universal claim fails.
options.D: The counterexample is what produces the claim.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bharat has $60=2^{2}\times 3\times 5$ and $90=2\times 3^{2}\times 5$. He wants their HCF from these prime factorisations.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Answer "common primes", naming that phrase instead of writing the HCF value.
options.B: Say that the HCF is what produces the shared primes, instead of reading the shared primes from the factorisations to build the HCF.
options.C: Keep only the common primes with the smaller count in each: $2^{1}\times 3^{1}\times 5^{1}=30$.
options.D: Report $60$, copying the smaller of the two given numbers because $60$ is printed first, without using the minimum powers.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Diya has $84 = 2^{2} \times 3 \times 7$ and $126 = 2 \times 3^{2} \times 7$. She wants their HCF from these prime factorisations.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: The HCF is the phrase common primes, with no value written.
options.B: Keep only primes that appear in both factorisations.
options.C: Use the smaller power of each shared prime: $2^{1} \times 3^{1} \times 7^{1} = 42$.
options.D: Report $84$, copying the smaller given number because $84$ is printed first.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tejas has $48=2^{4}\times 3$ and $72=2^{3}\times 3^{2}$. He wants their HCF from these prime factorisations.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The HCF is the phrase common primes.
options.B: The HCF is what produces the shared primes in the factorisations.
options.C: Keep only the common primes with the smaller count in each: $2^{3}\times 3^{1}=24$.
options.D: The HCF is $48$, copying the smaller given number.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Asha hears two bells: one every $4$ minutes and one every $6$ minutes. They ring together at $9{:}00$. She wants the next time they ring together.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Name any common multiple such as $24$ minutes, skipping that the earliest common ring is the LCM.
options.B: Replace the common-multiple question with a full prime-factor write-up used only to name an HCF.
options.C: The first common ring is after $\operatorname{lcm}(4,6)=12$ minutes, so at $9{:}12$.
options.D: Choose $4$ minutes only because the printed number $4$ stands out in the stem.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Harsh hears two bells: one every $8$ minutes and one every $12$ minutes. They ring together at $9{:}00$. He wants the next time they ring together.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: Add $8$ and $12$ to get $20$, and use $20$ minutes as the wait.
options.B: The wait is a common multiple of $8$ and $12$.
options.C: The least common multiple is $24$, so they next ring together at $9{:}24$.
options.D: Report $8$ alone, because $8$ is the smaller printed interval.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tejas cuts paper strips of $9\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $12\,\mathrm{cm}$ to make matching-length torans. He wants the shortest common length both strip sizes can make.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Any common multiple of $9$ and $12$ is the shortest common length.
options.B: The shortest common length is $9\times 12=108\,\mathrm{cm}$, with no smaller shared multiple.
options.C: The shortest common length is the LCM of $9$ and $12$, which is $36\,\mathrm{cm}$.
options.D: The shortest common length is $9+12=21\,\mathrm{cm}$ because those are the printed strip lengths.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Xavier has $12=2^{2}\times 3$ and $18=2\times 3^{2}$. He wants their LCM from these prime factorisations.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Call the finished product a "common multiple" label only, without taking each prime to the highest power needed.
options.B: Keep only primes that appear in both factorisations, and drop the extra $2$ from $12$ and the extra $3$ from $18$.
options.C: Take each prime to the highest power that appears: $2^{2}\times 3^{2}=36$.
options.D: Report $18$ as the LCM only because $18$ is the larger of the two printed numbers.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nila has $20=2^{2}\times 5$ and $30=2\times 3\times 5$. She wants their LCM from these prime factorisations.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Find any common multiple of $20$ and $30$, and treat that common multiple as the LCM.
options.B: Take each prime with the greatest power needed: $2^{2}\times 3\times 5=60$.
options.C: Use only the primes that appear in both factorisations, so take $2\times 5=10$.
options.D: The LCM is $30$, because $30$ is the larger printed factorisation on the page.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sagar has $24=2^{3}\times 3$ and $36=2^{2}\times 3^{2}$. He wants their LCM from these prime factorisations.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Take each prime to the highest power that appears: $2^{3}\times 3^{2}=72$.
options.B: Keep only the lower powers shared by both factorisations: $2^{2}\times 3=12$.
options.C: Call the finished product a common multiple only.
options.D: The LCM is $36$, because $36$ is the larger of the two printed numbers.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Vivek notices that $8$ is a factor of $24$.

Which claim about HCF and LCM is correct?

options.A: $24$ is a common multiple of $8$ and $24$, so $24$ must be their HCF.
options.B: Their HCF is $8$ and their LCM is $24$, even if $8$ did not divide $24$.
options.C: Their HCF is $8$ and their LCM is $24$.
options.D: $8$ is a factor of $24$, so $8$ is their LCM.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Sia notices that $6$ is a factor of $30$.

parts.text: Which claim about HCF and LCM is correct?

options.text: Call both answers multiple, with no HCF or LCM named.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sagar notices that $9$ is a factor of $36$.

Which claim about HCF and LCM is correct?

options.A: Their HCF is $9$ and their LCM is $36$.
options.B: $36$ is a common multiple of $9$ and $36$, so $36$ must be their HCF.
options.C: Their HCF is $9$ and their LCM is $36$, even if $9$ did not divide $36$.
options.D: $9$ is a factor of $36$, so $9$ is their LCM.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri knows $\mathrm{HCF}(12,18)=6$. She multiplies both numbers by $5$ to get $60$ and $90$.

Which claim about $\mathrm{HCF}(60,90)$ is correct?

options.A: The HCF is the common multiplier $5$ alone, so $\mathrm{HCF}(60,90)=5$.
options.B: After multiplying by $5$, the HCF is still $6$, with no new common factor to include.
options.C: The shared factor $5$ is part of the HCF, and the old common factors still contribute, so $\mathrm{HCF}(60,90)=30$.
options.D: The HCF is $90$, because $90$ is the larger printed number.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Avni writes the numbers $14 \times 6$ and $14 \times 9$. She wants their highest common factor.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the answer the common multiplier $14$, and stop with HCF $= 14$.
options.B: Say HCF $= 14$ even when the remaining factors $6$ and $9$ still share a common factor.
options.C: HCF $= 14 \times \mathrm{HCF}(6, 9) = 14 \times 3 = 42$, because $14$ joins any leftover shared factor.
options.D: Choose $14$ only because $14$ is the largest printed number among $14$, $6$, and $9$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Farhan writes this common-division table for $24$ and $36$:

$2 \mid 24\quad 36$

$2 \mid 12\quad 18$

$3 \mid 6\quad 9$

$\phantom{2\mid} 2\quad 3$

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The HCF is the phrase common division, so the answer is that label rather than a product of factors.
options.B: The HCF is $2\times 2\times 3=12$ and the LCM is $2\times 2\times 3\times 2\times 3=72$.
options.C: The HCF is $2\times 2\times 3\times 2\times 3=72$ and the LCM is $2\times 2\times 3=12$.
options.D: The HCF equals $24+36$ because those are the two starting numbers in the table.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Rohan writes this common-division table for $18$ and $30$:

$2 \mid 18\quad 30$

$3 \mid 9\quad 15$

$\phantom{2\mid} 3\quad 5$

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: The HCF is the phrase common division, so that label replaces any product of factors.
options.B: The HCF is $2 \times 3 = 6$, the product of the common divisors removed.
options.C: The LCM is $2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 5 = 90$, the common divisors times the leftover factors.
options.D: Choose $18$ as the HCF because $18$ is the first number printed in the table.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Isha takes the two numbers $12$ and $18$. Their HCF is $6$ and their LCM is $36$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The product $12\times18$ equals the LCM $36$ alone.
options.B: The LCM $36$ is greater than the product $12\times18=216$.
options.C: HCF $\times$ LCM equals the product: $6\times36=12\times18=216$, and the LCM $36$ is not greater than that product.
options.D: HCF $\times$ LCM equals the product only for prime numbers, so not for $12$ and $18$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Avni takes the two numbers $8$ and $12$. Their HCF is $4$ and their LCM is $24$.

parts.text: Which claim is correct?

options.text: The product $8\times12$ equals the LCM $24$ alone.
HCF $\times$ LCM equals the product: $4\times24=8\times12=96$, and the LCM $24$ is not greater than that product.
The LCM $24$ is greater than the product $8\times12=96$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
In the decimal 36.82, each digit has a place value.

What does the digit 8 stand for?

options.A: 8 tenths
options.B: 8 hundredths
options.C: 8 ones
options.D: 8 tens

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
In the decimal $45.307$, each digit has a place value.

What does the digit $3$ stand for?

options.A: $3$ tenths
options.B: $3$ hundredths
options.C: $3$ ones
options.D: $3$ thousandths

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
In the decimal $81.506$, each digit has a place value.

Which two claims correctly read the place-value parts?

options.A: The digit $5$ stands for $5$ tenths.
options.B: The digit $5$ stands for $5$ hundredths.
options.C: The digit $6$ stands for $6$ thousandths.

subject: maths
stem:
Nitin multiplies $1.2 \times 0.4$.

Which method is correct?

options.A: Call $12$ the finished product, without placing any decimal point.
options.B: Multiply $12 \times 4 = 48$, then place the decimal using only one decimal place, skipping that $1.2$ and $0.4$ contribute $1+1=2$ places.
options.C: Multiply $12 \times 4 = 48$, then place the decimal point so the product has $2$ decimal places: $0.48$.
options.D: Say the decimal places in the product are what create the factors $1.2$ and $0.4$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tanya multiplies $2.5 \times 0.3$.

Which method is correct?

options.A: Call $75$ the finished product, and place no decimal point.
options.B: Multiply $25 \times 3 = 75$, then place the decimal using only one decimal place, even though $2.5$ and $0.3$ contribute two places in total.
options.C: Multiply $25 \times 3 = 75$, then place the decimal point so the product has $2$ decimal places: $0.75$.
options.D: Say the decimal places in the product are what create the factors $2.5$ and $0.3$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Urvashi multiplies $1.5 \times 0.4$.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims are correct?

options.A: The finished product is the whole number $60$.
options.B: Multiply $15 \times 4 = 60$, then place the decimal so the product has $2$ decimal places: $0.60$.
options.D: The $2$ decimal places in the product are what create the factors $1.5$ and $0.4$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Farhan multiplies $0.3 \times 0.4$.

Compared with both factors, where does the product sit?

options.A: Call the product "greater than both" as a label, without checking either factor against $1$.
options.B: Say being less than both factors is what produces the factors $0.3$ and $0.4$.
options.C: Less than both factors, because each factor is between $0$ and $1$, so the product $0.12$ is smaller than $0.3$ and than $0.4$.
options.D: Settle the size by treating the digits as place-value regrouping of whole numbers only.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yash multiplies $0.2 \times 0.5$.

Compared with both factors, where does the product sit?

options.A: Call the product greater than both as a fixed label.
options.B: Being less than both factors is what produces the factors $0.2$ and $0.5$.
options.C: Less than both factors, because each factor is between $0$ and $1$, so the product $0.1$ is smaller than $0.2$ and than $0.5$.
options.D: Settle the size by treating the digits as place-value regrouping of whole numbers only.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Urvashi multiplies $0.4 \times 0.6$.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims are correct?

options.A: The product is greater than both factors.
options.B: The product is less than both factors.
options.C: The product equals $0.24$.
options.D: Being less than both factors is what produces the factors $0.4$ and $0.6$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ekta asks whether $\dfrac{3}{4}$ can be written as a terminating decimal by finding an equivalent fraction with denominator $10$, $100$, $1000$, and so on.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Write $0.3$ from the numerator $3$ alone, without making an equivalent fraction whose denominator is $10$, $100$, or $1000$.
options.B: Say that writing $0.75$ is what creates the equivalent fraction with denominator $100$, instead of building that equivalent first.
options.C: Yes: multiply numerator and denominator by $25$ to get $\dfrac{75}{100}=0.75$, a terminating decimal.
options.D: Apply the same denominator-$10/100/1000$ rewrite to convert a ratio of map lengths, beyond this fraction-to-decimal hinge.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Leela asks whether $\dfrac{7}{20}$ can be written as a terminating decimal by finding an equivalent fraction with denominator $10$, $100$, $1000$, and so on.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: $\dfrac{7}{20}$ cannot become a terminating decimal, even though an equivalent fraction $\dfrac{35}{100}$ exists.
options.B: Writing the terminating decimal $0.35$ is what creates the equivalent fraction $\dfrac{35}{100}$.
options.C: Yes: $\dfrac{7}{20} = \dfrac{35}{100} = 0.35$, a terminating decimal.
options.D: Rewrite $\dfrac{7}{20}$ as a continuing never-ending decimal only, and stop.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Urvashi asks whether $\dfrac{9}{25}$ can be written as a terminating decimal by finding an equivalent fraction with denominator $10$, $100$, $1000$, and so on.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims are correct?

options.A: Multiply numerator and denominator by $4$ to get the equivalent fraction $\dfrac{36}{100}$.
options.B: $\dfrac{9}{25}$ can be written as the terminating decimal $0.36$.
options.C: $\dfrac{9}{25}$ cannot become a terminating decimal because $25$ is not already $10$, $100$, or $1000$.
options.D: Writing $0.36$ is what creates the original fraction $\dfrac{9}{25}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Isha uses long division for $7 \div 4$. After the ones place she has remainder $3$ and wants to continue into decimals.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Call the answer "remainder" only, without regrouping leftover ones into tenths.
options.B: Continue writing digits after the ones place but skip placing the decimal point in the quotient when ones are regrouped into tenths.
options.C: Regroup the remainder $3$ ones as $30$ tenths, continue dividing, and place the decimal point in the quotient when ones become tenths: $1.75$.
options.D: Use the same tenths-regrouping plan for a division that already finished with remainder $0$ at the ones place.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Ishan uses long division for $9 \div 4$. After the ones place he has remainder $1$ and wants to continue into decimals.

parts.text: Which claim correctly states how to extend the division?

options.text: Stop at remainder $1$, and report the remainder as the final answer label.
Regroup the leftover $1$ one as $10$ tenths, continue dividing, and place the decimal point in the quotient when tenths begin.
Treat any leftover as a new whole-number division problem outside place-value regrouping.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tejas uses long division for $11 \div 4$. After the ones place he has remainder $3$ and wants to continue into decimals.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Regroup the remainder $3$ ones as $30$ tenths, continue dividing, and place the decimal point in the quotient when ones are regrouped into tenths.
options.B: Stop with remainder $3$ as the finished answer.
options.C: Continue writing digits after the ones place with no decimal point in the quotient.
options.D: Use the same tenths-regrouping plan when the remainder at the ones place is already $0$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Arnav divides 9.6 by 4.

Which claim keeps the quotient decimal point in the correct place?

options.A: The important label is counting-number divisor, so the quotient is 4.
options.B: Divide 96 by 4 to get 24 and leave the decimal point out of the quotient.
options.C: Place the decimal point in the quotient above the decimal point in 9.6, then divide to get 2.4.
options.D: The quotient is 9.6, because that is the printed decimal in the stem.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Vihaan divides $8.4$ by $3$.

Which claim keeps the quotient decimal point in the correct place?

options.A: Call the answer counting-number divisor, and stop with no quotient written.
options.B: $8.4 \div 3 = 84$, moving past the tenths with no decimal point in the quotient.
options.C: $8.4 \div 3 = 2.8$, placing the decimal point in the quotient before dividing the tenths.
options.D: $8.4 \div 3 = 8.4$, because $8.4$ is already printed in the stem.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tejas divides $7.5$ by $5$.

Which claim keeps the quotient decimal point in the correct place?

options.A: $7.5\div 5=1.5$, placing the decimal point in the quotient before dividing the tenths.
options.B: The answer is counting-number divisor, with no quotient written.
options.C: $7.5\div 5=75$, moving past the tenths with no decimal point in the quotient.
options.D: $7.5\div 5=7.5$, because $7.5$ is already printed in the stem.

stem: Naveen must compute $4.8 \div 0.6$.

stem:
Sameer must compute $126 \div 2.5$ by making the divisor a counting number.

Which two claims correctly carry out the plan?

options.A: Call the answer the dividend $126$, and stop there.
options.B: Multiply both $126$ and $2.5$ by $10$, giving the equivalent division $1260 \div 25$.
options.C: Then $1260 \div 25 = 50.4$, which equals $126 \div 2.5$.
options.D: Say the counting-number divisor $25$ is what creates the original decimal divisor $2.5$.

subject: maths
stem:
Aditya carries out the long division $5 \div 6$. After the decimal point, each new digit leaves remainder $2$, then again remainder $2$, and the pattern continues.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The decimal quotient ends after a few digits even while remainder $2$ keeps returning.
options.B: Repeating remainder $2$ only means the digit $5$ in the dividend is a chapter label, not a signal about the quotient.
options.C: Because remainder $2$ repeats, the decimal quotient does not end; the repeating remainders produce repeating digits.
options.D: The answer is remainder because $2$ is the standout printed number in the division.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Vihaan carries out the long division $1 \div 3$. After the decimal point, each new digit leaves remainder $1$, then again remainder $1$, and the pattern continues.

parts.text: Which claim about the decimal quotient is correct?

options.text: Because remainder $1$ repeats, the decimal quotient does not end.
The decimal quotient ends after a few digits even while remainder $1$ keeps returning.
The answer is remainder, because $1$ is the standout printed leftover.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

subject: maths
stem:
Swati computes $6\div 0.5$ and obtains $12$.

options.A: The quotient must be less than $6$ whenever division is used.
options.B: Because the divisor $0.5$ is between $0$ and $1$, the quotient $12$ is greater than the dividend $6$.
options.C: Any decimal divisor forces the quotient to equal the dividend.
options.D: Division by $0.5$ is the same as multiplication by $0.5$, so the result should be $3$.

stem:

options.C: Any decimal divisor forces the quotient to equal the dividend $8$.
options.D: Division by $0.25$ is the same as multiplication by $0.25$, so the result should be $2$.

subject: maths
stem:
Earth's year is about $365.2422$ days. A common calendar year has $365$ days. Sana asks which years get an extra leap day under the usual calendar divisibility rules.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The leap-day rule is just another name for the decimal $0.2422$ itself.
options.B: Every year needs a leap day because $365$ is shorter than $365.2422$.
options.C: A year gets a leap day when it is divisible by $4$, with the usual century exceptions.
options.D: A year gets a leap day when its last digit is $2$, because $0.2422$ begins with $2$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kabir knows a common calendar year has $365$ days and Earth's revolution is about $365.2422$ days.

Which two claims correctly reason about leap-day adjustments?

options.A: Earth revolution is the calendar rule's name, so divisibility need not be checked.
options.B: The extra about $0.2422$ day accumulates, so about every $4$ years an extra day is added.
options.C: Under the usual rules, a year divisible by $4$ is a leap year, with century-year exceptions.
options.D: A year is a leap year when the digits of the year look symmetric.

stem:

stem:

options.B: The number of pieces is $15.6$, because that is the longer printed measure.
options.C: Divide $15.6$ by $1.2$ to get $13$ pieces.
options.D: The number of pieces is $1.2$, because that is the piece length printed on the rope.

subject: maths
stem:
Ritu's teacher asks the class: "How many books do students in our class usually carry?"

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The prompt is statistical: it is about data with expected variation across students.
options.B: It is not statistical because the exact answer is not known yet.
options.C: It is only a fixed fact about one named student, so it is not statistical.
options.D: Any question that contains the word "how many" is automatically statistical.

options.text: The prompt is statistical: it asks about data with expected variation across students.

stem:

options.A: The prompt is statistical: it asks about travel times with expected variation across students.

options.C: A question can be statistical even when the answer is not known yet, if it expects data with variation.
options.D: It is only a fixed fact about one named student, so it is not statistical.

stem:
Javed compares two class teams. Team A has 4 players and scored 40 goals in all. Team B has 10 players and scored 70 goals in all. He wants a fair comparison of typical scoring when the teams have different sizes.

Which basis is appropriate?

options.A: Use the totals 40 and 70 only, and say Team B is ahead because 70 is larger.
options.B: Compare goals per player (10 versus 7), because the teams have different sizes.
options.C: Compare only whichever team has the single larger total printed in the stem.
options.D: Say Team A is ahead because 4 is smaller than 10, using team size alone as the score.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Feroz compares two class teams. Team A has $5$ players and scored $45$ goals in all. Team B has $9$ players and scored $63$ goals in all. He wants a fair comparison of typical scoring when the teams have different sizes.

parts.text: Which claim chooses a fair representative basis?

options.text: Use the totals $45$ and $63$ only, and say Team B is ahead because $63$ is larger.
Compare goals per player ($9$ versus $7$), because the teams have different sizes.
Say Team A is ahead because $5$ is smaller than $9$, using team size alone as the score.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

stem: Vikram compares two class teams. Team P has $6$ players and scored $48$ points in all. Team Q has $8$ players and scored $56$ points in all. He wants a fair comparison of typical scoring when the teams have different sizes.

parts.text: Which claim correctly chooses a fair basis for the comparison?

options.text: Compare the per-player averages: Team P averages $8$ points and Team Q averages $7$ points.
Compare the totals only: Team Q scored $56$ and Team P scored $48$.
Compare the team sizes only: Team Q has $8$ players and Team P has $6$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

options.B: The mean produces the data total, so the total of the four values must be 7.
options.C: The mean is (4 + 6 + 8 + 10) ÷ 4 = 7, the equal share of the total.
options.D: Report the median of the ordered list instead of the total divided by 4.

stem: Lochan's data are $5$, $7$, $9$, and $11$. He wants the arithmetic mean as the equal-share value of that list.

parts.text: Which claim correctly gives the mean?

options.text: The mean is $11$, the largest value in the list.
The mean is $8$, from $(5+7+9+11)\div 4$.
The mean is $32$, the total of the four values.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice that uses total and number of values.

stem:
Lavanya's data are $3$, $5$, $7$, and $9$. She wants the arithmetic mean as the equal-share value of that list.

options.A: Add only $3$ and $9$, then divide by $2$, leaving $5$ and $7$ out of the total.
options.B: The mean is $(3 + 5 + 7 + 9) \div 4 = 6$, the equal share of the total.
options.C: If the four values shared the total equally, each share would be $6$.
options.D: Report the median of the ordered list instead of the total divided by $4$.
