subject: maths
stem:
Ritu records runs in five matches: $12$, $0$, $8$, dash (did not play), and $10$. She wants the mean runs per match played.

How should she form the mean?

options.A: Drop both the observed $0$ and the dash, treating each as a no-value label.
options.B: Average five entries by counting the dash as a played match with blank score.
options.C: Sum $12+0+8+10=30$ over the four played matches, so the mean is $30/4$; exclude the dash.
options.D: Replace the dash with a guessed score and average all five numbers.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Gaurav records points in six games: $9$, $0$, $14$, dash (did not play), $7$, and $10$. He wants the mean points per game played.

parts.text: Which claim correctly forms the mean?

options.text: Drop both the observed $0$ and the dash, treating each as a no-value label.
Sum $9+0+14+7+10=40$ over the five played games, so the mean is $40/5$; exclude the dash.
Average six entries by counting the dash as a played game with a blank score.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Vikram records marks in five tests: $15$, $0$, $12$, dash (absent), and $9$. He wants the mean marks per test taken.

parts.text: Which claim correctly forms the mean?

options.text: Drop both the observed $0$ and the dash, treating each as a no-value label.
Sum $15+0+12+9=36$ over the four tests taken, so the mean is $36/4$.
Average five entries by counting the dash as a taken test with a blank score.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Javed has the scores $4$, $9$, $2$, $7$, and $5$. He wants the median.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the answer sorted data, without naming the middle value after sorting.
options.B: Take the middle entry of the unsorted list and report $2$ as the median.
options.C: Sort as $2$, $4$, $5$, $7$, $9$; the middle value $5$ is the median.
options.D: Say that the median $5$ is what creates the sorted list $2$, $4$, $5$, $7$, $9$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Pihu has the scores $6$, $11$, $3$, $8$, and $4$. She wants the median.

parts.text: Which claim correctly gives the median?

options.text: The answer is the phrase sorted data, with no middle value named.
Sort as $3$, $4$, $6$, $8$, $11$; the middle value $6$ is the median.
Take the middle entry of the unsorted list and report $3$ as the median.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Vikram has the scores $9$, $2$, $6$, and $4$. He wants the median.

parts.text: Which claim correctly gives the median?

options.text: The answer is the phrase sorted data.
Sort as $2$, $4$, $6$, $9$; the median is midway between $4$ and $6$, so $5$.
Take the middle entry of the unsorted list and report $2$ as the median.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Soham's scores are $8$, $9$, $10$, and $40$. He wants a typical value for the main cluster.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Report the mean as typical for the cluster, skipping that $40$ pulls the mean away from $8$, $9$, and $10$.
options.B: Say that choosing the median is what creates the outlier $40$.
options.C: Prefer the median, because $40$ pulls the mean upward away from the cluster $8$, $9$, $10$, while the median stays with that cluster.
options.D: Use the same median-over-mean story for a list with no outlier, as if every data set needed it.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Rudra's scores are $5$, $6$, $7$, $8$, and $30$. He wants a typical value for the main cluster.

parts.text: Which claim correctly chooses the better typical value?

options.text: The mean is better even when $30$ pulls the mean far from $5$, $6$, $7$, and $8$.
The median $7$ represents the main cluster better, because $30$ pulls the mean away from that cluster.
Choosing the median is what creates the outlier score $30$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Vikram's scores are $11$, $12$, $13$, $14$, and $45$. He wants a typical value for the main cluster.

parts.text: Which claim correctly chooses the better typical value?

options.text: The mean is better even when $45$ pulls the mean far from $11$, $12$, $13$, and $14$.
The median $13$ represents the main cluster better, because $45$ pulls the mean away from that cluster.
Choosing the median is what creates the outlier score $45$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Mona has monthly scores $4,7,4,9,7$ for months $1$ through $5$ in that order. She builds a dot plot of those scores on a number line.

options.A: Call the display a number line only, without reading frequencies, min, max, range, or clusters from the dots.
options.B: Read min $4$, max $9$, and frequencies from the dots, and also claim the dot plot still shows which month had which score, skipping that month order can be lost.
options.C: From the dots she can read values, frequencies (two $4$s, two $7$s, one $9$), min $4$, max $9$, and range $5$, but she cannot recover which month held which score from the dots alone.
options.D: Say that writing the frequencies is what creates the dots on the number line, instead of reading frequency from the dots already placed.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Meher records weekly scores $3,5,3,8,5$ for weeks $1$ through $5$ in that order. The diagram shows the dot plot of those scores on a number line.

Which claim about the dot plot is correct?

options.A: The number line alone is the distribution, so the dots are optional decoration.
options.B: The plot shows values and frequencies (two $3$s, two $5$s, one $8$), but it does not keep which week each score came from.
options.C: The dots create the number line marks $3$, $5$, and $8$.
options.D: The plot also reconstructs the exact onion-table week labels that were never drawn as dots.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Urvashi has daily scores $6,8,6,10,8$ for days $1$ through $5$ in that order. She builds a dot plot of those scores on a number line.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims about the dot plot are correct?

options.A: From the dots she can read values and frequencies (two $6$s, two $8$s, one $10$), min $6$, max $10$, and range $4$.
options.B: The display is a number line only, so the dots are optional.
options.C: The dot plot does not keep which day each score came from.
options.D: Writing the frequencies is what creates the dots on the number line.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The graph compares Maths and Science quiz marks for Ishaan, Rekha, and Tushar with adjacent bars, one common scale, and a legend.

Which claim correctly describes how the graph is built?

options.A: For each student, two adjacent bars share the category, use the same vertical scale, and the legend separates Maths from Science.
options.B: The display is finished by naming it a double column graph, without comparing any bar heights.
options.C: Drawing the clustered bars is what creates the Maths and Science quiz marks.
options.D: Only the tallest bar matters, because it is the most obvious height on the graph.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: The graph shows Class A and Class B student counts for Monday and Tuesday as adjacent bars on a common scale.

parts.text: Which claim correctly reads the graph?

options.text: Call the display a double column graph only, with no comparison of bar heights.
On Monday, Class A has $18$ students and Class B has $12$; on Tuesday, Class A has $22$ and Class B has $16$, read from adjacent bars on one scale.
Drawing adjacent bars is what creates the Monday and Tuesday categories.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Urvashi's graph compares English and Hindi marks for Divya, Kabir, and Neel with adjacent bars, one common scale, and a legend.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims correctly describe how the graph is built?

options.A: For each student, two adjacent bars share the category, use the same vertical scale, and the legend separates English from Hindi.
options.B: Bar heights on the common scale can be compared across English and Hindi for the same student.
options.C: The display is finished by naming it a double column graph, without comparing any bar heights.
options.D: Drawing the clustered bars is what creates the English and Hindi marks.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The graph shows how many books a class returned on four days.

Which conclusion is justified by the graph?

options.A: Tuesday has the tallest bar, so more books were returned on Tuesday than on any other labelled day.
options.B: The vertical axis is labelled Books, so the answer is the word Books.
options.C: Wednesday shows about $8$ books even though the scale marks are every $5$ books.
options.D: Books cause Tuesday to be busier than Monday.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ritu reads the graph of books borrowed on four days. The vertical axis is labelled books with marks $0,2,4,6,8$, and the bars show Mon $4$, Tue $6$, Wed $3$, Thu $5$.

Which claim correctly interprets the graph?

options.A: Call the answer the units on the vertical axis, and stop before reading the bars.
options.B: Read Tue as $6$ books even when that height is not tied to the marked scale.
options.C: First note the axes, scale, and bar heights, then conclude only that Tue is highest at $6$ books and Wed is lowest at $3$ books.
options.D: Conclude that more books were borrowed on Tue because students studied harder that day.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ananya records that three friends in her class each sleep about 8 hours on school nights. She wants a claim about sleep for all children in the state.

Which claim is warranted?

options.A: Every child in the state sleeps about 8 hours on school nights.
options.B: The three friends give a local note, but not a statewide sleep claim.
options.C: Statewide sleep is what produces the three friends' hours, so the state average must be 8.
options.D: Any sample of three is enough once the hours are written down.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Diya records that two classmates each read about $20$ pages on a school night. She wants a claim about reading for all children in the city.

Which claim is warranted?

options.A: Two classmates are enough for a citywide claim once the page counts are written down.
options.B: Citywide reading is what produces the two classmates' page counts, so the city average must be $20$.
options.C: The two classmates give a local note, but not a citywide reading claim.
options.D: Any pair of page counts may be used as a city estimate for every school subject, not only reading.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Vivek marks endpoints X and Y. He finds two points P and Q so that each is the same distance from X as from Y. He draws the line through P and Q.

What is that line?

options.A: The line that must pass through the endpoints X and Y only.
options.B: A line that creates equal distances from X and Y after it is drawn.
options.C: The perpendicular bisector of segment XY.
options.D: A guide for tiling a rectangle with 2 by 1 tiles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Misha looks at the diagram. Endpoints $X$ and $Y$ are marked. Points $P$ and $Q$ each lie at the same distance from $X$ as from $Y$. Line $m$ is drawn through $P$ and $Q$.

Which claim correctly names line $m$?

options.A: Line $m$ is the perpendicular bisector of segment $XY$.
options.B: Line $m$ is the segment $XY$ itself.
options.C: Equal distances from $X$ and $Y$ appear only after line $m$ is already drawn.
options.D: Line $m$ is named by the letter $m$ alone, because $m$ is printed largest.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Adeel looks at the diagram. Endpoints $X$ and $Y$ are marked. Points $P$ and $Q$ each lie at the same distance from $X$ as from $Y$. Line $n$ is drawn through $P$ and $Q$, and it meets $XY$ at $M$ with a right-angle mark.

parts.text: Which claim correctly names line $n$?

options.text: Line $n$ is the perpendicular bisector of segment $XY$.
Line $n$ is the segment $XY$ itself.
Equal distances from $X$ and $Y$ appear only after line $n$ is already drawn.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Omkar must construct a $90^\circ$ angle at point O on a given straight line.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Keep O on the line, but skip making O the midpoint of a segment on that line.
options.B: First draw a line through O that looks upright, then mark equal distances from O.
options.C: Mark points X and Y on the line at equal distances from O so that O is the midpoint of XY, then construct the perpendicular bisector of XY.
options.D: Treat O as a point outside the line and drop a perpendicular from outside.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Amaya looks at the diagram. Point $O$ lies on a straight line, and a right angle is to be built at $O$.

Which plan correctly constructs the $90^\circ$ angle at $O$?

options.A: Mark points $X$ and $Y$ on the line at equal distances from $O$ so that $O$ is the midpoint of $XY$, then construct the perpendicular bisector of $XY$.
options.B: Keep $O$ on the line and draw any upright ray from $O$.
options.C: First draw a line that looks upright through $O$, then mark equal distances from $O$.
options.D: Treat $O$ as a point off the line and drop a perpendicular from outside.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Wafa looks at the diagram. Point $R$ lies on a straight line, and a right angle is to be built at $R$.

Which plan correctly constructs the $90^\circ$ angle at $R$?

options.A: Mark $X$ and $Y$ on the line with $XR = RY$, then draw the perpendicular bisector of $XY$ through $R$.
options.B: Mark any point $P$ above the line and join $P$ to $R$, without making $R$ the midpoint of a segment on the line.
options.C: First draw a $60^\circ$ angle at $R$ by an equilateral triangle, then halve it to get $30^\circ$.
options.D: Treat the finished right angle at $R$ as what chooses the equal points $X$ and $Y$ on the line.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Farid must bisect $\angle XOY$ with ruler and compass.

Which construction is correct?

options.A: Name the vertex O as the bisector, and draw no equal marks on the arms.
options.B: First draw a ray from O and say that ray is what creates equal marks OA, OB, AC, and BC.
options.C: Mark A on OX and B on OY with $OA = OB$, then mark C with $AC = BC$, and draw ray OC.
options.D: Trace only the printed angle symbol at O, and treat that printed mark as the bisector.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ishita looks at the diagram. She must bisect $\angle XOY$ with ruler and compass. Equal marks show $OA=OB$ on the arms and $AC=BC$ with ray $OC$ drawn.

Which claim correctly states what that construction produces?

options.A: Name the vertex $O$ as the bisector, and treat equal marks on the arms as unnecessary.
options.B: Say that the finished bisector ray is what creates the equal marks $OA$, $OB$, $AC$, and $BC$.
options.C: Ray $OC$ bisects $\angle XOY$, because the equal marks build congruent triangles that force the two half-angles equal.
options.D: Trace only the printed angle arc at $O$, and treat that printed mark as the bisector.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: The diagram shows $\angle POQ$. Mukul must bisect $\angle POQ$ with ruler and compass. Equal marks show $OA = OB$ on the arms and $AC = BC$ with ray $OC$ drawn.

parts.text: Which claim correctly states what that construction produces?

options.text: Ray $OC$ bisects $\angle POQ$, because the equal marks build congruent triangles that force the two half-angles equal.
Name the vertex $O$ as the bisector, and treat the equal marks as unnecessary.
Say that the finished ray $OC$ is what creates the equal marks $OA$, $OB$, $AC$, and $BC$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Vivek must make an exact copy of $\angle PQR$ at a new vertex $S$ on a fresh ray.

Which construction copies the angle?

options.A: Name the new vertex $S$ as the copied angle, and transfer no arc or chord from $\angle PQR$.
options.B: Draw any arc at $S$ only, and skip matching the arc radius and the chord used on $\angle PQR$.
options.C: From $Q$ and from $S$ draw arcs of the same radius; then transfer the chord between the arc hits on $\angle PQR$ onto the new arc, and join that mark to $S$.
options.D: Say the finished equal angle at $S$ is what produces the matching arc radius and chord, instead of transferring those lengths from $\angle PQR$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Diya must make an exact copy of $\angle PQR$ at a new vertex $S$ on a fresh ray.

Which construction copies the angle?

options.A: Name the new vertex $S$ as the copied angle, and transfer no lengths from $\angle PQR$.
options.B: Draw any arc at $S$ only, and leave the chord from $\angle PQR$ unmatched.
options.C: From $Q$ and from $S$ draw arcs of the same radius; transfer the chord between the arc hits on $\angle PQR$ onto the new arc, and join to form the equal angle at $S$.
options.D: The finished equal angle at $S$ is what produces the matching arc radius and chord.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Wafa must make an exact copy of $\angle ABC$ at a new vertex $T$ on a fresh ray.

Which construction copies the angle?

options.A: Naming the new vertex $T$ completes the copy.
options.B: Any arc centred at $T$ copies $\angle ABC$.
options.C: From $B$ and from $T$ draw arcs of the same radius; then transfer the chord between the arc hits on $\angle ABC$ onto the new arc.
options.D: The matching arc and chord create $\angle ABC$ at $B$ rather than a copy at $T$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Omkar has line $m$ and wants a line through point $P$ parallel to $m$ by copying a corresponding angle from a transversal.

Which plan works?

options.A: Copy an angle at $P$ with no transversal that intersects line $m$, and claim the new line is parallel to $m$.
options.B: Say that the finished parallel line is what creates the transversal through $m$, instead of choosing the transversal first.
options.C: Draw a transversal through $P$ that cuts $m$, copy the corresponding angle at $P$, and draw the new line along that copied angle; it is parallel to $m$.
options.D: Use only a set-square to slide a parallel, and treat that tool method as this corresponding-angle copy hinge.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lila looks at the diagram. Line $m$ is given, point $P$ is off $m$, and transversal $t$ cuts $m$ at $E$. The marked angle $\alpha$ at $E$ is copied at $P$ so that new line $n$ through $P$ makes the corresponding angle $\alpha$ with $t$.

Which claim correctly states what that construction produces?

options.A: Copy an angle at $P$ with no transversal that cuts line $m$, and claim the new line is parallel to $m$.
options.B: Say that the finished parallel line is what creates transversal $t$ through $m$.
options.C: Line $n$ through $P$ is parallel to $m$, because the corresponding angle $\alpha$ was copied from transversal $t$.
options.D: Slide a set-square along $m$ and treat that tool method as this corresponding-angle copy.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Wafa has line $k$ and wants a line through point $R$ parallel to $k$ by copying a corresponding angle from a transversal.

Which plan works?

options.A: Copy an angle at $R$ with no transversal that cuts line $k$, and claim the new line is parallel to $k$.
options.B: The finished parallel line is what creates the transversal through $k$.
options.C: Draw a transversal through $R$ that cuts $k$, copy the corresponding angle at $R$, and draw the new line through $R$.
options.D: Slide a set-square along $k$ and treat that tool method as this corresponding-angle copy.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Wasim must draw a symmetric rangoli petal pattern with ruler and compass. Equal arm lengths and a mirror line are required before the outer arcs are traced.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Call the finished picture support lines only, without fixing equal arms or the mirror line first.
options.B: Trace the outer arcs first, and treat equal arm lengths and the mirror line as optional afterward.
options.C: First construct the mirror line and equal arm lengths (and any equal repeated angles needed); then trace the outer arcs along those constraints.
options.D: Say that tracing the outer arcs is what creates the mirror line and equal arms, instead of building those supports first.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Avni must draw a symmetric rangoli petal pattern with ruler and compass. Equal arm lengths and a mirror line are required before the outer arcs are traced.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Name the finished rangoli as the mirror line alone, and transfer no equal arm lengths.
options.B: Trace the outer arcs first, and leave the mirror line and equal arm lengths unconstructed.
options.C: Construct the mirror line and mark equal arm lengths first, then trace the outer arcs from those supports.
options.D: The finished outer arcs are what create the mirror line and the equal arm lengths.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Wafa constructs a six-petal flower with ruler and compass. Equal radii from the centre and equal $60^{\circ}$ turn angles are required before the outer petal arcs are traced.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Equal radii and $60^{\circ}$ turns are names only, so the flower is finished with no support construction drawn.
options.B: Trace the outer petal arcs first, and add equal radii and $60^{\circ}$ turns afterwards.
options.C: Construct the equal radii and $60^{\circ}$ support angles first, then trace the outer petal arcs.
options.D: Tracing the outer petal arcs is what creates the equal radii and $60^{\circ}$ turn angles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qadir must construct an exact $15^{\circ}$ angle using equal-radius arcs and angle bisection.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Call the answer fifteen degrees only, without building $60^{\circ}$ from an equilateral triangle and then bisecting.
options.B: Build a $60^{\circ}$ angle from equal-radius arcs, then stop without bisecting to $30^{\circ}$ and again to $15^{\circ}$.
options.C: Construct an equilateral triangle for $60^{\circ}$, bisect to $30^{\circ}$, then bisect again to obtain $15^{\circ}$.
options.D: Say that drawing $15^{\circ}$ is what creates the equilateral $60^{\circ}$ angle, instead of starting from $60^{\circ}$ and bisecting twice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Rohan must construct an exact $15^{\circ}$ angle at point $A$ on ray $AX$ in the diagram, using equal-radius arcs and angle bisection.

Which two claims correctly describe the plan?

options.A: Name ray $AX$ as the finished $15^{\circ}$ angle, and stop before drawing any arcs.
options.B: Build a $60^{\circ}$ angle at $A$ with equal-radius arcs that form an equilateral triangle.
options.C: Bisect that $60^{\circ}$ angle to $30^{\circ}$, then bisect again to obtain $15^{\circ}$.
options.D: The repeated bisections are what create the equal-radius arcs of the equilateral step.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Vikram must construct an exact $15^{\circ}$ angle at point $P$ on ray $PQ$, using equal-radius arcs and angle bisection.

parts.text: Which first step is correct?

options.text: Construct an equilateral triangle from equal-radius arcs to obtain a $60^{\circ}$ angle at $P$.
Name ray $PQ$ as the finished $15^{\circ}$ angle.
Draw a $45^{\circ}$ angle at $P$ as the starting angle.
Bisect a $15^{\circ}$ angle to create the equal-radius arcs.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows six congruent equilateral triangles meeting at a common point.

Why can they be assembled to form a regular hexagon?

options.A: Each triangle angle is $60^{\circ}$, six of them make $360^{\circ}$ at the centre, and the outer sides are equal.
options.B: A regular hexagon is simply the label for any figure built from triangles.
options.C: Any six triangles around a point form a regular hexagon.
options.D: The same assembly also builds a regular pentagon from five equilateral triangles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows six triangles meeting at centre $O$.

Which claim explains why these triangles form a regular hexagon?

options.A: Six congruent equilateral triangles fit around $O$ because six $60^{\circ}$ angles sum to $360^{\circ}$, so the outer boundary has equal sides and equal $120^{\circ}$ angles.
options.B: Call the answer regular hexagon, and stop with no angle sum at $O$.
options.C: Any six triangles around $O$ form a regular hexagon, even when the triangles are not congruent and not equilateral.
options.D: The same assembly also builds a regular pentagon from five such triangles around $O$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Vikram cuts six congruent equilateral paper triangles and joins them at a common point to build a regular hexagon.

parts.text: Which claim explains why the assembly forms a regular hexagon?

options.text: Six congruent equilateral triangles fit around a common point because six $60^{\circ}$ angles sum to $360^{\circ}$, so the outer boundary has equal sides and equal $120^{\circ}$ angles.
The answer is the name regular hexagon, with no angle sum at the common point.
Any six triangles around a common point form a regular hexagon, even when the triangles are not congruent and not equilateral.
The same assembly also builds a regular pentagon from five such triangles around a common point.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Yash wants to cover a 3-by-5 grid of unit squares with 2-by-1 tiles. Tiles must not overlap and must not leave gaps.

parts.text: Can the grid be tiled completely?

options.text: Yes
No
Only if the tiles may overlap

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Krish's 5-by-3 grid of unit squares. He wants to cover it with 2-by-1 tiles. Tiles must not overlap and must not leave gaps.

Can the grid be tiled?

options.A: No. The grid has 15 unit squares, so 2-by-1 tiles cannot cover it.
options.B: The tiling decision is the label "unit squares" on the grid.
options.C: Yes. Any block of 15 cells can be paired into 2-by-1 tiles.
options.D: Pairing tiles along rows is what creates the 5-by-3 grid size.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Parth colours a $4$-by-$4$ grid in checkerboard black and white, then removes two white corner squares. He wants to cover the remaining region with $2 \times 1$ tiles that do not overlap and leave no gaps.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: The remaining region has even area $14$, so it can be tiled by $2 \times 1$ tiles.
options.B: Every $2 \times 1$ tile covers one black square and one white square.
options.C: The remaining region has $8$ black squares and $6$ white squares, so it cannot be tiled by $2 \times 1$ tiles.
options.D: Only the total number of squares matters for tiling with $2 \times 1$ tiles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows a $4$-by-$4$ grid coloured in checkerboard black and white. Nitya removes the two opposite white corner squares marked in the figure. She wants to cover the remaining region with $2 \times 1$ tiles that do not overlap and leave no gaps.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The answer is the word checkerboard, because that colouring word is printed with the grid.
options.B: Yes: the remaining region has $14$ squares, an even count, so $2 \times 1$ tiles can cover it.
options.C: No: each $2 \times 1$ tile covers one black and one white square, but the remaining region has unequal black and white counts.
options.D: The same colouring argument also settles tiling of every even-area shape, including shapes with no grid colouring.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Poonam asks which shapes can tile the entire plane, covering without gaps or overlaps, rather than only a finite floor region.

Which claims are correct? Two options are correct.

options.A: Report the word tiling as the shape that covers the entire plane.
options.B: Repeated copies of a square can tile the entire plane.
options.C: Repeated copies of a regular hexagon can tile the entire plane.
options.D: Covering only a classroom floor with squares proves those squares tile the entire plane.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows a $4$-by-$4$ block of square tiles on Sameer's classroom floor. He asks which claim about tiling is correct.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The answer is the word tiling printed near the square tiles.
options.B: Repeated copies of a square can tile the entire plane, covering without gaps or overlaps.
options.C: Covering only the classroom floor with squares proves those squares tile the entire plane.
options.D: Plane tiling is what creates the square shape of each tile.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kavya has a weighing scale that is balanced. The left pan holds one sealed packet and a 20 g weight. The right pan holds a 50 g weight.

How can she find the mass of the packet?

options.A: Remove the 20 g weight from the left pan only, then read the right pan.
options.B: Add the packet mass to both pans so the scale tips.
options.C: Remove 20 g from each pan so the packet alone balances a 30 g weight.
options.D: Compare the pans while the scale is tipped and unbalanced.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nila has a weighing scale that is balanced, as in the diagram. The left pan holds one sealed packet and a $15\,\mathrm{g}$ weight. The right pan holds a $40\,\mathrm{g}$ weight.

How can she find the mass of the packet?

options.A: Remove the $15\,\mathrm{g}$ weight from the left pan only, then read the unbalanced pans as the packet mass.
options.B: The remaining comparison after removing equal weights from both pans is what first created the balanced pans.
options.C: Remove $15\,\mathrm{g}$ from both pans (take the $15\,\mathrm{g}$ weight off the left and replace the right $40\,\mathrm{g}$ with $25\,\mathrm{g}$), leaving the packet balanced against $25\,\mathrm{g}$.
options.D: Compare the pans while the scale is still tipped, using an unbalanced reading as the packet mass.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows a level balance scale. The left pan holds sealed tin $P$ and a $100\,\mathrm{g}$ weight. The right pan holds a $350\,\mathrm{g}$ weight.

Which claim correctly gives the mass of tin $P$?

options.A: The mass of tin $P$ is $450\,\mathrm{g}$.
options.B: The mass of tin $P$ is $350\,\mathrm{g}$.
options.C: The mass of tin $P$ is $250\,\mathrm{g}$.
options.D: The mass of tin $P$ is $100\,\mathrm{g}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Chitra builds matchstick squares in a row. Position 1 uses 4 sticks, position 2 uses 7 sticks, and position 3 uses 10 sticks. She wants the position number n whose arrangement uses 40 sticks.

Which approach is correct?

options.A: Describe only the matchstick arrangement in words, without a rule in n.
options.B: Use the rule 3n + 1 for any pretty drawing, even one not in this sequence.
options.C: Use the rule 3n + 1 for this sequence and solve 3n + 1 = 40 to find n.
options.D: Pick n = 40, because 40 is the target number printed in the question.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows a growing dot pattern. Position $1$ has $4$ dots, Position $2$ has $7$ dots, and Position $3$ has $10$ dots. Rohan wants the position where the pattern has $25$ dots.

Which two claims correctly form the rule and the equation?

options.A: The number of dots at Position $n$ is $3n + 1$.
options.B: Call the answer matchstick arrangement, and stop with no rule in $n$.
options.C: Set $3n + 1 = 25$ to find the needed position.
options.D: The number of dots at Position $n$ is $25$, because $25$ is the printed target.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yamini stacks paper cups for a display. Position $1$ uses $5$ cups, position $2$ uses $8$ cups, and position $3$ uses $11$ cups. She wants the position number $n$ whose arrangement uses $32$ cups.

Which approach is correct?

options.A: Solve $5n = 32$ for the position number.
options.B: Solve $n + 3 = 32$ for the position number.
options.C: Solve $3n + 2 = 32$ for the position number.
options.D: The position number is $32$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Soham is given the equation 2n + 3 = 11. A classmate proposes n = 4.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Call 4 the solution because it is a whole number written near the equation.
options.B: Writing n = 4 is what creates the equation 2n + 3 = 11.
options.C: Accept n = 4, because substituting gives LHS 2 \times 4 + 3 = 11, equal to the RHS.
options.D: Express a second unknown in terms of n before any substitution test.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Anvi is given the equation $3k - 5 = 10$. A classmate proposes $k = 4$.

parts.text: Which claim about $k = 4$ is correct?

options.text: Accept $k = 4$, because 4 is a whole number written near the equation.
Reject $k = 4$, because substituting gives LHS $3\times4 - 5 = 7$, which is not equal to RHS 10.
Writing $k = 4$ is what creates the equation $3k - 5 = 10$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Niharika is given the equation $5m + 2 = 17$. A classmate proposes $m = 3$.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Accept $m = 3$, because $3$ is a whole number written near the equation.
options.B: Writing $m = 3$ is what creates the equation $5m + 2 = 17$.
options.C: Accept $m = 3$, because substituting gives LHS $5 \times 3 + 2 = 17$, equal to the RHS.
options.D: Express a second unknown in terms of $m$ before any substitution test.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Komal must solve $3x + 5 = 17$ by isolating $x$. The two sides are already equal.

Which first move preserves equality and removes the unwanted $+5$?

options.A: Write "inverse operations" as the solution, without performing any step on the equation.
options.B: Subtract $5$ from the left side only, leaving the right side as $17$.
options.C: Subtract $5$ from both sides to get $3x = 12$, then divide both sides by $3$ to get $x = 4$.
options.D: Take $x = 17$, because $17$ is the largest number printed on the right-hand side.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Rohan must solve $4x + 7 = 23$ by isolating $x$. The two sides are already equal.

Which two claims correctly describe equality-preserving moves?

options.A: Write inverse operations as the solution, naming the phrase instead of changing both sides.
options.B: Subtract $7$ from both sides to get $4x = 16$.
options.C: Then divide both sides by $4$ to get $x = 4$.
options.D: Take $x = 23$, because $23$ is the largest number printed on the right-hand side.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yamini must solve $5x + 9 = 29$ by isolating $x$. The two sides are already equal.

Which first move preserves equality and removes the unwanted $+9$?

options.A: The first move is the label "inverse operations".
options.B: Subtract $9$ from the left side only, writing $5x = 29$.
options.C: Subtract $9$ from both sides, writing $5x = 20$.
options.D: Take $x = 29$, because $29$ is the largest printed number.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Chitra solves $3x+5= x+17$, where the unknown $x$ appears on both sides.

Which first move correctly clears the matching unknown terms?

options.A: Answer "like terms", naming that phrase instead of removing a matching $x$ term from both sides.
options.B: Subtract $x$ from one side only, or subtract a different letter-number, as if the matching-same-letter condition were optional.
options.C: Subtract $x$ from both sides to get $2x+5=17$, then isolate $x$.
options.D: Say that isolating $x$ is what creates the unknown terms on both sides, instead of first removing the matching $x$ terms.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Neil solves $5x+3=2x+18$, where the unknown $x$ appears on both sides.

parts.text: Which first move correctly clears the matching unknown terms?

options.text: Answer "like terms", naming that phrase instead of removing a matching $x$ term from both sides.
Subtract $2x$ from both sides to get $3x+3=18$, then isolate $x$.
Subtract $2x$ from one side only, treating the same-letter match as optional.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yamini solves $4x+7=x+19$, where the unknown $x$ appears on both sides.

Which first move correctly clears the matching unknown terms?

options.A: Subtract the constants $7$ and $19$ first, and treat the unknown terms as already cleared.
options.B: Subtract $x$ from the left side only, leaving $3x+7=x+19$.
options.C: Subtract $x$ from both sides to get $3x+7=19$.
options.D: Add $x$ to both sides to get $5x+7=19$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bharat's number machine multiplies an unknown start by $3$ and then adds $5$, and the display shows $20$.

Which claim models the situation correctly?

options.A: Write $3x+5$ without equating the expression to the stated total $20$.
options.B: Write operations multiply-by-$3$ and add-$5$ with no total to equal, as if an equation were still fixed.
options.C: Let the unknown be $x$; then $3x+5=20$.
options.D: Pick an equation only because the printed $20$ stands out, without translating the operations on $x$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Nitya's number machine multiplies an unknown start by $4$ and then subtracts $3$; the display shows $17$.

parts.text: Which equation models the situation?

options.text: $4x - 3$, with no equals $17$
$4 \times 17 - 3 = x$

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yamini buys $6$ identical pens and a sharpener that costs $\mathrm{Rs}\,8$. The bill is $\mathrm{Rs}\,50$. Let $p$ be the cost of one pen in rupees.

Which claim models the situation correctly?

options.A: The model is the expression $6p+8$.
options.B: The situation is modeled by the operations multiply-by-$6$ and add-$8$ alone.
options.C: The correct model is $6p+8=50$.
options.D: The unknown $p$ equals $50$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Uma knows two numbers sum to $50$, and the larger is $8$ more than the smaller. She wants one equation in one unknown.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Write $x+y=50$ and stop, skipping that one unknown must be rewritten in terms of the other using the "$8$ more" relation.
options.B: Say that solving for both numbers is what creates the "$8$ more" relation, instead of using that relation to reduce to one variable first.
options.C: Let the smaller be $x$; then the larger is $x+8$, so $x+(x+8)=50$.
options.D: Set up a two-equation elimination system in $x$ and $y$ without first expressing one quantity in terms of the other, beyond this one-variable reduction.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Tara knows two numbers sum to $48$, and the larger is $10$ more than the smaller. She wants one equation in one unknown.

parts.text: Which plan correctly reduces the two unknowns to one variable?

options.text: Keep both unknowns separate and write two unrelated equations with no link between them.
Let the smaller be $x$ and the larger be $x+10$, then write $x+(x+10)=48$.
Say that forming the equation is what creates the sum $48$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Wafa knows two numbers sum to $36$, and the larger is $6$ more than the smaller. She wants one equation in one unknown.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Let the smaller be $x$; then the larger is $x+6$, so $x+(x+6)=36$.
options.B: Write $x+y=36$ and stop.
options.C: Solving for both numbers is what creates the "$6$ more" relation.
options.D: Use elimination on a pair of equations in $x$ and $y$ as the first step.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anjali knows that $x=5$ satisfies $x+3=8$. She wants a new equation that still has solution $x=5$.

Which equation works?

options.A: $2x+3=16$, multiplying only the left side by $2$.
options.B: $x^2-1=24$, an equation not built by the same operation on both sides of $x+3=8$.
options.C: $2(x+3)=16$, multiplying both sides of $x+3=8$ by $2$.
options.D: $x+3=8$ itself, because the printed $8$ is already visible.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sameer knows that $x=4$ satisfies $x+6=10$. He wants new equations that still have solution $x=4$.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: $3x+6=30$ works, multiplying only the left side of $x+6=10$ by $3$.
options.B: $3(x+6)=30$ works, multiplying both sides of $x+6=10$ by $3$.
options.C: $(x+6)+2=12$ works, adding $2$ to both sides of $x+6=10$.
options.D: $x+6=10$ itself is the only allowed equation, because $10$ is already printed.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Wafa knows that $x=6$ satisfies $x-2=4$. She wants a new equation that still has solution $x=6$.

Which equation works?

options.A: $2(x-2)=8$, multiplying both sides of $x-2=4$ by $2$.
options.B: $2x-2=8$, multiplying only the left side of $x-2=4$ by $2$.
options.C: $x-2=4$ itself is the only allowed equation, because $4$ is already printed.
options.D: $x+2=4$, reversing the subtraction into addition on the left side only.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ishaan solves $3(x-2)=12$. Four solution steps are offered.

Which steps preserve equality and handle the brackets and coefficients correctly? One or more options may be correct.

options.A: Write $x=6$ at once, without checking any transformation from $3(x-2)=12$.
options.B: Expand to $3x-6=12$, distributing $3$ over $(x-2)$.
options.C: Then write $3x=18$ by adding $6$ to both sides.
options.D: Accept a step because the handwriting looks neat, without checking signs or brackets.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Anvi solves $2(x+3)=14$. A classmate writes the next line as $2x+3=14$.

parts.text: Is that step correct?

options.text: Incorrect: distributing $2$ must give $2x+6=14$, so the $+3$ was left undoubled.
Correct, because the final answer might still be checked later.
Correct, because the handwriting looks neat.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Diya solves $7x+5=3x+17$ using the form $Ax+B=Cx+D$ with $x=\dfrac{D-B}{A-C}$.

Which claim is correct?

options.B: $A=5$, $B=7$, $C=17$, $D=3$, matching the four printed numbers from smallest to largest.
options.D: Only $A$ and $C$ are used; $B$ and $D$ are left out of the formula.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kabir rewrites $5x+8=2x+20$ in the form $Ax+B=Cx+D$ and then uses $x=\dfrac{D-B}{A-C}$.

Which claim correctly identifies the values and the solution?

options.A: Call the answer the letter $B$ alone, and stop.
options.B: Use $x=\dfrac{D-B}{A-C}$ even when the equation is not first put in $Ax+B=Cx+D$ form.
options.D: Say that dividing for $x$ is what creates the $Ax+B=Cx+D$ layout of the equation.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
A school has lockers numbered 1 to 9, all starting closed. Student 1 toggles every locker. Student 2 toggles every 2nd locker. Student 3 toggles every 3rd, and so on, up to student 9.

After every student has finished, which lockers are open?

options.A: Lockers 1, 4, and 9
options.B: Lockers 2, 3, 5, and 7
options.D: Lockers 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yash's school has lockers numbered 1 to 16. Every locker starts closed. Student 1 toggles every locker. Student 2 toggles every 2nd locker. Student 3 toggles every 3rd, and so on, up to student 16.

Which two claims are correct after every student has finished?

options.A: The lockers that stay open are the prime-numbered lockers.
options.B: Lockers 1, 4, 9, and 16 stay open.
options.C: A locker stays open when it is toggled an odd number of times.
options.D: Every even-numbered locker stays open.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Inaya lines up $16$ closed school lockers numbered $1$ to $16$. Student $k$ toggles every $k$-th locker, for $k=1,2,\ldots,16$, starting from all closed.

parts.text: Which claim correctly names the lockers that remain open?

options.text: Lockers $1$, $4$, $9$, and $16$ remain open.
Every even-numbered locker remains open.
Only locker $1$ remains open.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri studies lockers numbered 1 to 12. A locker is touched exactly twice when its number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.

Which list shows only lockers touched exactly twice?
author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ishaan studies school lockers numbered $1$ to $15$. A locker is touched exactly twice when its number has exactly two factors, $1$ and itself.

Which list shows only lockers touched exactly twice?

options.A: The list of every locker number that has a factor other than $1$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Zubin studies classroom lockers numbered $1$ to $20$. A locker is touched exactly twice when its number has exactly two factors, $1$ and itself.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims are correct?

options.A: Lockers $1$, $2$, $3$, $5$ and $7$ are all touched exactly twice.
options.B: Lockers $2$, $3$, $5$, $7$, $11$, $13$, $17$ and $19$ are touched exactly twice.
options.C: Locker $1$ is not touched exactly twice.
options.D: Locker $20$ is touched exactly twice because $20$ is the last locker number.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yamini asks whether 36 is a square number and how to write it with square notation.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: 36 is only a 'perfect square' label, not a square number.
options.B: Because 36 is a square number it produces a perfect square, so she writes 6 as 36².
options.C: 36 = 6 × 6 = 6², so 36 is a perfect square.
options.D: 36 is a square number because a square array splits into two triangular-number parts.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Imran asks whether 49 is a square number and how to write it with square notation.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: 49 is only a "perfect square" label, not a square number.
options.B: Because 49 is a square number it produces a perfect square, so he writes 7 as $49^2$.
options.C: 49 = $7 \times 7 = 7^2$, so 49 is a perfect square.
options.D: 49 is a square number because a square array splits into two triangular-number parts.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ojasvi asks whether $64$ is a square number and how to write it with square notation.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: $64$ is only a "perfect square" label, not a square number.
options.B: Because $64$ is a square number it produces a perfect square, so she writes $8$ as $64^{2}$.
options.C: $64 = 8 \times 8 = 8^{2}$, so $64$ is a perfect square.
options.D: $64$ is a square number because a square array splits into two triangular-number parts.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Omkar asks whether $47$ can be a perfect square.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call $47$ a perfect-square label without testing its digits.
options.B: Say being a perfect square is what produces a forbidden units digit, reversing the digit test.
options.C: No: a perfect square cannot end in $7$, so $47$ is not a perfect square.
options.D: Reject $47$ only because the printed tens digit $4$ looks even.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Vihaan asks whether $83$ can be a perfect square.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call $83$ a perfect-square label rather than a number checked by its last digit.
options.B: Being a perfect square is what produces a forbidden units digit, so the digit test runs backwards from the square claim.
options.C: No: a perfect square cannot end in $3$, so $83$ is not a perfect square.
options.D: Reject $83$ only because the printed tens digit $8$ looks even.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Zubin lists $38$, $49$, and $70$ and wants to rule out impossible perfect squares using last-digit patterns. Perfect squares end only in $0$, $1$, $4$, $5$, $6$, or $9$.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims are correct?

options.A: $38$ is a perfect-square label.
options.B: $38$ cannot be a perfect square, because a perfect square cannot end in $8$.
options.C: $49$ cannot be ruled out by last digit alone, because $9$ is an allowed ending.
options.D: Reject $70$ only because the printed tens digit $7$ looks odd.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri looks at the consecutive squares $7^2 = 49$ and $8^2 = 64$.

Which claim about the gap is correct?

options.A: Call "gap" the label $64$, without subtracting the consecutive squares.
options.B: Say the gap is what produces the squares $49$ and $64$.
options.C: The gap is $15$, and there are $14$ whole numbers strictly between $49$ and $64$, because consecutive squares differ by consecutive odd numbers and the count between is one less than the gap.
options.D: Report $8$ alone, because that digit is printed in $8^2$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Avni looks at the consecutive squares $9^{2}=81$ and $10^{2}=100$.

Which two claims about the gap are correct?

options.A: Call the gap the label $100$, with no subtraction of the consecutive squares.
options.B: The gap is $19$, because consecutive squares differ by consecutive odd numbers and $100-81=19$.
options.C: There are $18$ whole numbers strictly between $81$ and $100$, one less than the gap $19$.
options.D: The gap $19$ is what produces the squares $81$ and $100$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Zubin looks at the consecutive squares $11^{2}=121$ and $12^{2}=144$.

Which claim about the gap is correct?

options.A: The gap is $144$, the larger square.
options.B: The gap $23$ is what produces the squares $121$ and $144$.
options.C: The gap is $23$, and there are $22$ whole numbers strictly between $121$ and $144$.
options.D: The gap is $12$, the larger base printed in $12^{2}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tara tests whether $36$ is a perfect square by subtracting consecutive odd numbers starting from $1$: $36-1=35$, $35-3=32$, $32-5=27$, and so on.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the process odd numbers only, without checking whether the subtractions reach $0$.
options.B: Stop after any single subtraction, skipping the need to continue through consecutive odds until $0$ or a pass below $0$.
options.C: Keep subtracting $1$, $3$, $5$, $\ldots$ in order; reaching exactly $0$ after six steps shows $36=6^{2}$.
options.D: Decide from the printed digit $6$ in $36$ alone, without the odd-number test.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Vihaan tests whether $25$ is a perfect square by subtracting consecutive odd numbers starting from $1$: $25-1=24$, $24-3=21$, $21-5=16$, and so on.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the process a sum of odd numbers and treat that label alone as the decision.
options.B: Subtract odd numbers that skip ahead or start after $1$, and treat a later return to $0$ as proof that $25$ is square.
options.C: Keep subtracting $1$, $3$, $5$, $7$, $9$ in order; reaching exactly $0$ after five steps shows $25=5^{2}$.
options.D: Decide from the printed digit $5$ in $25$ alone.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Zubin tests whether $49$ is a perfect square by subtracting consecutive odd numbers starting from $1$: $49-1=48$, $48-3=45$, $45-5=40$, and so on.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims are correct?

options.A: $49$ is a perfect square because the test is a sum of odd numbers.
options.B: Continuing $1$, $3$, $5$, $7$, $9$, $11$, $13$ in order reaches exactly $0$ after seven steps, so $49=7^{2}$.
options.C: The sum of the first seven odd numbers starting at $1$ equals $49$.
options.D: $49$ is a perfect square because its units digit is $9$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Jatin lists triangular numbers $1$, $3$, $6$, $10$ and wants to connect them to square-number patterns.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the answer "square number" only, without joining two adjacent triangular totals.
options.B: Say that the square totals are what create the triangular numbers $1$, $3$, $6$, $10$, instead of pairing adjacent triangular numbers to make squares.
options.C: Two adjacent triangular numbers make a square: $1+3=4$, $3+6=9$, $6+10=16$, so extending the triangular pattern also builds the related square pattern.
options.D: Pick $10$ as a square only because $10$ is the largest printed triangular number in the list.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Yash's triangular dot pattern with rows of 1, then 2, then 3 dots, and a square 3-by-3 dot array.

Which claim connects the triangular pattern to the square pattern?

options.A: Two adjacent triangular totals join into a square: $3+6=9$, matching the 3-by-3 array.
options.B: The whole display is only a square-number pattern, so the triangular rows need no role.
options.C: The square 3-by-3 array is what creates the triangular rows of 1, 2, and 3 dots.
options.D: The answer is 9 only because 9 is the largest count printed beside the arrays.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Yamini's triangular dot pattern with rows of 1, then 2, then 3, then 4 dots, and a square 4-by-4 dot array.

Which claim connects the triangular pattern to the square pattern?

options.A: Two adjacent triangular totals join into a square: $6+10=16$, matching the 4-by-4 array.
options.B: The whole display is only a square-number pattern, so the triangular rows need no role.
options.C: The square 4-by-4 array is what creates the triangular rows of 1, 2, 3, and 4 dots.
options.D: The answer is 16 only because 16 is the largest count printed beside the arrays.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
A square floor tile has area 81 cm². Shreya needs the side length of the tile.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The square roots of 81 are +9 and −9, and −9 cm can be used as the side length of the tile.
options.B: The side length produces the perfect square, so the side length is 81 cm.
options.C: The side length is 9 cm, the positive square root of 81.
options.D: A negative number is an allowed physical side length for this tile.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: A square floor tile has area $64$ cm$^{2}$. Ritu needs the side length of the tile.

parts.text: Which claim is correct?

options.text: The side length produces the perfect square, so the side length is $64$ cm.
The side length is $8$ cm, the positive square root of $64$.
A side length of $-8$ cm is allowed for this tile.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Yamini's square garden patch with area $121\,\mathrm{m}^{2}$. She needs the side length of the patch.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The side length is $11\,\mathrm{m}$, the positive square root of $121$.
options.B: The square roots of $121$ are $+11$ and $-11$, and $-11\,\mathrm{m}$ can be used as the side length.
options.C: The side length produces the perfect square, so the side length is $121\,\mathrm{m}$.
options.D: A negative number is an allowed physical side length for this patch.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Smita writes the prime factorisation $576 = 2^{6} \times 3^{2}$. She wants to know whether $576$ is a perfect square and, if it is, what its square root is.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Report the words factor pair as the square root of $576$.
options.B: Finding a factor pair is what creates the prime factorisation $2^{6} \times 3^{2}$.
options.C: $576$ is a perfect square because the primes split into two identical groups $2^{3} \times 3$ and $2^{3} \times 3$, so $\sqrt{576} = 24$.
options.D: Read $576$ as a perfect cube and take its cube root instead of pairing the prime factors.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Nitya writes the prime factorisation $360=2^3\times 3^2\times 5$.

parts.text: Which claim correctly decides whether $360$ is a perfect square?

options.text: Call the answer a factor pair of $360$, and stop.
$360$ is not a perfect square, because in the prime factorisation the exponents of $2$ and of $5$ are not even.
Say that listing a factor pair is what creates the prime factorisation of $360$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kabir wants a whole-number bound for $\sqrt{50}$. He knows $7^{2} = 49$ and $8^{2} = 64$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: $\sqrt{50}$ lies between 7 and 8, because $49 < 50 < 64$.
options.B: $\sqrt{50} = 25$, by halving 50.
options.C: $\sqrt{50}$ is between 7 and 8 only when 50 is a perfect square.
options.D: The nearby squares 49 and 64 settle $\sqrt{50}$ as exactly 7.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Vihaan wants a whole-number bound for $\sqrt{80}$. He knows $8^{2}=64$ and $9^{2}=81$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: $\sqrt{80}=40$, by halving $80$.
options.B: $\sqrt{80}$ lies between $8$ and $9$ only when $80$ is a perfect square.
options.C: $\sqrt{80}$ lies between $8$ and $9$, because $64<80<81$.
options.D: The nearby squares $64$ and $81$ settle $\sqrt{80}$ as exactly $8$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Megha checks which of these whole numbers are perfect cubes and computes simple cubes.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: $8$ is a perfect cube because $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$.
options.B: $9$ is a perfect cube because $3 \times 3 = 9$.
options.C: $27$ is a perfect cube because $3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27$.
options.D: Every odd whole number is a perfect cube because $1$ and $27$ are cubes.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tara checks whether whole numbers are perfect cubes and computes simple cubes.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call $64$ a perfect cube label only, with no check that some whole number cubes to $64$.
options.B: $100$ is a perfect cube because it ends with two zeros.
options.C: $4^{3} = 64$, so $64$ is a perfect cube; also $3^{3} = 27$.
options.D: $27$ is a perfect cube even when the edge length is not a whole number of unit cubes.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Irfan uses last-digit and trailing-zero patterns to test whether a whole number can be a perfect cube.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: A perfect cube can end only in $0$, $1$, $4$, $5$, $6$, or $9$, as for perfect squares.
options.B: A whole number ending in exactly two zeros can be a perfect cube.
options.C: A perfect cube may end in any digit $0$ through $9$, and trailing zeros in a perfect cube come in groups of three.
options.D: Every whole number ending in $8$ is a perfect cube because $2^{3}=8$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ira checks whether $2500$ and $8000$ could be perfect cubes by using last-digit and trailing-zero patterns.

Which two claims correctly apply those patterns?

options.A: Call the full answer the label units digit, and stop there.
options.B: $8000$ may be a perfect cube: trailing zeros in a cube come in groups of three.
options.C: $2500$ cannot be a perfect cube: a cube cannot end in exactly two zeros.
options.D: Call $2500$ a cube only because the printed $25$ looks largest on the page.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sahil notes that $1729=1^{3}+12^{3}$ and $1729=9^{3}+10^{3}$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: $1729$ is a taxicab number because $1729$ is itself a perfect cube.
options.B: Writing the two cube sums is what creates the digits of $1729$.
options.C: $1729$ is a taxicab number because it is a sum of two positive cubes in two different ways.
options.D: $1729$ is a taxicab number because it ends with $9$, like $9^{3}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Meher studies numbers that can be written as a sum of two positive cubes in two different ways.

parts.text: Which number is a taxicab number of that kind?
Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Neel knows that some cubes equal a block of consecutive odd numbers.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: $8=3+5$, so $8$ is $2^{3}$ written as two consecutive odd numbers.
options.B: Every sum of consecutive odd numbers is a cube.
options.C: $27=7+9+11$, so $27$ is $3^{3}$ written as three consecutive odd numbers.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Avni knows that some cubes equal a block of consecutive odd numbers.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: $64=13+15+17+19$, so $64$ is $4^{3}$ written as four consecutive odd numbers.
options.B: Every sum of consecutive odd numbers is a cube.
options.C: The cube $64$ is what produces the odd addends only after the sum is named a square.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sana works with the perfect cube $27=3^{3}$.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: The cube root of $27$ can be decided with no link to a number that cubes to $27$.
options.B: The cube root of $27$ is $3$.
options.C: The cube root of $3^{3}$ is $3$.
options.D: The cube root of $27$ is $27\div 3=9$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Ritu works with the perfect cube $125=5^{3}$.

parts.text: Which claim is correct?

options.text: The cube root of $125$ is $5$.
The cube root of $125$ can be decided with no link to a number that cubes to $125$.
The cube root of $125$ is $125\div 5=25$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Arjun writes $216=2^{3}\times 3^{3}$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: $216$ is a perfect cube with no need to group its prime factors in threes.
options.B: The cube root produces the prime factorisation $2^{3}\times 3^{3}$, rather than reading one factor from each triplet.
options.C: $216$ is a perfect cube and its cube root is $2\times 3=6$.
options.D: The same triplet test also settles every even number, not only perfect-cube checks.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Krish writes the prime factorisation $1728=2^{6}\times 3^{3}$ and checks for a perfect cube and its cube root.

parts.text: What should he conclude?

options.text: 1728 is a perfect cube and its cube root is 12.
1728 is a perfect cube and its cube root is 24.
1728 is not a perfect cube because an exponent is even.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Heena lists $1$, $4$, $9$, $16$ (squares) and $1$, $8$, $27$, $64$ (cubes).

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Both lists are square sequences under one shared name.
options.B: For squares, first differences being odd is enough; second differences need not be constantly $2$.
options.C: For squares, first differences are odd and second differences are constantly $2$; cubes need further difference levels before a constant appears.
options.D: The constant-second-difference rule for squares also classifies every cube list without further differences.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Anvi lists $1,4,9,16,25$ and forms first differences $3,5,7,9$, then second differences $2,2,2$. She compares this pattern with perfect squares and perfect cubes.

parts.text: What should she conclude?

options.text: The second differences stay at 2, which matches a sequence of perfect squares.
The second differences stay at 2, which matches a sequence of perfect cubes.
Constant first differences mean the sequence is cubes.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sahil folds a sheet so each fold doubles the current thickness. The starting thickness is 0.1 mm. He wants the thickness after k folds.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Add 2 mm at each fold to the starting thickness.
options.B: Multiply the starting thickness by k only, ignoring that each fold acts on the current thickness.
options.C: Replace "double" with "add two" and sum 0.1 + 2 + 2 + … for k folds.
options.D: Start at 0.1 mm and multiply by 2 at each fold (repeated multiplication).

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Kavya starts with a dough ball of mass 50 g. Each rise doubles the current mass. She wants the mass after n rises.

parts.text: Which claim models the mass correctly?

options.text: Start at 50 g and multiply by 2 at each rise.
Start at 50 g and add 2 g at each rise.
Multiply the starting 50 g by n only.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sia starts a culture with $3$ cells. Every hour the count becomes three times the count from the hour before.

Which two claims correctly decide how to model the count after $4$ hours?

options.A: Add $3$ four times to the starting count to get the count after $4$ hours.
options.B: Multiply the starting count by $3$ once for each of the $4$ hours.
options.C: The count after $4$ hours is $3\times 3\times 3\times 3\times 3$.
options.D: The starting count is the product of four hourly triples.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Komal writes the product 5 × 5 × 5 × 5 and wants exponential notation with the correct base and exponent.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Write 4^5, treating the count of factors as the base.
options.B: Write 5^4 and also allow 5 × 4 as the same meaning.
options.C: Write 5^4: base 5 with exponent 4, meaning four factors of 5.
options.D: The exponent is the value being multiplied, so here the base may be ignored.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kavya writes the product $4 \times 4 \times 4 \times 4 \times 4$ and wants exponential notation with the correct base and exponent.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: The exponent is $4$, because $4$ is the number being multiplied.
options.B: The base is $4$, the repeated factor in the product.
options.C: The exponent is $5$, because $4$ appears as a factor five times.
options.D: The notation $4^5$ means $4$ multiplied by $5$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Abhay writes the product $6 \times 6 \times 6$ and wants exponential notation with the correct base and exponent.

parts.text: Which notation is correct?

options.text: $6 \times 3$

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Chitra has the prime factorisation 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 and wants it in exponential form.

Which writing is correct?

options.A: Write 2 × 3 only, dropping the repeated factors instead of grouping them as exponents.
options.B: Write 2³ × 3², grouping three factors of 2 and two factors of 3.
options.C: Start from 2³ × 3² to invent the product, as if the exponential form produced the primes.
options.D: Divide the prime factors instead of multiplying them when writing the factorisation.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Diya has the prime factorisation $2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 3$ and wants it in exponential form.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: Write $2 \times 3$ only, dropping the repeated factors instead of grouping them as exponents.
options.B: Write $2^2 \times 3^3$, grouping two factors of 2 and three factors of 3.
options.C: Each repeated prime becomes a base, and the count of repeats becomes its exponent.
options.D: Start from $2^2 \times 3^3$ to invent the product, as if the exponential form produced the primes.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Prisha has the prime factorisation $2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 5 \times 5$ and wants it in exponential form.

Which writing is correct?

options.A: Write $2 \times 5$ only, dropping the repeated factors instead of grouping them as exponents.
options.B: Start from $2^{4} \times 5^{2}$ to invent the product, as if the exponential form produced the primes.
options.C: Write $2^{4} \times 5^{2}$, grouping four factors of $2$ and two factors of $5$.
options.D: Divide the prime factors instead of multiplying them when writing the factorisation.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sahil simplifies $3^{4}\times 3^{3}$.

Which step is valid?

options.A: Write $3^{4}\times 5^{3}=3^{7}$, adding the exponents even though the bases are not the same.
options.B: Write $3^{4}+3^{3}=3^{7}$, extending the product rule to a sum of powers.
options.C: Write $3^{4}\times 3^{3}=3^{7}$, adding the exponents because the bases are the same.
options.D: Choose $3^{7}$ only because $7$ is the largest single digit printed among $3$, $4$, and $3$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Nitya simplifies $5^{3} \times 5^{4}$.

parts.text: Which step is valid?

options.text: Write $5^{3} \times 5^{4} = 5^{7}$, adding the exponents because the bases are the same.
Write $5^{3} \times 7^{4} = 5^{7}$, adding the exponents even though the bases are not the same.
Choose $5^{7}$ only because $7$ is the largest single digit among $5$, $3$, and $4$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Abhay simplifies $2^{5} \times 2^{3}$.

parts.text: Which step is valid?

options.text: Write $2^{5} \times 2^{3} = 2^{8}$, adding the exponents because the bases are the same.
Write $2^{5} \times 3^{3} = 2^{8}$, adding the exponents for different bases.
Choose $2^{8}$ because $8$ is the sum of the printed digits $2$, $5$, and $3$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Komal simplifies $(2^{3})^{4}$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the answer inner exponent, without multiplying the exponents.
options.B: Say that $2^{12}$ is what creates the written form $(2^{3})^{4}$.
options.D: Choose $2^{4}$ only because $4$ is the largest single printed exponent.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sameer simplifies $(3^{2})^{5}$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The answer is the inner exponent $2$, with no product of the exponents.
options.B: $3^{10}$ is what creates the written form $(3^{2})^{5}$.
options.D: Write $3^{5}$ only, because $5$ is the largest single printed exponent.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Abhay simplifies $(5^{2})^{3}$.

parts.text: Which claim is correct?

options.text: $5^{6}$ is what creates the written form $(5^{2})^{3}$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yamini must simplify $3^{4}\times 2^{4}$.

Which rewrite is correct?

options.A: Call the answer same exponent only, without combining the bases.
options.B: Write $3^{4}\times 2^{4}=6^{8}$, adding the exponents as if the bases were already the same.
options.C: Write $3^{4}\times 2^{4}=(3\times 2)^{4}=6^{4}$, because the exponents match.
options.D: Also rewrite $3^{4}+2^{4}$ as $(3+2)^{4}$ by the same base-combining step, beyond products and quotients of matching powers.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anaya rewrites products and quotients of powers that share an exponent.

Which two claims correctly combine powers with the same exponent?

options.A: Call the rewrite a base product and treat that label alone as the simplification.
options.B: $2^{5}\times 3^{5}=6^{5}$, because five copies of $2$ times five copies of $3$ regroup as five copies of $6$.
options.C: $8^{4}\div 2^{4}=4^{4}$, because four copies of $8$ divided by four copies of $2$ regroup as four copies of $4$.
options.D: Combine $5^{3}\times 2^{4}$ the same way even though the exponents differ.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Abhay must simplify $5^{3}\times 4^{3}$.

parts.text: Which rewrite is correct?
Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nitin sets a $3$-digit lock code. Each digit may be $0$ through $9$, and $0$ is allowed in the first place. He wants the total number of codes.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Count $9$ choices for the first digit by forbidding $0$ there, skipping that $0$ is allowed as a first-digit choice on this lock.
options.B: Say that writing the total $1000$ is what creates the ten choices in each digit place, instead of multiplying the per-stage choices to get the total.
options.C: Multiply the choices at each stage: $10\times10\times10=1000$ codes.
options.D: Also count ordered meal combos from a different menu with this same $10\times10\times10$ product, beyond this lock-code stage count.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ira builds a 2-stage snack code: first she picks one of 4 chutneys, then one of 3 breads. Every chutney–bread pair is allowed.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: There are only 3 codes, because the bread count alone is the total.
options.B: The total number of codes is $4\times3=12$, the product of the choices at each stage.
options.C: Equal choice counts across stages can be written with powers; here the stages differ, so the product $4\times3$ is the right form.
options.D: Any meal price list is also counted by this same $4\times3$ product.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Zubin designs a school badge in two stages: first he picks one of 5 colours, then one of 3 pin shapes. Every colour–shape pair is allowed.

Which plan gives the total number of badges?

options.A: Count only the 5 colours, because the pin shapes do not change the total.
options.B: The 3 pin shapes produce the 5 colours, so start from shapes and ignore colour choices.
options.C: Multiply the stage counts: $5\times3=15$ badges.
options.D: Count only badges that use the first colour, so the total is $1\times3=3$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Manav simplifies $\dfrac{5^{7}}{5^{3}}$ for counting-number exponents with the same nonzero base.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: $\dfrac{5^{7}}{2^{3}}=5^{7-3}$, as if different bases still allowed subtracting exponents.
options.B: $\dfrac{5^{3}}{5^{7}}=5^{3-7}$ is covered by the same stated rule for $a>b$ counting exponents with no further condition.
options.C: $\dfrac{5^{7}}{5^{3}}=5^{7-3}=5^{4}$, because the bases are the same and nonzero.
options.D: The value is $5$, because $5$ is the printed base shown most clearly.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Neil simplifies $\dfrac{7^{8}}{7^{3}}$ for counting-number exponents with the same nonzero base.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: $\dfrac{7^{8}}{3^{3}}=7^{8-3}$, as if different bases still allowed subtracting exponents.
options.B: $\dfrac{7^{3}}{7^{8}}=7^{3-8}$ is covered by the same stated rule for $a>b$ counting exponents with no further condition.
options.C: $\dfrac{7^{8}}{7^{3}}=7^{8-3}=7^{5}$, because the bases are the same and nonzero.
options.D: The value is $7$, because $7$ is the printed base shown most clearly.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Zubin simplifies $\dfrac{3^{9}}{3^{4}}$ for counting-number exponents with the same nonzero base.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims are correct?

options.A: $\dfrac{2^{9}}{3^{4}}$ also equals a single power by subtracting the exponents $9-4$.
options.C: The bases match and are nonzero, so subtracting the exponents is allowed.
options.D: The answer is $3^{9}$ because $9$ is the largest exponent printed in the fraction.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kabir evaluates $5^{0}$ and $(-3)^{0}$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: $5^{0} = 0$, because the exponent is zero.
options.B: $5^{0} = 1$ and $(-3)^{0} = 1$, for these nonzero bases.
options.C: $5^{0} = 1$ only when the base is positive; $(-3)^{0}$ is undefined.
options.D: Any base to the power 0 equals 1, including $0^{0}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Aarav simplifies powers with a nonzero base. He uses the zero-exponent rule.

Which two claims correctly state and justify $7^0$?

options.A: Write $7^0=1$ even when the same cancellation $7^a/7^a=1$ for nonzero $7$ is not available.
options.B: $7^0=1$, because $7^a\div 7^a=1$ for nonzero $7$, and that matches the zero-exponent rule.
options.C: The zero-exponent rule for nonzero bases gives $7^0=1$.
options.D: Apply $x^0=1$ also when the base is $0$, treating $0^0$ the same way.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Parth works with the nonzero base $5$ and integer exponents.

Which two claims are correct?
author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anaya works with the nonzero base $4$ and integer exponents.

Which two claims are correct?
author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sameer compares the powers $3^{7}$ and $3^{4}$ with the same positive base.

Which claim correctly compares them?

options.A: Report the words exponent difference as the value of $3^{7}$.
options.B: The larger exponent is what creates the base $3$.
options.D: $3^{7}$ is larger because $7$ is the digit printed largest.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ishaan compares the powers $5^{6}$ and $5^{4}$ with the same positive base.

Which two claims correctly use the exponent difference?

options.A: Call the answer same positive base only, with no comparison of $5^{6}$ and $5^{4}$.
options.C: Because the exponents differ by $2$ and the base $5>1$, $5^{6}$ is greater than $5^{4}$.
options.D: $5^{4}$ is greater than $5^{6}$, because the usual order of the exponents is read backwards.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tanvi writes the place value of each digit in $405.27$ using powers of $10$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Report the words power of $10$ as the digit $4$.
options.B: The $2$ in $405.27$ has place value $2\times 10^{2}$.
options.D: The value is $405$, because those digits are printed largest before the point.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Adil writes the place value of each digit in $3.74$ using powers of $10$.

parts.text: Which product correctly writes the place value of the digit $7$?
Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sameer writes $45200$ in scientific notation.

Which claim is correct?

options.B: The form $10^{4}\times 4.52$ is what creates the rule $1\le x<10$.
options.C: $45200=4.52\times 10^{4}$, with coefficient $4.52$ satisfying $1\le x<10$.
options.D: $4.52\times 10^{4}$ is also the scientific form of $0.452$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yash must write $59000$ in scientific notation, with coefficient $x$ satisfying $1 \le x < 10$.

Which claim is correct?

options.B: The exponent $4$ is what creates the coefficient $5.9$.
options.D: Also allow $0.59 \times 10^{5}$ under the same scientific-notation rule.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Vimal compares $4.2\times 10^{5}$ and $3.8\times 10^{6}$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Compare only the coefficients $4.2$ and $3.8$ and ignore the powers of $10$.
options.B: The same comparison ranks every pair of numbers, including those not written with powers of $10$.
options.C: $3.8\times 10^{6}$ is larger because the exponent $6$ is greater than $5$.
options.D: Add each coefficient to its exponent ($4.2+5$ versus $3.8+6$) to decide the order.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sameer compares $5.1\times 10^{4}$ and $4.7\times 10^{5}$.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: Compare only the coefficients $5.1$ and $4.7$ and ignore the powers of $10$.
options.B: $4.7\times 10^{5}$ is larger because the exponent $5$ is greater than $4$.
options.C: Order of magnitude is checked first; the larger exponent decides before coefficients are compared.
options.D: Add each coefficient to its exponent ($5.1+4$ versus $4.7+5$) to decide the order.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Irfan estimates how many heartbeats a person has in one year. He takes about $70$ beats each minute.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The yearly total is the word "estimate".
options.B: The length of one year is what produces the rate of $70$ beats each minute.
options.C: A close estimate is about $70 \times 60 \times 24 \times 365$ beats from the rate and the time factors.
options.D: Add $70+60+24+365$ to get the yearly number of beats.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sameer estimates how many steps a walker takes in one year. He takes about $100$ steps each minute of walking and walks about $30$ minutes each day.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The yearly total is the word "estimate".
options.B: The length of one year is what produces the rate of $100$ steps each minute.
options.C: A close estimate is about $100 \times 30 \times 365$ steps from the rate and the time factors.
options.D: Add $100+30+365$ to get the yearly number of steps.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Megha compares two savings plans that both start with ₹100. Plan P adds ₹100 each month. Plan Q doubles the amount each month.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Both plans are linear growth because both use the number $100$.
options.B: Doubling each month is what creates the starting amount ₹100.
options.C: Plan P shows linear growth; Plan Q shows exponential growth.
