options.D: The linear and exponential labels also classify every pair of school marks as growth types.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anvi compares two savings plans starting at ₹1000.
Plan L: add ₹200 at the end of every month (linear growth).
Plan E: multiply the current amount by 1.1 at the end of every month (exponential growth).

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Both plans show linear growth by adding ₹200 each month.
options.B: Plan L shows exponential growth, and Plan E shows linear growth.
options.C: Plan L shows linear growth; Plan E shows exponential growth.
options.D: Only Plan E can be used for more than one month.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sahil matches large-number names to powers of $10$ in the Indian and international systems.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: $1$ crore equals $10^{6}$.
options.B: Large-number names need no powers of $10$; the names alone settle the size.
options.C: In the Indian system $1$ crore $=10^{7}$; in the international system $1$ million $=10^{6}$.
options.D: Any name that looks large is a crore because crore is a long word.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Imran matches large-number names to powers of 10. He knows 1 crore $=10^{7}$ in the Indian system and 1 million $=10^{6}$ in the international system.

Which claim is correct?

options.C: 1 crore $=10$ million.
options.D: 1 crore equals 1 million because both names are large.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Walia counts seven pebbles by matching each pebble to one clap in order, from clap 1 through clap 7.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The ordered clap sequence alone counts the pebbles even if some pebbles are skipped.
options.B: One-to-one matching works only with written Hindu numerals, not with claps.
options.C: Each pebble is matched exactly once to one clap, so the ordered claps show that there are seven pebbles.
options.D: Seven is correct because the word seven is the largest word written on the board.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Adil counts six mangoes by matching each mango to one bead in order, from bead 1 through bead 6.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The ordered bead sequence alone counts the mangoes even if some mangoes are left unmatched.
options.B: One-to-one matching works only when Hindu numerals are written on the beads.
options.C: Each mango is matched exactly once to one bead, so the ordered beads show that there are six mangoes.
options.D: Six is correct because the word six is the longest word Adil wrote beside the beads.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Boman has a pile of identical beads and an ordered clap sequence: first clap, second clap, third clap, and so on. He wants the clap sequence to represent how many beads are in the pile.

Which claim correctly states what he must do?

options.A: Match each bead to exactly one clap in order, with no bead left unmatched and no clap left unused for a bead.
options.B: Clap once for the whole pile, then name the size from the sound alone.
options.C: Match some beads to two claps so the sequence runs longer than the pile.
options.D: Skip matching the last few beads once the claps sound familiar.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Dev compares three ways to count a large pile of beads: the spoken list one, two, three, … ; a list that stops at twenty; and a mark for each bead with no number words.

Which judgement is correct?

options.A: Call the stopping-at-twenty list an unending sequence, because it uses number words.
options.B: The spoken list one, two, three, … works even if he scrambles the order of the words.
options.C: The ordered list one, two, three, … keeps going and stays usable for large piles; the finite list stops, and single marks become cumbersome.
options.D: Choose the darkest bead in the pile as the count.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Farhan compares three counting plans for a large bag of marbles: the spoken list one, two, three, … ; a fixed list that stops at thirty; and a single chalk mark for each marble with no number words.

parts.text: Which claim correctly judges those plans for a large collection?

options.text: Call the answer the phrase unending sequence, and stop there.
The spoken list keeps going and stays usable; the list that stops at thirty is finite; chalk marks alone can continue but become cumbersome.
Prefer chalk marks because each mark is the largest printed symbol on the board.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bina compares three plans for counting a large jar of rice grains: the spoken list one, two, three, \ldots ; a list that stops at fifty; and a tick mark for each grain with no number words.

Which judgement is correct?

options.A: The tick marks alone are best because they carry the label of an unending sequence.
options.B: The list that stops at fifty works for any jar size.
options.C: The spoken list one, two, three, \ldots can continue and stays usable for a large jar.
options.D: Fifty is the correct plan because fifty is the largest number named.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tara learns Gumulgal number names: urapon means 1 and ukasar means 2. Longer names are built as sums of these group words, so ukasar-urapon means 3 and ukasar-ukasar means 4.

Which reading of ukasar-ukasar-urapon is correct?

options.A: The name means urapon, because urapon is the last word printed.
options.B: The name is just a new unrelated label, ignoring the known meanings of 1 and 2.
options.C: The name means 5, because it is 2 + 2 + 1.
options.D: Treating the parts as independent labels is what builds the total.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Krish learns Gumulgal number names: urapon means 1 and ukasar means 2. Longer names are built as sums of these group words, so ukasar-urapon means 3 and ukasar-ukasar means 4.

Which reading of ukasar-ukasar-ukasar is correct?

options.A: The name means urapon, because urapon is the usual leftover word.
options.B: The name is just a new unrelated label, ignoring the known meanings of 1 and 2.
options.C: The name means 6, because it is $2 + 2 + 2$.
options.D: Treating the three parts as independent labels is what builds the total 6.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Rahul learns Gumulgal number names: urapon means $1$ and ukasar means $2$. Longer names are built as sums of these group words, so ukasar-urapon means $3$ and ukasar-ukasar means $4$. He wants the correct name for a count of $5$ sticks.

parts.text: Which claim is correct?

options.text: The name for $5$ is ukasar-ukasar-urapon, because it is $2 + 2 + 1$.
The name for $5$ is urapon, because urapon is the leftover word for any odd count.
Any new string of syllables may be used for $5$, ignoring the known meanings of $1$ and $2$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit writes numbers with Roman landmarks: I $=1$, V $=5$, X $=10$, L $=50$. He wants to represent $48$.

Which plan follows landmark decomposition?

options.A: Answer "Roman numerals", naming the system instead of building $48$ from landmarks.
options.B: String any mix of I, V, X, L without taking as many of the largest useful landmark as possible first.
options.C: Take one XL for $40$ (the largest useful landmark not past $48$), then VIII for the remaining $8$, writing XLVIII.
options.D: Copy the Hindu–Arabic digits $4$ and $8$ as shapes, and treat those drawn shapes as the Roman form.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ishaan writes numbers with Roman landmarks: I $=1$, V $=5$, X $=10$, L $=50$. He wants to represent $39$.

Which plan follows landmark decomposition?

options.A: Answer "Roman numerals", naming the writing system instead of building $39$ from landmarks.
options.B: Place any mix of I, V, X, and L in any order until the symbols look long enough.
options.C: Take one XXX for $30$ (the largest useful landmark not past $39$), then IX for the remaining $9$.
options.D: Copy the digits $3$ and $9$ as drawn shapes and treat those shapes as the Roman form.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bina writes numbers with Roman landmarks: I $=1$, V $=5$, X $=10$, L $=50$. She wants to represent $27$.

Which plan follows landmark decomposition?

options.A: The plan is the label "Roman numerals".
options.B: Write twenty-seven I marks only.
options.C: Take two X for $20$, one V for $5$, and two I for $2$, giving XXVII.
options.D: Pick XXVII only because $27$ is the printed target.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Padma looks at landmarks $1$, $5$, $25$, $125$, where each new landmark is $5$ times the previous one.

Does this sequence form a base-$n$ system, and why?

options.A: Call the answer a fixed multiplier label only, without asking whether landmarks are repeated powers of one base.
options.B: Say it is base-$5$ even when the multipliers jump as $5$, then $3$, then $7$, with no single fixed $n$.
options.C: Yes: the first landmark is $1$ and each next landmark is the previous times the same fixed $n=5$, so the landmarks are powers of $5$.
options.D: Decide yes only because $125$ is the largest printed landmark in the list.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Ritu looks at landmarks $1$, $4$, $16$, $64$, where each new landmark is $4$ times the previous one.

parts.text: Does this sequence form a base-$n$ system, and which claim is correct?

options.text: Call the answer a fixed-multiplier label only, with no check that landmarks are powers of one base.
Yes: the first landmark is $1$ and each next landmark is the previous times the same fixed $n=4$, so the landmarks are powers of $4$.
Yes, even when the multipliers jump as $4$, then $3$, then $7$, with no single fixed $n$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bina looks at landmarks $1$, $6$, $36$, $216$, where each new landmark is $6$ times the previous one.

Does this sequence form a base-$n$ system, and why?

options.A: The answer is the fixed multiplier $6$, with no check that the landmarks are powers of one base.
options.B: Yes, it is base-$6$ even if the multipliers jumped as $6$, then $5$, then $8$.
options.C: Yes: the first landmark is $1$ and each next landmark is the previous times the same fixed $n=6$, so the landmarks are powers of $6$.
options.D: Yes, because $216$ is the largest printed landmark in the list.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Chitra adds in a base-$10$ landmark system. In one place she has $10$ copies of the $1$-landmark.

Which claim is correct before she reads the sum?

options.A: Call the answer regrouping, without exchanging the $10$ ones for one ten-landmark.
options.B: Leave all $10$ copies of the $1$-landmark unregrouped in the written sum.
options.C: Exchange the $10$ copies of the $1$-landmark for one copy of the $10$-landmark before reading the result.
options.D: Only repeat the chapter word landmark, without exchanging $10$ copies for the next landmark.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Rohan adds in a base-$5$ landmark system. In the ones place he holds $5$ copies of the $1$-landmark.

parts.text: Which claim is correct before he reads the sum?

options.text: Leave the $5$ ones unexchanged and read five ones as the ones digit.
Exchange the $5$ ones for one copy of the $5$-landmark, then read the sum.
Call the step regrouping and stop after naming that label.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bina adds in a base-$4$ landmark system. In the ones place she holds $4$ copies of the $1$-landmark.

Which claim is correct before she reads the sum?

options.A: Regrouping is the correct answer for this sum.
options.B: The written sum keeps all $4$ copies of the $1$-landmark in the ones place.
options.C: Exchange the $4$ copies of the $1$-landmark for one copy of the $4$-landmark before reading the result.
options.D: In a base-$10$ system the same $4$ ones may also stay unregrouped.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ritu works in base $10$. She multiplies the landmark $100$ by $10$, then multiplies $23=20+3$ by $10$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the answer landmark only, without moving among powers of $10$ or distributing across grouped parts.
options.B: Treat $100\times10$ as a power move to $1000$, but multiply $23\times10$ without distributing over $20+3$.
options.C: Landmark $100\times10=1000$ (power up by $1$); then $23\times10=(20+3)\times10=200+30=230$ by distributing.
options.D: Say that writing $230$ is what creates the landmark move $100\times10=1000$, instead of using power moves and distribution to build products.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Adil works in base ten with landmark powers of 10. He multiplies the landmark $100$ by $10$, then multiplies the grouped number $300+40$ by $10$.

parts.text: Which claim treats landmark products as moves among powers and then distributes across the grouped parts?

options.text: $100\times10$ becomes the next landmark $1000$, and $10\times(300+40)=3000+400$.
The work is only about naming landmark powers, so no multiplication step is needed.
Add the landmarks $100+10$ and $300+40$ instead of multiplying by 10.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Abhay works in base ten with landmark powers of 10. He multiplies the landmark $1000$ by $10$, then multiplies the grouped number $200+30$ by $10$.

parts.text: Which claim treats landmark products as moves among powers and then distributes across the grouped parts?

options.text: $1000\times10$ becomes the next landmark $10000$, and $10\times(200+30)=2000+300$.
The work is only about naming landmark powers, so no multiplication step is needed.
Add the landmarks $1000+10$ and $200+30$ instead of multiplying by 10.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Divya compares writing large numbers with a new landmark symbol for every power, versus using place value.

Which claim correctly explains place-value numerals?

options.A: Place value still works if each digit keeps a fixed absolute value in every position.
options.B: Writing a new landmark symbol for each power is what creates place value.
options.C: The same digit can mean ones or sixties depending on its position, so no new symbol is needed for each landmark.
options.D: Place value is found by squaring a digit's position number.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Avni compares writing large numbers with a new landmark symbol for every power, versus using place value.

Which two claims correctly explain place-value numerals?

options.A: Place value still works if each digit keeps a fixed absolute value in every position.
options.B: The same digit can mean ones or sixties depending on its position, so no new symbol is needed for each landmark.
options.C: Place value uses position to decide a symbol's value rather than inventing a separate symbol for every landmark number.
options.D: Place value is found by squaring a digit's position number.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Abhay reads the base-ten numeral $405$. He compares giving every digit a fixed value with reading each digit by its place.

parts.text: Which claim correctly explains how place value reads $405$?

options.text: $405$ means $4\times100+0\times10+5\times1$, so the digit $4$ counts hundreds because of its position.
Each digit always means the same absolute amount, so the $4$ in $405$ equals the $4$ in $4$.
Position is ignored; the numeral is read by adding the digit symbols $4$, $0$, and $5$ alone.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Naina has $3$ hundreds and $5$ ones, with no tens. She writes a place-value numeral for that amount.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Write $35$, placing the $3$ and the $5$ next to each other.
options.B: Write $350$, treating the empty tens place as if it held the ones digit $5$ shifted left.
options.C: Write $305$, using $0$ as a placeholder in the tens place.
options.D: Write $3$ and $5$ only, and leave the empty tens place blank with no digit.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Diya records three hundreds and two ones in a place-value numeral. The tens place is empty.

Which claim correctly fills that empty place?

options.A: Call the answer the word placeholder alone, and stop.
options.B: Leave the tens place blank and still claim the numeral clearly shows three hundreds and two ones.
options.C: Write $0$ in the tens place so the numeral $302$ keeps hundreds and ones in their correct positions.
options.D: Carry tens into the next place the way base-$n$ addition carries when there are $n$ copies of a unit.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Omkar reads that the Mayan landmark numbers are $1$, $20$, $360$, $7200$, and so on, written in vertical place value with a zero symbol.

parts.text: Which classification fits this system?

options.text: Almost base-$20$, because the third landmark is $360$ rather than $400$.
Exact base-$20$, because every landmark is a pure power of $20$.
Base-$10$, because the landmarks must match Hindu place values.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice that uses the third landmark.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Rohan reads that Mayan landmark numbers are $1$, $20$, $360$, $7200$, and so on, written in vertical place value with a zero symbol.

parts.text: Which claim correctly classifies this place-value system?

options.text: It is a pure base-$20$ system because every place is exactly a power of $20$.
It is almost base-$20$: places use $20$ for the second landmark, but $360$ (not $400$) breaks a pure power-of-$20$ tower, while still using vertical place value and zero.
The zero symbol alone turns any vertical list into base-$10$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Malini compares older numeral systems with the Hindu number system.

Which claim correctly states what makes the Hindu number system the efficient modern form?

options.A: The answer is the label digits $0$–$9$ alone.
options.B: Ten digits are enough; base-$10$ place value and zero as both a digit and a number are not needed.
options.C: Ten digits, base-$10$ place value, and zero as both a digit and a number make the system efficient.
options.D: Compact writing of any number is what creates the ten digits and the place-value structure.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Kavya compares older numeral systems with the Hindu number system used today.

parts.text: Which claim states what makes the Hindu number system efficient?

options.text: Ten digits $0$–$9$, base-$10$ place value, and zero as both a digit and a number.
Call the answer digits $0$–$9$ only, with no place value and no role for zero.
Place value is what creates the ten digits, so the digits come after places are named.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Parul sorts four closed shapes: a square; a triangle; a circle; and a five-sided polygon with straight sides.

Which shape is a quadrilateral?

options.A: The square
options.B: The triangle
options.C: The circle
options.D: The five-sided polygon

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows a closed shape drawn on Sana's slate, with vertices labelled A, B, C and D.

Which claim about the figure is correct?

options.A: The figure is a quadrilateral: it has four straight sides.
options.B: The figure is a triangle: it has three straight sides.
options.C: The figure is a circle: its side is a single curve.
options.D: The figure is a five-sided polygon: it has five straight sides.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows figure $F$ drawn for Karan's geometry class.

Which claim correctly classifies figure $F$?

options.A: Figure $F$ is a quadrilateral because it has four straight sides.
options.B: Figure $F$ is not a quadrilateral because two sides have different lengths.
options.C: Figure $F$ is a triangle because one corner looks sharper than the others.
options.D: Figure $F$ is a circle because the longest side bends the eye along a curve.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Harish draws several parallelograms, measures their opposite angles, and sees they match each time. He wonders whether opposite angles of every parallelogram are equal.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The measurements alone prove the property for every parallelogram.
options.B: The property is false, because measuring always reverses the true angles.
options.C: The measurements suggest a useful pattern, but a general property needs a deduction from known geometric facts.
options.D: Only a single measured parallelogram is enough to settle every quadrilateral property.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tara looks at the diagram of parallelogram $ABCD$. She measures $\angle DAB = 68^{\circ}$ and $\angle ABC = 112^{\circ}$ and notices the opposite angles match in this drawing. She wonders whether opposite angles of every parallelogram are equal.

Which claim correctly decides what her measurements justify?

options.A: The matching angles in this one drawing prove the property for every parallelogram.
options.B: Equal opposite angles are what create the parallelogram sides in the diagram.
options.C: The measurements support the pattern in this parallelogram; a general property still needs geometric reasoning from known facts.
options.D: Any four-sided shape on the page has equal opposite angles once two angles are measured.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Chetan draws several rhombi, measures their opposite sides, and sees they match each time. He wonders whether opposite sides of every rhombus are equal.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The matching measures on his drawings prove the property for every rhombus.
options.B: Measuring produces the general property, so geometric reasoning is not needed.
options.C: A general property needs geometric reasoning from known facts, not only the measured pattern.
options.D: The property checked on these rhombi also covers every quadrilateral.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Zaid has quadrilateral ABCD in which ∠A = ∠B = ∠C = ∠D = 90°.

Can he classify ABCD as a rectangle without separately checking that opposite sides are equal?

options.A: He should call the figure a right angle, not a rectangle.
options.B: Yes, even if A, B, C, D were only three rays and not a closed quadrilateral.
options.C: Yes: a quadrilateral with all angles 90° is a rectangle; opposite-side equalities then follow.
options.D: The same rule also classifies any open broken line of four right turns as a rectangle.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows quadrilateral ABCD. Anvi measures $\angle A = \angle B = \angle C = \angle D = 90^\circ$.

Can she classify ABCD as a rectangle without separately checking that opposite sides are equal?

options.A: Yes: a quadrilateral with all angles $90^\circ$ is a rectangle; opposite-side equalities then follow.
options.B: She should call the figure a right angle, not a rectangle.
options.C: Yes, even if A, B, C, D were only three rays and not a closed quadrilateral.
options.D: The same rule also classifies any open broken line of four right turns as a rectangle.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows quadrilateral $PQRS$. Sarika measures $\angle P = \angle Q = \angle R = \angle S = 90^\circ$.

Can she classify $PQRS$ as a rectangle without separately checking that opposite sides are equal?

options.A: Yes: a quadrilateral with all angles $90^\circ$ is a rectangle; opposite-side equalities then follow.
options.B: She should call the figure a right angle, not a rectangle.
options.C: Yes, even if $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ were only three rays and not a closed quadrilateral.
options.D: The same rule also classifies any open broken line of four right turns as a rectangle.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Parul asks whether calling a quadrilateral a rectangle is the same as saying its diagonals are equal and bisect each other.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: It is a rectangle from equal diagonals alone, skipping that the diagonals must also bisect each other in the parallelogram setting.
options.B: Equal bisecting diagonals are produced by the rectangle name after the fact, so either label invents the other without checking.
options.C: Among parallelograms, equal diagonals (which already bisect) make a rectangle; outside that setting the two statuses are not freely interchangeable.
options.D: The same claim also makes any two equal crossing sticks on the desk a rectangle.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows quadrilateral ABCD with diagonals AC and BD meeting at O. Kavya measures $AC = BD$, $AO = OC$, and $BO = OD$.

Which claim about ABCD is correct?

options.A: ABCD is a rectangle, because its diagonals are equal and bisect each other.
options.B: ABCD is a rectangle from $AC = BD$ alone.
options.C: The rectangle name is what creates equal bisecting diagonals, so the measurements cannot start the claim.
options.D: The same measurements also make any two equal crossing sticks on the desk a rectangle.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows quadrilateral $WXYZ$ with diagonals $WY$ and $XZ$ meeting at $O$. Chetan measures $WY = XZ$, $WO = OY$, and $XO = OZ$.

Which claim about $WXYZ$ is correct?

options.A: $WXYZ$ is a rectangle, because its diagonals are equal and bisect each other.
options.B: $WXYZ$ is a rectangle from $WY = XZ$ alone.
options.C: The rectangle label for $WXYZ$ is what produces $WY = XZ$ and the bisections at $O$.
options.D: The same measurements also make any two equal crossing sticks a rectangle.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Harish has a quadrilateral with all four angles $90^\circ$ and side lengths $5$, $8$, $5$, $8$ in order around the shape.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call it a square as the label, without checking that all sides are equal.
options.B: Say being a square is what produces the four right angles here.
options.C: It is a rectangle but not a square, because all angles are right while adjacent sides $5$ and $8$ are unequal.
options.D: Report "$5$" as the type, because that numeral is printed first.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows quadrilateral $ABCD$ with all four angles $90^\circ$ and side lengths $6$, $4$, $6$, $4$ in order around the shape.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call it a square as the label, with no check that all sides are equal.
options.B: Being a square is what produces the four right angles here.
options.C: It is a rectangle but not a square, because all angles are right while adjacent sides $6$ and $4$ are unequal.
options.D: Report $6$ as the type, because that numeral is printed first on a side.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Chetan has a quadrilateral with all four angles $90^{\circ}$ and side lengths $7$, $3$, $7$, $3$ in order around the shape.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: It is a square because all four angles are $90^{\circ}$.
options.B: Being a square is what produces the four right angles in this shape.
options.C: It is a rectangle but not a square, because all angles are right while adjacent sides $7$ and $3$ are unequal.
options.D: It is a square because the first side length printed is $7$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Farid already knows a rectangle-diagonal construction. He asks what extra diagonal condition turns that construction into a square construction.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the answer "diagonal" only, without stating any extra square condition on the diagonals.
options.B: Say that naming the figure a square is what creates equal diagonals that meet at right angles, instead of using those diagonal conditions to build the square.
options.C: Require diagonals that are equal, bisect each other, and meet at right angles (they also bisect the square's angles).
options.D: Switch to a circle-and-radius construction for a regular hexagon, and treat that method as this square-diagonal condition.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows quadrilateral $ABCD$ with diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ meeting at $O$. Sia already knows the diagonals are equal and bisect each other, as in a rectangle. She asks what extra diagonal condition makes $ABCD$ a square.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The diagonals also meet at right angles at $O$, so $ABCD$ is a square.
options.B: Call the figure a diagonal construction and treat that label alone as the square test.
options.C: Meeting at right angles is what produces equal diagonals that bisect each other.
options.D: Treat $ABCD$ as a kite whose one symmetry diagonal alone settles the square test.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Chetan already knows how to build a rectangle from equal diagonals that bisect each other. He asks what extra diagonal condition turns that construction into a square.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The extra condition required is the word diagonal.
options.B: Naming the figure a square forces the diagonals to meet at right angles.
options.C: The diagonals must also meet at right angles (and then they bisect the square's angles).
options.D: A kite test with one symmetry diagonal turns the rectangle construction into a square.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Vivek asks whether a quadrilateral can have three interior angles of $90^\circ$ and a fourth interior angle that is not $90^\circ$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the figure an "interior angle" only, without using the quadrilateral angle-sum.
options.B: Say that drawing four sides is what forces the angle sum to be $360^\circ$, instead of using the $360^\circ$ sum to constrain the fourth angle.
options.C: No: the four interior angles sum to $360^\circ$, so three right angles force the fourth to be $90^\circ$ as well.
options.D: Answer "yes" only because the stem prints the numeral $90$ three times.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Meher's quadrilateral $ABCD$ with right-angle marks at $A$, $B$, and $D$, and with the remaining interior angle at $C$ labelled $x$.

Which claim about $x$ is correct?

options.A: $x$ must be $90^\circ$, because the four interior angles of a quadrilateral sum to $360^\circ$.
options.B: $x$ is only an interior-angle label, so the quadrilateral sum does not constrain it.
options.C: Drawing the four sides is what forces $x=90^\circ$, rather than the $360^\circ$ angle sum.
options.D: $x$ can be any size, because the diagram prints three right-angle marks.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Bina's quadrilateral $PQRS$ with right-angle marks at $P$, $Q$, and $R$, and with the remaining interior angle at $S$ labelled $x$.

Which claim about $x$ is correct?

options.A: $x$ must be $90^\circ$, because the four interior angles of a quadrilateral sum to $360^\circ$.
options.B: $x$ is only an interior-angle label, so the quadrilateral sum does not constrain it.
options.C: Drawing the four sides is what forces $x=90^\circ$, rather than the $360^\circ$ angle sum.
options.D: $x$ can be any size, because the diagram prints three right-angle marks.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Deepak sorts quadrilaterals. He asks which of these claims about parallelograms are true.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: A parallelogram must have four right angles.
options.B: A rectangle is a parallelogram.
options.C: A square is a parallelogram.
options.D: Every parallelogram is a rectangle.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows quadrilateral $ABCD$ with both pairs of opposite sides parallel. Sameer asks how rectangles and squares relate to parallelograms.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: $ABCD$ is a parallelogram; rectangles and squares are special parallelograms because their opposite sides are parallel.
options.B: $ABCD$ is a parallelogram only if all four angles are $90^{\circ}$.
options.C: Every parallelogram is a rectangle.
options.D: The same rule classifies any open broken line of four segments as a parallelogram.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows quadrilateral $PQRS$ with both pairs of opposite sides parallel. Bina asks how rectangles and squares relate to parallelograms.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: $PQRS$ is a parallelogram; rectangles and squares are special parallelograms because their opposite sides are parallel.
options.B: $PQRS$ is a parallelogram only if all four angles are $90^{\circ}$.
options.C: Every parallelogram is a square.
options.D: The same rule classifies any open path of four segments as a parallelogram.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
In parallelogram $PQRS$, $\angle P=70^\circ$.

Which claim about the angles is correct?

options.A: Adjacent $\angle Q=110^\circ$ and opposite $\angle R=70^\circ$.
options.B: Adjacent $\angle Q=70^\circ$ and opposite $\angle R=110^\circ$.
options.C: Every angle of $PQRS$ equals $70^\circ$.
options.D: Adjacent $\angle Q=70^\circ+110^\circ=180^\circ$ as a single angle measure at $Q$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kabir looks at the diagram of parallelogram $PQRS$. Angle $P$ is marked $70^{\circ}$.

Which claim correctly determines the adjacent and opposite angles?

options.A: Adjacent angle $Q$ is $110^{\circ}$ (co-interior with $P$ on parallel sides), and opposite angle $R$ equals angle $P$, so $R=70^{\circ}$.
options.B: Call $PQRS$ a parallelogram even when the co-interior pair on parallel sides is not used to find angle $Q$.
options.C: Say that equal adjacent angles are what create parallelogram $PQRS$.
options.D: Apply equality of opposite angles also to a kite that is not a parallelogram, using only the printed $70^{\circ}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Aditya has parallelogram $ABCD$ with $AB = 9$ cm and $AD = 5$ cm.

Which claim correctly states the side lengths that can be inferred?

options.A: Report the words opposite sides as the length of $AB$.
options.B: Equal opposite sides are what create parallelogram $ABCD$ from the lengths $9$ cm and $5$ cm.
options.C: $CD = 9$ cm and $BC = 5$ cm, because opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal.
options.D: Diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ must each equal $9$ cm.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows parallelogram $ABCD$ with $AB=7$ cm and $AD=4$ cm.

Which claim correctly states the side lengths that can be inferred?

options.A: Report the words opposite sides as the length of $AB$.
options.B: Equal opposite sides are what create parallelogram $ABCD$ from the lengths $7$ cm and $4$ cm.
options.C: $CD=7$ cm and $BC=4$ cm, because opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal.
options.D: Diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ must each equal $7$ cm.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Ritu draws parallelogram $ABCD$ with diagonals $AC$ and $BD$.

parts.text: Which claim is correct?

options.text: The diagonals must be equal in length and must bisect each other.
The diagonals must bisect each other, but they need not be equal.
The diagonals must be equal in length, but they need not bisect each other.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice that uses a property of the diagonals.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows parallelogram $ABCD$ with diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ meeting at $O$.

Which claim about the diagonals is correct for every parallelogram?

options.A: The diagonals are equal in length, because the figure is labelled parallelogram.
options.B: Call the answer diagonal only, with no statement about $O$, $AC$, or $BD$.
options.C: The diagonals bisect each other: $O$ is the midpoint of both $AC$ and $BD$.
options.D: Bisection holds for $AC$ even when $O$ is not the midpoint of $BD$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Rehan studies a quadrilateral whose four sides are equal. Right angles are not required.

Which claim correctly classifies this quadrilateral?

options.A: It is a rhombus even when the four sides are not equal.
options.B: Being a parallelogram is what forces all four sides to be equal.
options.C: It is a rhombus because all sides are equal, and every rhombus is a parallelogram.
options.D: Every parallelogram is a rhombus.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Meher looks at the diagram of quadrilateral $ABCD$. All four sides carry the same tick mark. No right-angle mark is shown.

Which claim correctly classifies $ABCD$?

options.A: $ABCD$ is a rhombus and a parallelogram; it is not a square because no right angle is shown.
options.B: Call $ABCD$ a rhombus while the four sides are allowed to be unequal.
options.C: Being a parallelogram is what creates the four equal side lengths.
options.D: Call $ABCD$ a square under the same marks, with right angles that are not shown.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kunal knows one angle of a rhombus is $70^{\circ}$.

Which claim correctly finds the other three angles?

options.A: The answer is the words opposite angles.
options.B: The other three angles are $70^{\circ}$, $70^{\circ}$, and $70^{\circ}$ because $70$ is the printed angle.
options.C: The opposite angle is $70^{\circ}$ and each adjacent angle is $110^{\circ}$.
options.D: Find the other angles by using trapezium base-angle rules on the rhombus.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ira knows one angle of a rhombus is $70^{\circ}$. She needs the other three angles.

Which two claims correctly give those angles?

options.A: Call the full answer the label opposite angles, and stop there.
options.B: The opposite angle is also $70^{\circ}$.
options.C: Each adjacent angle is $110^{\circ}$.
options.D: All four angles are $70^{\circ}$, mixing in a rectangle's equal-angle pattern.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Komal studies the diagonals of a rhombus.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: The diagonals of a rhombus meet at $90^{\circ}$.
options.B: The diagonals of a rhombus are always equal in length.
options.C: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other.
options.D: Each diagonal of a rhombus equals a side of the rhombus.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Ritu studies the diagonals of a rhombus.

parts.text: Which claim is correct?

options.text: The diagonals of a rhombus meet at $90^{\circ}$ and bisect each other.
The diagonals of a rhombus are always equal in length.
Each diagonal of a rhombus equals a side of the rhombus.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tanvi studies kite $ABCD$ with $AB=AD$ and $CB=CD$.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: Report the words adjacent equal sides as diagonal $AC$.
options.B: $ABCD$ is a kite because $AB=AD$ and $CB=CD$.
options.C: Diagonal $AC$ bisects diagonal $BD$ at right angles.
options.D: Bisecting $BD$ at right angles is what creates the equal sides $AB=AD$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows kite $ABCD$ that Krish draws. Equal marks show $AB=AD$ and $CB=CD$. Diagonal $AC$ is drawn solid; diagonal $BD$ is dashed.

Which claim about the kite and its special diagonal is correct?

options.A: The kite has all four sides equal because the diagram shows four sides.
options.B: Diagonal $BD$ is the axis of symmetry of the kite.
options.C: Diagonal $AC$ is the axis of symmetry; it bisects $BD$ at right angles.
options.D: The figure is a kite because it is labelled $ABCD$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sameer has trapezium $PQRS$ with $PQ\parallel SR$ and $\angle P=75^{\circ}$. Angle $S$ lies on the same non-parallel side $PS$.

Which claim correctly gives $\angle S$?

options.A: Report the words parallel sides as the measure of $\angle S$.
options.B: $\angle S$ equals $75^{\circ}$.
options.C: $\angle S$ equals $105^{\circ}$, because the angles on the same non-parallel side between the parallel sides add to $180^{\circ}$.
options.D: The parallel sides $PQ\parallel SR$ are produced by the $105^{\circ}$ angle.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows trapezium $ABCD$ with $AB\parallel DC$. Angle $DAB=70^\circ$. Imran wants angle $ADC$ on the same non-parallel side as angle $DAB$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Angle $ADC=70^\circ$ because angle $ADC$ must equal angle $DAB$ in a trapezium.
options.B: Angle $ADC$ cannot be found from the parallel sides alone.
options.C: Angle $ADC=110^\circ$ because the angles on the same non-parallel side between the parallel sides add to $180^\circ$.
options.D: Angle $ADC=70^\circ$ because $AB$ equals $DC$ on the diagram.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bela has trapezium $ABCD$ with $AB\parallel DC$ and equal non-parallel sides $AD=BC$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Report the words non-parallel sides as $\angle A$.
options.B: Equal base angles are what create $AD=BC$.
options.C: $\angle A=\angle B$ and $\angle D=\angle C$, because the non-parallel sides are equal.
options.D: $\angle A$ equals $90^{\circ}$ because $AB$ looks horizontal.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows trapezium $ABCD$ with $AB\parallel DC$ and equal non-parallel sides $AD=BC$. Diya studies whether the base angles are equal.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The trapezium has equal base angles because it is labelled $ABCD$.
options.B: Angles at $A$ and $D$ are equal because they sit on leg $AD$.
options.C: Angles at $A$ and $B$ are equal, and angles at $D$ and $C$ are equal.
options.D: Every trapezium has equal base angles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tanya keeps the four numbers 3, 4, 5 and 6 fixed. She only changes the + and − signs between them, writing expressions of the form 3 ± 4 ± 5 ± 6.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Every such value has the same parity; for these four consecutive numbers that common parity is even.
options.B: Changing one sign can flip the parity of the value.
options.C: The common parity depends on a sign written before the first number 3.
options.D: Parity here is settled by whether 3 divides each partial sum.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yash keeps the four numbers 2, 3, 4 and 5 fixed. He only changes the + and − signs between them, writing expressions of the form 2 ± 3 ± 4 ± 5.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: Changing one sign can flip the parity of the value.
options.B: Every such value has the same parity.
options.C: Changing the + and − signs cannot change the parity of the value.
options.D: The common parity depends on a sign written before the first number 2.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Karan forms values with the four fixed numbers $7$, $4$, $2$, and $1$ by writing $7\pm 4\pm 2\pm 1$ and choosing each sign independently.

Which claim correctly decides whether changing the signs can change the odd/even parity of the value?

options.A: Yes: each sign change flips the parity of the value.
options.B: No: every choice of signs gives a value with the same parity.
options.C: Only the sign in front of $7$ can change the parity.
options.D: Yes when the four numbers are consecutive, and no for these four numbers.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit checks which expression must always be even for integer values of the letters. He compares 4m + 2q with x^2 + 2.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: 4m + 2q is always even, because it equals 2(2m + q).
options.B: x^2 + 2 is always even, because the constant 2 is even.
options.C: An expression is even only when the letters themselves are even.
options.D: x^2 + 2 is always even whenever 4m + 2q is even, with no further check.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ishaan checks which expressions must always be even when the letter-numbers are integers. He compares $4m + 2q$ with $x^{2} + 2$.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: $4m + 2q$ is always even, because $4m + 2q = 2(2m + q)$ for every integer $m$ and $q$.
options.B: $x^{2} + 2$ is always even, because the added constant $2$ is even.
options.C: $x^{2} + 2$ is not always even: when $x$ is odd, $x^{2}$ is odd, so $x^{2} + 2$ is odd.
options.D: Integer values of the letters are what the even-or-odd conclusion creates.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Damini checks which expression must always be even for integer values of the letters. She compares $6a + 2b$ with $n^{2} + 1$.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: $6a + 2b$ is always even only when $a$ and $b$ are even.
options.B: Integer values of the letters are produced by an expression being even.
options.C: $6a + 2b$ must always be even, while $n^{2} + 1$ is not always even.
options.D: $n^{2} + 1$ must always be even because the constant $1$ sits next to a square.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Deepak looks at two even numbers and asks when their sum is a multiple of 4.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Any sum of two even numbers may be labeled a multiple of 4.
options.B: Every sum of two even numbers is a multiple of 4, with no further check.
options.C: The sum is a multiple of 4 when the two even numbers leave the same remainder on division by 4.
options.D: The same remainder rule also applies unchanged when one addend is odd.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Imran looks at two even numbers and asks when their sum is a multiple of 4.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: The sum is a multiple of 4 when the two even numbers leave the same remainder on division by 4.
options.B: Every sum of two even numbers is a multiple of 4, with no further check.
options.C: One multiple of 4 plus one number of the form $4q+2$ gives a sum that is not a multiple of 4.
options.D: The same remainder rule also applies unchanged when one addend is odd.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tania checks the even numbers $6$ and $10$ and asks whether their sum is a multiple of $4$.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Any sum of two even numbers may be labeled a multiple of $4$.
options.B: Every sum of two even numbers is a multiple of $4$, with no further check.
options.C: $6$ and $10$ both leave remainder $2$ on division by $4$, so their sum $16$ is a multiple of $4$.
options.D: The same remainder rule also applies unchanged when one addend is odd.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tanya knows that $6$ divides $18$ and $6$ divides $30$.

What follows for $18+30$ and for a split of a multiple of $6$?

options.A: Conclude that $6$ divides $48$ from the sum looking convenient, with no check that $6$ divides both $18$ and $30$.
options.B: From $6$ dividing $48$, conclude that every split of $48$ into two addends has both addends multiples of $6$.
options.C: Then $6$ divides $18+30$; but if $6$ divides a total, its addends need not both be multiples of $6$.
options.D: Use the same closure when $4$ divides $18$ and $6$ divides $30$, with no shared divisor for both numbers.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Farhan knows that $4$ divides $12$ and $4$ divides $20$.

Which two claims keep the direction of the divisibility rule straight?

options.A: Then $4$ divides $12+20$ even if $4$ divides only one of $12$ or $20$.
options.B: Then $4$ divides $12+20$ and $4$ divides $20-12$.
options.C: If $4$ divides a total such as $32$, a split into two addends need not make both addends multiples of $4$.
options.D: The same closure holds when $3$ divides $12$ and $5$ divides $20$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Damini knows that $5$ divides $15$ and $5$ divides $35$.

What follows for $15+35$ and for a split of a multiple of $5$?

options.A: $5$ divides $15+35$ when $5$ divides only one of $15$ or $35$.
options.B: Because $5$ divides $50$, both addends in every split of $50$ must be multiples of $5$.
options.C: $5$ divides $15+35=50$; a multiple of $5$ can still split into addends that are not both multiples of $5$.
options.D: The same closure also applies when different divisors act on $15$ and $35$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit knows that $12$ is divisible by $3$.

Which claim follows?

options.A: Skip the given that $12$ is divisible by $3$, and treat whether multiples of $12$ are divisible by $3$ as unknown.
options.B: Say that divisibility by $3$ is what creates the number $12$ itself.
options.C: Every multiple of $12$ is divisible by $3$, and $12$ is divisible by every factor of $3$.
options.D: Infer that $12$ is divisible by every multiple of $3$, such as $6$ or $9$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Neil knows that $15$ is divisible by $5$.

Which two claims follow?

options.A: Treat whether multiples of $15$ are divisible by $5$ as unknown, dropping the given that $15$ is divisible by $5$.
options.B: Every multiple of $15$ is divisible by $5$.
options.C: $15$ is divisible by every factor of $5$.
options.D: $15$ is divisible by every multiple of $5$, such as $10$ or $20$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Damini knows that $18$ is divisible by $6$.

Which claim follows?

options.A: Whether multiples of $18$ are divisible by $6$ cannot be decided from the given.
options.B: Divisibility by $6$ is what creates the number $18$.
options.C: Every multiple of $18$ is divisible by $6$, and $18$ is divisible by every factor of $6$.
options.D: $18$ is divisible by every multiple of $6$, such as $12$ or $24$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Uday wants to prove that $180$ is divisible by $12$. He knows $12=2^{2}\times 3$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Check divisibility by $2$ alone and stop, skipping that $12$ also needs the factor $3$ and enough factors of $2$.
options.B: Say that proving divisibility by $12$ is what creates the prime factors of $12$.
options.C: Use tests that together supply $2^{2}$ and $3$ — for example divisible by $4$ and by $3$ — because those combine to prove divisible by $12$.
options.D: Use the same combined-test idea to prove divisibility by a prime such as $7$, where a single prime test already settles it.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Vihaan wants to prove a whole number is divisible by $24$. He knows $24=2^{3}\times 3$.

Which two claims correctly choose factor tests whose combined force proves divisibility by $24$?

options.A: Checks by $4$ and by $6$ together prove divisibility by $24$.
options.B: Checks by $8$ and by $3$ together prove divisibility by $24$, because $\operatorname{lcm}(8,3)=24$.
options.C: The tests by $8$ and by $3$ work because their prime powers together supply $2^{3}\times 3$.
options.D: Divisibility by $24$ is what produces the separate checks by $8$ and by $3$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Damini wants to prove that $126$ is divisible by $18$. She knows $18=2\times 3^{2}$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: A check that $126$ is divisible by $2$ proves divisibility by $18$.
options.B: Proving divisibility by $18$ creates the prime factors $2$ and $3^{2}$.
options.C: Tests that together supply $2$ and $3^{2}$ — for example divisible by $2$ and by $9$ — prove divisibility by $18$, since $\operatorname{lcm}(2,9)=18$.
options.D: Checks that $126$ is divisible by $2$ and by $3$ prove divisibility by $18$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Komal works with numbers that leave remainder $2$ when divided by $5$. She wants to reason with that remainder form without full division each time.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Write $5k+2$ but skip reducing a combined remainder again when the sum of remainders reaches $5$ or more.
options.B: Say that the form $5k+2$ is what creates remainder $2$ on division by $5$, instead of remainder $2$ justifying that form.
options.C: Write each such number as $5k+2$ (or $5k-3$), combine remainder parts in sums or products, then reduce again by $5$ as needed.
options.D: Use the same $5k+2$ form for numbers that leave remainder $2$ when divided by $7$, beyond divisor $5$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yash says a whole number leaves remainder 3 when divided by 5. He writes numbers of that kind as $5k+3$ with whole number $k$, and keeps the remainder strictly between 0 and 4.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Every such number may also be written as $5k+5$, because remainder size does not matter.
options.B: The divisor 5 is produced by the remainder 3, rather than 5 and $k$ producing remainder 3.
options.C: Numbers leaving remainder 3 on division by 5 are exactly those of the form $5k+3$ with $0\le3<5$.
options.D: The same $5k+3$ form also covers numbers that leave remainder 4 when divided by 5.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Chetan works with whole numbers that leave remainder $4$ when divided by $7$. He writes them as $7k+4$ with whole number $k$, and keeps the remainder strictly between $0$ and $6$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Any form $7k+r$ is fine even when $r$ is 7 or larger, because the $7k$ part is present.
options.B: The divisor $7$ is produced by the remainder $4$, so start from $4$ and ignore the $7k$ term.
options.C: Numbers of that kind are $7k+4$, and the remainder stays less than the divisor $7$.
options.D: Write every such number as $4k+7$, swapping the places of the remainder $4$ and the divisor $7$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yash says a whole number is divisible by 10 exactly when its units digit is 0.

Why does this last-digit shortcut work?

options.A: Units digit is the name of the rule, so that label is the reason.
options.B: The units digit produces place value, so place value comes from the units digit alone.
options.C: Every higher place value in a whole number is a multiple of 10, so only the units digit can affect divisibility by 10.
options.D: The answer is place value because those words are the most obvious label in the idea.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Ritu says a whole number is divisible by $10$ exactly when its units digit is $0$.

parts.text: Which claim correctly explains why this last-digit shortcut works?

options.text: Units digit is the name of the rule, so that label is the reason.
Every higher place value in a whole number is a multiple of $10$, so only the units digit can affect divisibility by $10$.
The units digit produces place value, so place value comes from the units digit alone.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Chetan expands $370$ by place value as $3\times100+7\times10+0\times1$. He asks why divisibility by $10$ depends only on the units digit being $0$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Every higher place is a multiple of $10$, so only the units digit can stop the whole number from being a multiple of $10$; here that digit is $0$.
options.B: The label that matters is the units digit alone, so place value plays no role in the shortcut.
options.C: The units digit is what creates place value, so start from that digit and ignore the expansion.
options.D: The answer is $0$ only because $0$ is the last digit printed in $370$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Harsh checks whether $378$ is divisible by $9$ and by $3$ by using the sum of its digits $3+7+8=18$.

Which claims are correct? Two options are correct.

options.A: Report the words divisibility by $9$ as the value of the digit sum $18$.
options.B: $378$ is divisible by $9$ because the digit sum $18$ is divisible by $9$.
options.C: $378$ is divisible by $3$ because the digit sum $18$ is divisible by $3$.
options.D: $378$ is divisible by $9$ because its units digit is $8$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Nitya asks whether $2\,457$ is divisible by $9$. She may use the sum of its digits.

parts.text: Which claim correctly applies the digit-sum test?

options.text: Call the answer "divisibility by $9$" as a label only, and stop.
Sum the digits $2+4+5+7=18$; because $18$ is divisible by $9$, so is $2\,457$.
Say that divisibility by $9$ is what creates the digit sum $18$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Leela tests 2178 for divisibility by 11 using alternating digit sums, starting from the units digit.

parts.text: Which claim is correct?

options.text: $8 - 7 + 1 - 2 = 0$, so 2178 is divisible by 11.
$2 + 1 + 7 + 8 = 18$, so check divisibility by 9 instead for the 11 test.
$8 + 7 + 1 + 2 = 18$, and 18 is a multiple of 11.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice that uses alternating place values.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sia tests $3520$ for divisibility by $11$ using alternating digit sums, starting from the units digit: $0-2+5-3$.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: Only the units digit $0$ needs to be checked for divisibility by $11$.
options.B: The alternating sum $0-2+5-3=0$ is divisible by $11$, so $3520$ is divisible by $11$.
options.C: A zero alternating sum counts as a multiple of $11$, so the divisibility test passes.
options.D: Alternating digit sums are what create the place values of $3520$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Arjun finds the digital root of $459$ by repeated digit sums: $4+5+9=18$, then $1+8=9$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Digital root $9$ is only a label for the digit-sum steps, not remainder information for $9$.
options.B: Remainder information for $9$ is what creates the digit sums $18$ and $9$, rather than the digit sums preserving the remainder.
options.C: Digital root $9$ means $459$ is a multiple of $9$, so it leaves remainder $0$ on division by $9$.
options.D: Digital root $9$ because the units digit of $459$ is $9$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tara finds the digital root of $378$ by repeated digit sums: $3+7+8=18$, then $1+8=9$.

Which two claims correctly interpret that digital root?

options.A: Call the answer repeated digit sum only, with no link to a remainder on division by $9$.
options.B: The digital root $9$ matches the remainder information for $378$ on division by $9$ (a multiple of $9$ reports digital root $9$).
options.C: Because $378 = 9 \times 42$, the digit-sum process agrees with remainder $0$ on division by $9$, reported as digital root $9$.
options.D: The digital root is what creates the number $378$, so the sums run backwards from $9$ to rebuild $378$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Neel studies this cryptarithm. Each letter stands for a digit, and different letters stand for different digits.

$$\begin{array}{c@{}c} & A & B \\ + & A & B \\ \hline & C & A \end{array}$$

Which claim correctly narrows a digit before trying every full substitution?

options.A: Letter $C$ must be twice letter $A$, with no carry anywhere.
options.B: Any digits for $A$, $B$, and $C$ work as long as each letter is a single digit.
options.C: From the units column, $A$ equals the units digit of $2B$ after the carry is placed, so each choice of $B$ leaves only one possible $A$.
options.D: The sum $CA$ must be smaller than one addend $AB$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yash works on a multiplication cryptarithm. Each letter stands for one digit, different letters different digits, and he wants to narrow possible digits before trying every full substitution.

Which two claims correctly help him narrow the digits first?

options.A: Call the full answer the label letter-number, and stop there.
options.B: A leading letter of a multi-digit number cannot be $0$.
options.C: The units digit of the product constrains which digit pairs are still possible.
options.D: Listing every full substitution is what creates the leading-digit rule.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Xavier multiplies the outside factor through the bracket: $3(x - 4)$.

Which expansion is correct?
author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Adil multiplies the outside factor through the bracket: $4(y - 3)$.

parts.text: Which expansion is correct?
Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Inaya expands $5(2x-3)$ for her algebra homework.

parts.text: Which claim correctly states the expanded form?
Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qasim multiplies $(x + 3)(x - 2)$ by forming every cross-product.

Which expansion is correct?

options.D: $x^{2}$, because $x$ is the most obvious letter in the product.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kavya multiplies $(y + 4)(y - 3)$ by forming every cross-product exactly once and reading each sign from its two factors.

Which expansion is correct?
author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Eklavya multiplies $(z + 5)(z - 1)$ by forming every cross-product exactly once and reading each sign from its two factors.

parts.text: Which expansion is correct?
Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Hassan starts with the product $12 \times 15$. The factors are then changed to $13 \times 17$.

By how much does the product increase?

options.A: Report only the adjustments $+1$ and $+2$, and call those adjustments the change in the product.
options.B: Say the adjustments $+1$ and $+2$ are what produce the original product $12 \times 15$.
options.C: By $41$, because $(12+1)(15+2) = 12\times15 + 12\times2 + 15\times1 + 1\times2$, so the change is $24 + 15 + 2$.
options.D: Rewrite $12$ as $10+2$ and multiply by a special identity, without expanding the adjusted product.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Diya starts with the product $8 \times 11$. The factors are then changed to $10 \times 13$.

parts.text: By how much does the product increase?

options.text: By $16$, from the $8\times2$ change term alone.
By the adjustments $+2$ and $+2$ to the factors.
By $42$, because $(8+2)(11+2)=8\times11 + 8\times2 + 11\times2 + 2\times2$ and the change is $16+22+4=42$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Umesh starts with the product $9 \times 14$. The factors are then changed to $11 \times 16$.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims are correct?

options.A: Report only the adjustments $+2$ and $+2$, and call those adjustments the change in the product.
options.B: The product increases by $50$, because $(9+2)(14+2) = 9\times14 + 9\times2 + 14\times2 + 2\times2$ and the change is $18 + 28 + 4$.
options.C: The change from the original product is $9\times2 + 14\times2 + 2\times2$.
options.D: Say the adjustments $+2$ and $+2$ are what produce the original product $9 \times 14$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Xavier expands and then simplifies $2a^{2} + 3a + a^{2}$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the variable part $a$ the whole simplified result, without combining like terms.
options.B: Combine $2a^{2}$ with $3a$ into one term, skipping that only identical variable parts (including exponents) may be combined.
options.C: Combine $2a^{2}$ with $a^{2}$ to get $3a^{2}$, leave $3a$ as it is, and report $3a^{2} + 3a$.
options.D: Report only the printed coefficient $2$ as the simplified expression, ignoring the variable parts.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Tara expands and then simplifies $3b^{2} + 4b + 2b^{2}$.

parts.text: Which claim is correct?

options.text: Call the variable part $b$ the whole simplified result.
Combine $3b^{2}$ with $4b$ into one term.
Combine $3b^{2}$ with $2b^{2}$ to get $5b^{2}$, leave $4b$ as it is, and report $5b^{2} + 4b$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Eklavya expands and then simplifies $4c^{2} + 5c + c^{2}$.

parts.text: Which claim is correct?

options.text: $4c^{2} + c^{2} = 5c^{2}$, so the simplified form is $5c^{2} + 5c$.
$4c^{2}$, $5c$, and $c^{2}$ all combine into the single term $5c^{3}$.
The simplified form is $9c^{2}$, from adding the coefficients $4$, $5$, and $1$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qasim expands $(x+3)^{2}$.

Which expansion is correct?

options.A: Call the answer $x^{2}$ only, without writing the product of two identical binomials.
options.B: Write $x^{2}+9$, squaring $x$ and $3$ separately and skipping the two equal cross-products.
options.D: Replace the expansion with a full factorisation algorithm for a cubic, beyond this squared-sum identity.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Avni expands $(y+4)^{2}$.

Which expansion is correct?

options.A: Write $y^{2}$ only, naming the squared first term as the whole expansion.
options.B: Write $y^{2}+16$, squaring $y$ and $4$ separately and leaving out the two equal cross-products.
options.D: Replace the expansion with a full factorisation algorithm for a cubic polynomial.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows a square of side $z+5$ split into four rectangles.

Eklavya expands $(z+5)^{2}$.

parts.text: Which expansion is correct?
Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Zaid expands $(x-5)^{2}$.

Which expansion is correct?

options.A: Call the answer $x^{2}$ only, without writing the product of two identical differences.
options.B: Say that writing $x^{2}-10x+25$ is what creates $(x-5)^{2}$, instead of expanding the product.
options.C: Write $(x-5)(x-5)=x^{2}-5x-5x+25=x^{2}-10x+25$, so the combined cross-term is negative.
options.D: Expand as $x^{2}+25$ by squaring each part, then add a positive cross-term as in $(x+5)^{2}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anaya expands $(8-3)^{2}$.

Which expansion is correct?

options.A: Call the result negative cross-products and treat that label alone as the expansion.
options.B: Negative cross-products are what produce the squared difference $(8-3)^{2}$.
options.D: $(8-3)^{2}=8^{2}-3^{2}=55$, as if the square were a plain difference of squares.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows a square of side $x-3$ split into four labelled regions.

Eklavya expands $(x-3)^{2}$.

parts.text: Which expansion is correct?
Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Omkar wants to expand $(x+5)(x-5)$ by recognising a conjugate pair.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Treat $(x+5)(x+5)$ as the conjugate pair for this expansion, skipping that the connecting signs must be opposite.
options.B: Say that getting $x^2-25$ is what creates the opposite signs in $(x+5)(x-5)$, instead of using those opposite signs to cancel the cross-terms.
options.C: The factors are conjugates: same terms $x$ and $5$ with opposite signs, so $(x+5)(x-5)=x^2-25$.
options.D: Use the same conjugate cancellation when adding $(x+5)+(x-5)$, beyond this product expansion.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ira expands $(y+7)(y-7)$ by looking for conjugate factors.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: $(y+7)(y+7)$ is the conjugate pair for this expansion.
options.B: The factors use the same terms $y$ and $7$ with opposite connecting signs, so the cross-terms cancel.
options.C: The product is $y^2-49$.
options.D: The same cross-term cancel also applies to the sum $(y+7)+(y-7)$ in place of the product.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Damini wants to expand $(z+9)(z-9)$ by recognising a conjugate pair.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: $(z+9)(z-9)=z^{2}+81$, keeping both signs as addition in the product.
options.B: The expanded difference $z^{2}-81$ is what creates the factors $(z+9)$ and $(z-9)$.
options.C: $(z+9)(z-9)=z^{2}-81$, because the factors share the same terms with opposite signs.
options.D: $(z+9)(z-9)=z^{2}+18z-81$, as if both middle terms stay after expansion.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Pallavi asks whether $(x+3)^{2}=x^{2}+6x+9$ is an identity.

Which claim correctly decides?

options.A: Name the left-hand side only, without comparing a simplified right-hand side.
options.B: Matching one trial value on the left-hand side is what creates an identity.
options.C: Expand and simplify both sides; they agree for every permitted $x$, so the equality is an identity.
options.D: It is an identity because the trial $x=1$ made both sides equal.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Krish asks whether $(2x-1)(x+4)=2x^{2}+7x-4$ is an identity.

Which two claims correctly decide?

options.A: Call the left-hand side the identity, because that is the printed first expression.
options.B: Expand both sides and simplify; they match for every permitted $x$, so the equality is an identity.
options.C: Matching simplified forms on both sides settles the identity question for all permitted values.
options.D: Try $x=1$ only; agreement at that one value proves the equality is an identity.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Damini asks whether $(x+5)^{2}=x^{2}+10x+25$ is an identity.

Which claim correctly decides?

options.A: Expand the left-hand side: $(x+5)^{2}=x^{2}+10x+25$, matching the right-hand side for every permitted $x$, so the equality is an identity.
options.B: The work is only about naming the left-hand side, so no expansion is needed.
options.C: The left-hand side is what produces an identity, so matching simplified forms is unnecessary.
options.D: It is an identity because the printed constant $25$ looks like a perfect square.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Leela wants an easier way to compute $48 \times 52$.

Which claims correctly rewrite the product without changing its value? Two options are correct.

options.A: $48 \times 52 = 50 \times 50$, replacing each factor by 50.
options.C: $48 \times 52 = 48 \times (50 + 2) = 48 \times 50 + 48 \times 2$.
options.D: $48 \times 52 = 48 + 52$, because a product means combine the two numbers by addition.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Aarav wants an easier way to compute $48\times 52$ while keeping the same value.

Which two claims correctly choose and justify a decomposition?

options.A: Call the answer the place-value base $10$ alone, and stop.
options.B: Write $48\times 52=(50-2)(50+2)=50^2-2^2$, which equals the original product.
options.C: The identity $(a-b)(a+b)=a^2-b^2$ preserves the value of $48\times 52$ when $a=50$ and $b=2$.
options.D: Choose the decomposition only because $50$ is the largest printed number nearby.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Naina builds a matchstick pattern. Step $1$ uses $4$ matchsticks for one square. Each new step adds one square that shares one side with the previous square, so $3$ new matchsticks are added each time.

Which expression gives the number of matchsticks at Step $k$?

options.D: Only Step $1$ has a matchstick count; later steps have no expression in $k$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Rohan's matchstick pattern. Step $1$ uses $4$ matchsticks for one square. Each new step adds one square that shares one side with the previous square, so $3$ new matchsticks are added each time.

options.D: Only Step $1$ has a matchstick count; later steps have no expression in $k$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sahil describes the same shaded rectangle of width $2$ and length $x+3$ in two ways: $2(x+3)$ and $2x+6$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The two expressions match because both contain $x$ and $3$, with no need to expand.
options.B: Expanding $2x+6$ into $2(x+3)$ is what creates the rectangle from width $2$ and length $x+3$.
options.C: Expanding gives $2(x+3)=2x+6$, so both expressions describe the same rectangle.
options.D: Equivalence of $2(x+3)$ and $2x+6$ also proves every pair of algebra expressions names the same region.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Ishaan describes the same shaded rectangle of width $3$ and length $x+4$ in two ways: $3(x+4)$ and $3x+12$.

parts.text: Which claim correctly tests that the two expressions match?

options.text: Expand $3(x+4)$ to $3x+12$; both name the same whole rectangle.
The expanded form $3x+12$ is what creates the factor form $3(x+4)$.
Treat $3(x+4)$ and $3x+12$ as matching even when they describe different wholes.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ira mixes juice and water in the ratio 2 : 5.

What does this ratio mean?

options.A: For every 5 parts of juice there are 2 parts of water.
options.B: Juice and water are equal, because a ratio always means equal shares.
options.C: For every 2 parts of juice there are 5 parts of water.
options.D: The whole mix is divided by adding 2 and 5 only after swapping the order.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kavya mixes sand and cement in the ratio 3 : 1.

What does this ratio mean?

options.A: Sand and cement are equal shares, because a ratio always means equal parts.
options.B: For every 1 part of sand there are 3 parts of cement.
options.C: For every 3 parts of sand there is 1 part of cement.
options.D: The whole mix is found by adding 3 and 1 only after swapping the order of sand and cement.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Boman says the ratio of red marbles to blue marbles in his pouch is $2:5$.

Which two claims correctly keep each term attached to its named colour?

options.A: For every $5$ red marbles there are $2$ blue marbles.
options.B: For every $2$ red marbles there are $5$ blue marbles.
options.C: Red to blue is the same comparison as $2$ to $5$ in that order.
options.D: Blue to red is already written as $2:5$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anya records two linked quantities. At first, juice is 2 cups and water is 5 cups. Later, juice is 6 cups and water is 15 cups.

Is the change proportional?

options.A: Yes, because juice rose by 4 cups and that additive rise alone settles the question.
options.B: Yes for any pair of increases, even when the two quantities grow by unrelated amounts.
options.C: Yes, because both quantities were multiplied by the same factor 3.
options.D: Yes, because 15 is the largest number printed among the four amounts.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Farhan records juice and water. At first, juice is $2$ cups and water is $5$ cups. Later, juice is $6$ cups and water is $15$ cups.

parts.text: Which claim correctly decides whether the change is proportional?

options.text: The change is proportional: both quantities are multiplied by the same factor $3$.
The change is proportional because each quantity grew by adding $4$ cups.
Call the answer corresponding quantities, and stop there.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Firoz records paint and thinner. At first, paint is $3$ litres and thinner is $4$ litres. Later, paint is $9$ litres and thinner is $12$ litres.

Is the change proportional?

options.A: Yes, because each quantity increased by adding the same number of litres.
options.B: No, because a common factor of $3$ is larger than $1$.
options.C: Yes, because paint and thinner are both multiplied by the same factor $3$.
options.D: Yes, because the later thinner amount is $12$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Uday compares the ratios 2 : 3 and 4 : 6.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: They are proportional even if he matches 2 with 4 and 3 with 6 in crossed positions without checking corresponding places.
options.B: He must convert both ratios into percentages before he can compare them.
options.C: Yes, they are proportional: both reduce to 2 : 3, and 2 \times 6 = 3 \times 4.
options.D: Convert 2 : 3 into centimetres using a length-conversion table, then compare.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Krish compares the ratios $3 : 5$ and $6 : 10$.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: They are proportional even if he matches 3 with 10 and 5 with 6 without checking products.
options.B: He must convert both ratios into percentages before he can compare them.
options.C: Yes, they are proportional: both reduce to $3 : 5$, and $3 \times 10 = 5 \times 6$.
options.D: Convert $3 : 5$ into centimetres using a length-conversion table, then compare.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Vidya compares the ratios $4 : 7$ and $8 : 14$.

parts.text: Which claim is correct?

options.text: Yes, they are proportional: both reduce to $4 : 7$, and $4 \times 14 = 7 \times 8$.
They are proportional even if she matches $4$ with $14$ and $7$ with $8$ without checking products.
She must convert both ratios into percentages before she can compare them.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

subject: maths
stem:
Isha has the proportion $3 : 5 :: 6 : x$. The first ratio matches the second under one common factor.

What is $x$?

options.A: The answer is "common factor", naming that phrase instead of finding $x$.
options.B: Compute a fourth number by any arithmetic on $3$, $5$, and $6$, without treating the pairs as a true proportion.
options.C: $x = 10$, because the factor that changes $3$ to $6$ is $2$, so $5$ becomes $10$ (or $3x = 5\times 6$).
options.D: Replace the fourth-proportional step with a percentage conversion of $3 : 5$ before naming $x$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ishaan has the proportion $4 : 7 :: 12 : x$. The first ratio matches the second under one common factor.

What is $x$?

options.A: The answer is "common factor", naming that phrase instead of finding $x$.
options.B: Compute a fourth number by any arithmetic on $4$, $7$, and $12$, treating the pairs as unrelated.
options.C: $x = 21$, because the factor that changes $4$ to $12$ is $3$, so $7$ becomes $21$ (or $4x = 7\times 12$).
options.D: Replace the fourth-proportional step with a percentage conversion of $4 : 7$ before naming $x$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Firoz has the proportion $5 : 8 :: 15 : x$. The first ratio matches the second under one common factor.

What is $x$?

options.A: $x$ is the common factor.
options.C: $x = 24$, because the common factor $3$ changes $5$ to $15$ and $8$ to $24$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anya compares two juice mixes: Mix P uses $3$ cups concentrate in $12$ cups water; Mix Q uses $2$ cups concentrate in $6$ cups water. She wants the stronger concentrate mix.

Which comparison is fair?

options.A: Compare the absolute concentrate amounts $3$ and $2$ alone, without matching water on a common reference.
options.B: Say that a fair comparison is what creates the matching units, instead of placing both mixes on a common concentrate or water amount first.
options.C: Rewrite both as concentrate per the same water amount (or an equal ratio): P is $3:12=1:4$ and Q is $2:6=1:3$, so Q is stronger.
options.D: Replace the ratio comparison with an unrelated average of the four printed cups, outside this hinge.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Krish compares two paint mixes. Mix $P$ uses $4$ cups colour in $10$ cups water. Mix $Q$ uses $3$ cups colour in $6$ cups water. He wants the stronger colour mix.

Which claim correctly ranks the mixes?

options.A: Mix $P$ is stronger because its colour count $4$ is greater than $3$.
options.B: A fair strength ranking is what creates the matching water amounts.
options.C: Rewrite both on equal water: $P$ is $4:10=2:5$ and $Q$ is $3:6=1:2$, so $Q$ is stronger.
options.D: Rank the mixes by the average of the four printed cup counts $4$, $10$, $3$ and $6$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Firoz compares two syrup mixes. Mix $R$ uses $5$ cups syrup in $15$ cups water. Mix $S$ uses $3$ cups syrup in $6$ cups water. He wants the stronger syrup mix.

Which claim correctly ranks the mixes?

options.A: Mix $R$ is stronger because its syrup count $5$ is greater than $3$.
options.B: A fair strength ranking is what creates the matching water amounts.
options.C: Rewrite both on equal water: $R$ is $5:15=1:3$ and $S$ is $3:6=1:2$, so $S$ is stronger.
options.D: Rank the mixes by the average of the four printed cup counts $5$, $15$, $3$ and $6$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Deepak knows a job takes $6$ workers $8$ days. He wants how many days $12$ workers need for the same job.

Which claim is correct before any Rule-of-Three calculation?

options.A: Call the answer Rule of Three, without deciding whether the situation is directly proportional.
options.B: Say that applying the Rule of Three is what creates a direct-proportion relationship.
options.C: Do not treat it as direct proportion: more workers means fewer days for the same job, so the direct Rule of Three does not apply.
options.D: Divide the workforce in the ratio $6:12$ as if sharing a whole in a ratio were the same decision.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Rohan knows a job takes $6$ workers $8$ days. He wants how many days $12$ workers need for the same job.

parts.text: Which claim is correct before any Rule-of-Three calculation?

options.text: Treat workers and days as directly proportional and scale $8$ days by $12/6$.
Reject direct proportion here, because more workers must shorten the time for the same job.
Call the method the Rule of Three and apply it as a direct scale because that label fits.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.
