subject: maths
stem:
Firoz knows $4$ identical pumps empty a tank in $9$ hours. He wants how many hours $6$ identical pumps need to empty the same tank.

Which claim is correct before any Rule-of-Three calculation?

options.A: Rule of Three is the correct approach for this situation.
options.B: Applying the Rule of Three as a direct proportion creates the pumps-and-hours relationship.
options.C: Do not treat pumps and hours as directly proportional: more pumps means fewer hours for the same tank.
options.D: The $9$ hours should be divided in the ratio $4:6$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sahil must divide a whole of $60$ in the ratio $2:3$.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Call the answer ratio parts only, without finding one equal group's size from $2+3$.
options.B: Form parts $2\times60$ and $3\times60$, omitting the step that one group is $60/(2+3)$.
options.C: One group is $60/(2+3)=12$, so the parts are $2\times12=24$ and $3\times12=36$.
options.D: Also divide $60$ in the ratio $2:3$ by the same equal-group steps when the two parts must instead multiply to $60$, beyond sharing a whole.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Adil shares 48 laddoos in the ratio $5:3$ between two boxes. The ratio terms count equal-sized groups.

parts.text: Which claim divides the whole correctly?

options.text: One group is $48/(5+3)=6$ laddoos, so the parts are $5\times6=30$ and $3\times6=18$.
The answer is only the pair of ratio parts $5$ and $3$, so the whole 48 is unused.
Split 48 into 5 and 3 laddoos, ignoring that the parts must use all 48.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Eklavya shares 72 stickers in the ratio $4:5$ between two folders. The ratio terms count equal-sized groups.

The answer is only the pair of ratio parts $4$ and $5$, so the whole 72 is unused.
Split 72 into 4 and 5 stickers, ignoring that the parts must use all 72.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

subject: maths
stem:
A juice mix has 2 litres of mango pulp and 3 litres of water. Pooja wants the pulp-to-water ratio $2:5$ by adding only water.

options.A: Add mango pulp until the pulp matches the new water target.
options.B: Add 5 litres of water to reach the target water amount shown in the ratio.
options.C: Keep the 2 litres of mango pulp fixed, need 5 litres of water in total, so add 2 litres of water.
options.D: Add 5 litres of water because 2 and 3 are the printed amounts.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Anvi's drink mix has 3 litres of syrup and 5 litres of water. She wants a syrup-to-water ratio $3:7$ by adding only water.

parts.text: How much water must she add?

options.text: Add $2$ litres of water, so the new water amount is $7$ litres while syrup stays $3$ litres.
Add $4$ litres of water, treating both syrup and water as free to change.
Add $7$ litres of water, reading the target water number as the amount to pour in.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Eklavya's tea mix has $4$ litres of concentrate and $6$ litres of water. He wants a concentrate-to-water ratio $4:9$ by adding only water.

parts.text: Which claim correctly finds how much water to add?

options.text: Concentrate stays $4$ litres. For ratio $4:9$, water must be $9$ litres, so add $9-6=3$ litres of water.
The changing component is water, so ignore the fixed concentrate and repartition the original $10$ litres.
Add $9$ litres of water because $9$ is the new ratio part printed for water.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Parth converts $20^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to Fahrenheit. He also converts a length of $3\,\mathrm{m}$ to centimetres.

Which claim matches the kind of measurement to the correct conversion relation?

options.A: Use $F = \dfrac{9}{5}C$ with no offset for the temperature, and multiply the length by $100$.
options.B: Use $F = \dfrac{9}{5}C + 32$ for the temperature, and divide the length by $100$.
options.C: Use $F = \dfrac{9}{5}C + 32$ for the temperature, and multiply the length by $100$.
options.D: Use $F = \dfrac{9}{5}C + 32$ for both the temperature and the length.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Diya converts $2.5$ litres of juice into millilitres before comparing with a recipe that uses millilitres.

Which claim correctly chooses and applies the conversion?

options.A: Call the answer the target unit millilitre alone, and stop.
options.B: Say that naming millilitres is what creates the original litre amount $2.5$.
options.C: Use $1\,\mathrm{L}=1000\,\mathrm{mL}$, so $2.5\,\mathrm{L}=2500\,\mathrm{mL}$.
options.D: Decide from the printed digit $2$ alone, ignoring whether the measure is volume.

options.A: 40/100 of the class
options.B: 100/40 of the class
options.C: 40 of the class, with no whole chosen
options.D: 40 more students than the whole class

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:

Which two claims correctly read 25%?

options.A: 25% means 25 kg more than the whole bag of rice.
options.B: 25% means $\frac{25}{100}$ of the bag of rice.
options.C: 25% means 25 equal parts out of 100 equal parts of the bag of rice.
options.D: 25% means $\frac{100}{25}$ of the bag of rice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:

Which claim correctly states what $18\%$ means?

options.A: $18\%$ means $18$ out of every $10$ students in the class.
options.B: $18\%$ means $18$ out of every $100$ students in the class.
options.C: $18\%$ means $100$ out of every $18$ students in the class.
options.D: $18\%$ means $18$ students in total, with no reference to the whole class.

author: grok

options.B: Treat the part-to-part comparison $14:25$ itself as already a percentage.
options.C: $\dfrac{14}{25} = \dfrac{56}{100}$, so the percentage is $56\%$.

stem:

stem:

options.B: That 5% gives the same rupee amount on every bill, so the whole does not matter.
options.C: That the whole is ₹800, so the late fee is (5/100) × 800.
options.D: Start from a guessed late-fee amount and reverse to invent both the fees and the percent.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:

options.B: The whole is ₹450, so the discount is $(8/100)\times 450$.
options.C: The same 8% gives a different rupee amount if the book cost changes.
options.D: Start from a guessed discount amount and reverse to invent both the cost and the percent.

stem:

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:

options.C: Convert both to percentages first ($90\%$ and $88\%$), because the wholes $20$ and $25$ differ.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:

options.A: $21$ is larger than $16$, so the second score is the higher percent.
options.B: Convert both to percentages first ($80\%$ and $84\%$), because the wholes $20$ and $25$ differ.
options.C: A larger raw score need not be a larger percent when the totals differ.
options.D: Compare the raw scores on a third unrelated whole of $100$ marks she did not take.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri scores $14$ marks out of $20$ on one test and $18$ marks out of $25$ on another.

Which claim about comparing her percentages is correct?

options.A: $18 > 14$, so the second score is the higher percentage.
options.B: A fair percentage comparison is what forces the totals $20$ and $25$ to be equal.
options.C: Write $14/20 = 70\%$ and $18/25 = 72\%$; the wholes differ, so compare those percentages rather than the raw marks alone.
options.D: Compare the raw marks $18$ and $14$ directly while the totals stay $25$ and $20$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:

options.B: Add $10\%$ of $80$ to $5\%$ of a different value, skipping that the benchmarks must share the same whole.
options.D: Use the same benchmark story to compare lengths on an unrelated map scale.

stem:

options.C: Each benchmark piece is taken of the same whole $60$ before the pieces are added.
options.D: Use the same benchmark story to compare lengths on an unrelated map scale.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri finds $45\%$ of $80$ mentally using benchmark percentages.

Which method is correct?

options.A: The finished answer is the phrase "same whole", with no percent of $80$ computed.
options.D: Use the same benchmark story to compare lengths on an unrelated map scale.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri knows that $24$ is $30\%$ of an unknown whole $W$. She wants $W$ and then the remaining part of the whole.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Call the answer "unknown whole" only, without solving for $W$ from the percent.
options.B: Find the remaining part from $24$ before solving for $W$, skipping that the unknown whole must be found from the percent first.
options.C: Set $\dfrac{30}{100}=\dfrac{24}{W}$, so $W=80$; the remaining part is $80-24=56$.
options.D: Report $30$ as the whole only because $30$ is the printed percent numeral.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sia knows that $\mathrm{Rs}\,120$ is $15\%$ of an unknown whole bill $W$. She wants $W$.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Call $\mathrm{Rs}\,120$ the unknown whole and treat that label as $W$.
options.B: Set $15$ equal to $120/W$ and solve, dropping the percent-to-hundredths step.
options.C: Set $\dfrac{15}{100}=\dfrac{120}{W}$ and solve to get $W=800$.
options.D: Take $W=120$ because $120$ is the large printed amount on the bill.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri knows that $\mathrm{Rs}\,45$ is $25\%$ of an unknown whole amount $W$. She wants $W$.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: $\mathrm{Rs}\,45$ is the unknown whole $W$.
options.B: Solve $25=45/W$ for $W$.
options.C: Set $\dfrac{25}{100}=\dfrac{45}{W}$ and solve to get $W=180$.
options.D: The unknown whole is $W=25$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit hears that this year's collection is $150\%$ of last year's base of ₹$200$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Treat $150\%$ as more than the base after ignoring which amount was chosen as the $100\%$ base.
options.B: Say that collecting ₹$300$ is what creates the $150\%$ reading, instead of $150\%$ of the base giving ₹$300$.
options.C: $150\%$ means $1.5$ times the chosen base, so ₹$300$, which exceeds the ₹$200$ base.
options.D: Use "$150\%$ exceeds the base" to decide whether a fraction is greater than $1$ when no percentage base was chosen.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Meher's water tank holds 40 litres when full. Today's reading is 120% of that full amount.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: 120% is meaningful even if no base amount is named.
options.B: Being above 100% is what creates the 40 litre base, rather than comparing with that base.
options.C: 120% of the full tank means the quantity is more than the 40 litre base: $1.2\times40=48$ litres.
options.D: 120% always means a 20 litre increase, for every tank size.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Firoz hears that today's attendance is $125\%$ of yesterday's base of $80$ students.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: 125% means the same as the base of 80 students, because any percent names the base.
options.B: The base of 80 students is produced by today's attendance, so start from today and ignore the percent.
options.C: 125% of 80 is $1.25\times80=100$ students, which is more than the base.
options.D: 125% of 80 is 25 students, reading only the digits above 100.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tanya's book cost $\mathrm{Rs}\,400$. Its price rises to $\mathrm{Rs}\,460$.

What is the percentage increase?

options.A: $\dfrac{60}{460}\times100\%$ , using the new price as the base.
options.B: $\dfrac{460}{400}\times100\%$ , the new price as a percent of the original, not the percentage increase.
options.D: $60\%$, reading the printed rise of $60$ rupees as the percentage.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Imran's cricket bat cost $\mathrm{Rs}\,500$. Its price rises to $\mathrm{Rs}\,575$.

What is the percentage increase?

options.A: The increase is $15\%$, found by dividing $75$ by the new price $575$.
options.B: $575$ as a percent of $500$ is the percentage increase.
options.C: The increase is $15\%$, because $75$ divided by the original price $500$, times $100$, is $15$.
options.D: The percentage increase is $75$, the printed rise in rupees.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Firoz's school bag cost $\mathrm{Rs}\,800$. Its price rises to $\mathrm{Rs}\,920$.

What is the percentage increase?

options.A: $15\%$, because the increase $120$ is taken over the original amount $800$.
options.B: $13.04\%$ approximately, because the increase $120$ is taken over the new amount $920$.
options.C: $115\%$, because $920$ as a percent of $800$ is the percentage increase.
options.D: $920\%$, because $920$ is the largest rupee amount printed in the stem.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Omkar compares two statements about last year's fee of $\mathrm{Rs}\,5000$.
Statement 1: This year's fee is $120\%$ of last year's fee.
Statement 2: The fee rose by $20\%$.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: Statement 1 means this year's fee is $\mathrm{Rs}\,120$ only.
options.B: Statement 1 means this year's fee equals last year's fee plus $20\%$ of last year's fee.
options.C: Statement 2 also makes this year's fee equal to $120\%$ of last year's fee.
options.D: Statement 1 means the fee fell by $20\%$ from last year.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Kabir reads: "The final price is $80\%$ of the original price $₹500$."

parts.text: Which claim correctly reads that statement?

options.text: Call the answer the final amount alone as a bare label, and stop.
The final price is $0.8\times 500=₹400$, a final amount that is $80\%$ of the original, not an $80\%$ increase.
Treat $80\%$ as an increase of $₹80$ on $₹500$, so the final price is $₹580$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Diya buys a lamp for $\mathrm{Rs}\,800$. The tag shows $\mathrm{Rs}\,1000$. She sells the lamp for $\mathrm{Rs}\,900$.

Which two claims correctly name the prices before profit or discount is calculated?

options.A: $\mathrm{Rs}\,800$ is the selling price.
options.B: $\mathrm{Rs}\,800$ is the cost price.
options.C: $\mathrm{Rs}\,1000$ is the marked price and $\mathrm{Rs}\,900$ is the selling price.
options.D: Profit percent must use the marked price $\mathrm{Rs}\,1000$ as the $100\%$ base in every case.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Vihaan buys a bag for $\mathrm{Rs}\,450$. The tag shows $\mathrm{Rs}\,600$. He sells the bag for $\mathrm{Rs}\,540$.

parts.text: Which claim correctly names the three prices before profit or discount is calculated?

options.text: $\mathrm{Rs}\,450$ is the selling price, $\mathrm{Rs}\,600$ is the cost price, and $\mathrm{Rs}\,540$ is the marked price.
$\mathrm{Rs}\,450$ is the cost price, $\mathrm{Rs}\,600$ is the marked price, and $\mathrm{Rs}\,540$ is the selling price.
Profit percent must use the marked price $\mathrm{Rs}\,600$ as the $100\%$ base in every case.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bela invests $\mathrm{Rs}\,800$ in goods and sells them for $\mathrm{Rs}\,1000$. The profit amount is $\mathrm{Rs}\,200$.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: Report the words investment cost as the profit amount $\mathrm{Rs}\,200$.
options.B: Profit percentage on cost is $25\%$, using the investment $\mathrm{Rs}\,800$ as the base.
options.C: Profit percentage on sales is $20\%$, using the revenue $\mathrm{Rs}\,1000$ as the base.
options.D: Profit percentage is $200\%$, reading the printed profit $200$ as the percentage.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kavya invests $\mathrm{Rs}\,600$ in goods and sells them for $\mathrm{Rs}\,750$. The profit amount is $\mathrm{Rs}\,150$.

Which claim correctly states the profit percentage?

options.A: Call the answer investment cost only, with no percentage computed from the profit amount.
options.B: Profit percentage is $\dfrac{150}{750}\times 100\% = 20\%$, using the selling price as the base.
options.C: Profit percentage is $\dfrac{150}{600}\times 100\% = 25\%$, measured against the investment cost.
options.D: Profit percentage is $150\%$, reading the printed profit amount $150$ as the percentage.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
A bag is marked $\mathrm{Rs}\,800$. Sana gets a $10\%$ discount on the marked price.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The discount amount can be found with no reference to the marked price $\mathrm{Rs}\,800$.
options.B: The same $10\%$ discount settles every other tag in the shop with no further base.
options.C: Discount $=10\%$ of $800=\mathrm{Rs}\,80$, so the selling price is $\mathrm{Rs}\,720$.
options.D: Read the digit $8$ in $800$ alone to decide the discount.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ira sees a shirt with marked price ₹$500$. The shop offers a $10\%$ discount on that marked price.

Which claim correctly applies the discount?

options.A: The discount is ₹$50$ with no reference to the marked price ₹$500$.
options.B: The same $10\%$ discount step also settles a later profit percent after the discount.
options.C: Discount $= 10\%$ of ₹$500$ = ₹$50$, so the selling price is ₹$450$.
options.D: Selling price is ₹$10$ because $10$ is the largest printed number in the offer.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ritu deposits $\mathrm{Rs}\,5000$ at $10\%$ per year simple interest for 3 years.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Each year the interest is $10\%$ of the amount after adding the previous year's interest.
options.B: The interest for 3 years is $10\%$ of $\mathrm{Rs}\,5000$ once only.
options.C: Each year the interest is $10\%$ of the same principal $\mathrm{Rs}\,5000$.
options.D: Simple interest applies only in the first year, then the rate becomes zero.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Neil puts $\mathrm{Rs}\,4000$ in a simple-interest account at $8\%$ per year for $2$ years.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: Year-$2$ interest is $8\%$ of the amount after year $1$, so the principal has grown.
options.B: Each year the interest is $8\%$ of the same principal $\mathrm{Rs}\,4000$.
options.C: Over $2$ years the interest totals $\mathrm{Rs}\,640$, because $2\times 0.08\times 4000=640$.
options.D: Simple interest at $8\%$ also covers every loan and deposit Neil will ever open.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yogesh invests $\mathrm{Rs}\,5000$ at $10\%$ per year, compounded annually, for $2$ years.

Which claim correctly gives the amount after $2$ years?

options.A: Each year adds $\mathrm{Rs}\,500$ on the original $\mathrm{Rs}\,5000$ only, so the amount is $\mathrm{Rs}\,6000$.
options.B: Compounding also covers interest paid out each year with the principal kept fixed at $\mathrm{Rs}\,5000$.
options.C: After year $1$ the amount is $\mathrm{Rs}\,5500$; year $2$ interest on $\mathrm{Rs}\,5500$ gives amount $\mathrm{Rs}\,6050$.
options.D: The amount is $10\%$, the printed rate.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Avni invests $\mathrm{Rs}\,8000$ at $5\%$ per year, compounded annually, for $2$ years.

Which claim correctly gives the amount after $2$ years?

options.A: Each year adds $\mathrm{Rs}\,400$ on the original $\mathrm{Rs}\,8000$ only, so the amount is $\mathrm{Rs}\,8800$.
options.B: Compounding also covers interest paid out each year with the principal kept fixed at $\mathrm{Rs}\,8000$.
options.C: After year $1$ the amount is $\mathrm{Rs}\,8400$; year $2$ interest on $\mathrm{Rs}\,8400$ gives amount $\mathrm{Rs}\,8820$.
options.D: The amount is $5\%$, the printed rate.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Malini's school laptop costs $\mathrm{Rs}\,10000$. It depreciates by $10\%$ of its current value at the end of each year for $2$ years.

Which two claims correctly model that decline?

options.A: After $2$ years the value is $\mathrm{Rs}\,10000 \times 0.9 = \mathrm{Rs}\,9000$, using one $10\%$ decrease only.
options.B: After $1$ year the value is $\mathrm{Rs}\,10000 \times 0.9 = \mathrm{Rs}\,9000$.
options.C: After $2$ years the value is $\mathrm{Rs}\,9000 \times 0.9 = \mathrm{Rs}\,8100$.
options.D: Each year subtract $\mathrm{Rs}\,1000$ from $\mathrm{Rs}\,10000$ as if interest were taken on a fixed original principal.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Anvi's school printer is worth ₹8000. Each year it loses 10% of its value at the start of that year. After 2 years, what is its value?
author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kunal buys a bag with marked price $\mathrm{Rs}\,1000$. The shop gives a $20\%$ discount, then a further $10\%$ discount on the reduced price.

Which claim correctly finds the final price?

options.A: Final price $= \mathrm{Rs}\,1000 \times 0.7 = \mathrm{Rs}\,700$, adding the $20\%$ and $10\%$ labels.
options.B: Final price $= \mathrm{Rs}\,1000 \times 0.8 \times 0.9 = \mathrm{Rs}\,720$, applying $20\%$ then $10\%$ on the new base.
options.C: The same successive-base calculation is required when the shop gives only a single $20\%$ discount.
options.D: Final price $= \mathrm{Rs}\,1000$ because $20$ and $10$ are the printed percent labels.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
A jacket costs ₹1000. The shop raises the price by 20%, then offers 20% off the new price. Diya tracks the final price.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: The final price is ₹1000 because +20% and −20% cancel.
options.B: The final price is ₹960.
options.C: Each change uses the price after the previous change, so the factors multiply: $1.2\times 0.8$.
options.D: The final price is ₹1000−20=₹980 from the printed 20 labels.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Pia is told that length $A$ is $40\%$ of length $B$.

Which claim correctly states what percent $B$ is of $A$?

options.C: Saying $B$ is $250\%$ of $A$ is what creates the fact that $A$ is $40\%$ of $B$.
options.D: Reverse the comparison by multiplying successive percentage changes $0.4$ and $0.6$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Krish notes that 40 is 25% of 160.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: 160 is also 25% of 40.
options.C: Reversing the comparison changes the percentage because the whole changes.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qadir has a square of side 3 cm. He makes a new square whose side is 6 cm, so the side length is multiplied by 2.

Which statement about the area is correct?

options.A: The area becomes 2 times as large, matching the side factor.
options.B: The area stays the same because both figures are still squares.
options.C: The area becomes 4 times as large, because area scales with the square of the side factor.
options.D: The perimeter becomes 4 times as large, and that same factor rule applies to area.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows square P of side 2 cm and square Q of side 4 cm. The side length is multiplied by 2 from P to Q.

Which statement about the area is correct?

options.A: The area of Q is 4 times the area of P, because area scales with the square of the side factor.
options.B: The area of Q is 2 times the area of P, matching the side factor.
options.C: The perimeter becomes 4 times as large, and that same factor rule applies to area.
options.D: The area stays the same because both figures are still squares.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows square $S$ of side $3\,\mathrm{cm}$ and square $T$ of side $6\,\mathrm{cm}$.

Which claim correctly states how the area changes from $S$ to $T$?

options.A: The area of $T$ is twice the area of $S$ because the side length doubled.
options.B: The area of $T$ is four times the area of $S$ because the side length doubled.
options.C: The area of $T$ equals the area of $S$ because both shapes are squares.
options.D: The area of $T$ is six times the area of $S$, matching the new side length.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Indira starts with a square. She may build a new square on a diagonal of the given square, or join the midpoints of the given square's sides. She wants twice the area, and also half the area.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Double the area by joining the midpoints; halve it by building on the diagonal.
options.B: Double the area by building a square on the diagonal; halve it by joining the midpoints of the sides.
options.C: Joining the midpoints doubles the area, and building on the diagonal also doubles the area.
options.D: Building on the diagonal halves the area, with no separate midpoint construction.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ishaan studies the diagram of square $PQRS$. Dashed segment $PR$ is a diagonal. Grey points $M$, $N$, $O$, $T$ are the midpoints of the sides, joined to form square $MNOT$.

Which plan correctly doubles the area of $PQRS$ and which plan halves it?

options.A: Join the midpoints to double the area, and build on diagonal $PR$ to halve it.
options.B: Build a new square on diagonal $PR$ to double the area; join midpoints $M$, $N$, $O$, $T$ to halve it.
options.C: Use either construction for either goal, because the starting figure need not be a square.
options.D: Treat every inscribed quadrilateral inside $PQRS$ as a half-area square.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Hemant studies the diagram of square $ABCD$. Dashed segment $AC$ is a diagonal. Grey points $W$, $X$, $Y$, $Z$ are the midpoints of the sides, joined to form square $WXYZ$.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims are correct?

options.A: Build a new square on diagonal $AC$ to double the area of $ABCD$.
options.B: Join midpoints $W$, $X$, $Y$, $Z$ to form square $WXYZ$ and halve the area of $ABCD$.
options.C: Join the midpoints to double the area, and build on diagonal $AC$ to halve it.
options.D: Treat every inscribed quadrilateral inside $ABCD$ as a half-area square.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Asha has a right triangle whose two perpendicular sides are equal, each of length 5. She wants the relation for the hypotenuse c.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: c² = 2 × 5² = 50, because for equal perpendicular sides a, c² = 2a².
options.B: Equal legs are produced only after c² = 2a² is known, so the side lengths cannot start the relation.
options.C: The hypotenuse equals 5, renaming the equal legs as if they were already the hypotenuse.
options.D: Choose c = 5 because 5 is the number printed on both legs.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows right triangle PQR with right angle at P. Imran measures $PQ = PR = 6$ cm and wants the relation for the hypotenuse $c$.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: $c^2 = 2 \times 6^2 = 72$, because for equal perpendicular sides $a$, $c^2 = 2a^2$.
options.B: The hypotenuse equals 6 cm, renaming the equal legs as if they were already the hypotenuse.
options.C: Equal legs are produced only after $c^2 = 2a^2$ is known, so the side lengths cannot start the relation.
options.D: Choose $c = 6$ because 6 is the number printed on both legs.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows right triangle $LMN$ with right angle at $L$. Hemant measures $LM = LN = 8\,\mathrm{cm}$ and wants the relation for the hypotenuse $c$.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: $c^{2} = 2 \times 8^{2} = 128$, because for equal perpendicular sides $a$, $c^{2} = 2a^{2}$.
options.B: The hypotenuse equals $8\,\mathrm{cm}$.
options.C: Equal legs $LM$ and $LN$ are produced by the relation $c^{2} = 2a^{2}$.
options.D: Choose $c = 8$ because $8$ is the number printed on both legs.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qadir wants to place $\sqrt{2}$ between two decimals. He checks $1.4^{2}=1.96$ and $1.5^{2}=2.25$.

Which conclusion is correct?

options.A: Report $1.4$ and $1.5$ themselves as the value of $\sqrt{2}$.
options.B: Write $1.4<\sqrt{2}<1.5$ using $-1.4$ and $-1.5$ as the trial bounds as well.
options.C: Because $1.96<2<2.25$, it follows that $1.4<\sqrt{2}<1.5$.
options.D: Say that choosing the decimals $1.4$ and $1.5$ is what creates the number $\sqrt{2}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows a number line with $\sqrt{2}$ marked. Farhan checks $1.4^{2}=1.96$ and $1.5^{2}=2.25$.

Which conclusion is correct?

options.A: Because $1.96<2<2.25$, it follows that $1.4<\sqrt{2}<1.5$.
options.B: Report $1.4$ and $1.5$ themselves as the value of $\sqrt{2}$.
options.C: Write $1.4<\sqrt{2}<1.5$ using $-1.4$ and $-1.5$ as the trial bounds as well.
options.D: Say that choosing the decimals $1.4$ and $1.5$ is what creates the number $\sqrt{2}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows a number line with $\sqrt{2}$ marked. Hemant checks $1.41^{2}=1.9881$ and $1.42^{2}=2.0164$.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims follow?

options.A: Because $1.9881<2<2.0164$, it follows that $1.41<\sqrt{2}<1.42$.
options.B: Report $1.41$ itself as the exact value of $\sqrt{2}$.
options.C: The same bracketing also holds if the trial bounds are taken as $-1.41$ and $-1.42$.
options.D: Closer positive decimals whose squares still bracket $2$ keep $\sqrt{2}$ between those decimals.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Indira asks whether $\sqrt{2}$ can be written as a terminating decimal or as a fraction of counting numbers.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the answer terminating decimal, without deciding what $\sqrt{2}$ can equal.
options.B: Write $\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{m}{n}$ without requiring $m$ and $n$ to be counting numbers with $n$ nonzero.
options.C: $\sqrt{2}$ is neither a terminating decimal nor equal to $\dfrac{m}{n}$ for counting numbers $m$ and $n$.
options.D: Decide from the printed digit $2$ alone, without testing decimal or fraction form.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Imran asks whether $\sqrt{2}$ can be written as a terminating decimal or as a fraction of counting numbers.

parts.text: Which claim correctly settles both forms?

options.text: $\sqrt{2}$ is a terminating decimal.
$\sqrt{2}$ equals $\dfrac{m}{n}$ for counting numbers $m$ and $n$ with $n\neq 0$.
$\sqrt{2}$ is neither a terminating decimal nor equal to $\dfrac{m}{n}$ for counting numbers $m$ and $n$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Hemant asks which of these forms $\sqrt{2}$ can take: a terminating decimal, or a fraction $m/n$ of counting numbers $m$ and $n$.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims are correct?

options.A: $\sqrt{2}$ is correctly described as a terminating decimal.
options.B: $\sqrt{2}$ cannot be written as a terminating decimal.
options.C: $\sqrt{2}$ cannot equal $m/n$ for counting numbers $m$ and $n$ with $n\neq 0$.
options.D: $\sqrt{2}$ equals the terminating decimal $1.4$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Veena has a triangle with a right angle at $C$, and side lengths $a=BC$, $b=AC$, and $c=AB$.

Which claim applies $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$ correctly?

options.A: Write $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$ for the side lengths even when angle $C$ is not a right angle.
options.B: Say that writing $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$ is what creates the right angle at $C$, instead of using the right angle to name the hypotenuse.
options.C: Because $\angle C=90^{\circ}$, the hypotenuse is $AB=c$ opposite $C$, so $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$.
options.D: Also apply $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$ unchanged to every acute triangle with sides $a$, $b$, and $c$, beyond right-angled triangles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows $\triangle ABC$ with a right angle at $B$, $AB=5$, and $BC=12$. Vihaan wants the length of $AC$.

Which claim correctly applies $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$?

options.A: $AC$ is the hypotenuse opposite the right angle, so $5^{2}+12^{2}=AC^{2}$ and $AC=13$.
options.B: Apply $5^{2}+12^{2}=AC^{2}$ even when the right-angle mark at $B$ is removed.
options.C: The right angle at $B$ is produced only after $5^{2}+12^{2}=AC^{2}$ is written.
options.D: Treat $AC$ as a leg and set $AC^{2}+5^{2}=12^{2}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri has $\triangle PQR$ with a right angle at $P$, $PQ=6$, and $PR=8$. She wants the length of $QR$.

Which claim correctly applies $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$?

options.A: $6^{2}+8^{2}=QR^{2}$ even if angle $P$ were not a right angle.
options.B: The hypotenuse $QR$ is what creates the right angle at $P$.
options.C: $PQ$ and $PR$ are the perpendicular sides, so $6^{2}+8^{2}=QR^{2}$ and $QR=10$.
options.D: Treat $PQ$ as the hypotenuse, so $8^{2}+QR^{2}=6^{2}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Parul has a right-angled triangle with legs $a=6$ and $b=8$ and hypotenuse $c$. She wants $c$ from $a^2+b^2=c^2$.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Use $c=\sqrt{6^2+8^2}$ even if the triangle is not right-angled and $c$ is not the hypotenuse, skipping those conditions.
options.B: Find a missing leg by adding the known squares the same way, as when the unknown is a leg rather than the hypotenuse.
options.C: Rearrange to $c=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}=\sqrt{36+64}=\sqrt{100}=10$, taking the positive square root.
options.D: Compute $c=6^2+8^2=100$ and stop, leaving the value squared instead of taking the positive square root.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Yash's right-angled triangle $ABC$ with right angle at $A$, legs $AB=5$ and $AC=12$, and hypotenuse $BC=c$.

Which plan finds $c$ correctly?

options.B: Use $c=\sqrt{5^2+12^2}$ even when $c$ is treated as a leg rather than the hypotenuse.
options.C: Find a missing leg by adding the known squares the same way as for the hypotenuse.
options.D: Compute $c=5^2+12^2=169$ and leave the answer squared.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri has a right-angled triangle with legs $a=9$ and $b=12$ and hypotenuse $c$. She wants $c$ from $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$.

Which plan is correct?

options.B: $c=9+12=21$, treating the legs as already the hypotenuse length.
options.C: $c=\sqrt{12^{2}-9^{2}}$, subtracting the known squares as if $c$ were a leg.
options.D: $c=9^{2}+12^{2}=225$, leaving the sum of squares without the square root.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
A bamboo pole leans from the ground up to a wall. The diagram shows the right triangle formed by the pole, the wall, and the ground.

Before writing an \(a^2 + b^2 = c^2\) equation, what must Chirag identify?

options.A: The ground distance and the wall height as the two legs, and the pole as the hypotenuse opposite the right angle.
options.B: Perpendicular distances as the answer label, without naming which segments are legs or hypotenuse.
options.C: Write \(a^2 + b^2 = c^2\) first; checking that the lengths form a right triangle can wait.
options.D: Form the equation for any three lengths nearby, even if they do not make a right triangle.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows a ladder leaning from the ground to a wall, forming a right triangle.

Before writing an $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$ equation, what must Diya identify?

options.A: The ground distance and the wall height as the two legs, and the ladder as the hypotenuse opposite the right angle.
options.B: Perpendicular distances as the answer label on the diagram.
options.C: Write $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$ first; checking that the lengths form a right triangle can wait.
options.D: Form the equation for any three lengths nearby, even if they do not make a right triangle.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Poonam has the positive-integer triple $(7, 24, 25)$ and takes $25$ as the largest entry.

Which claim correctly classifies the triple?

options.A: Report the words legs $a$ and $b$ as the classification of $(7, 24, 25)$.
options.B: Naming legs $7$ and $24$ is what creates the integer triple $(7, 24, 25)$.
options.C: $(7, 24, 25)$ is a Baudhāyana triple because $7^{2} + 24^{2} = 25^{2}$.
options.D: $(7, 24, 25)$ is a Baudhāyana triple because $25$ is the standout largest printed number.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nitya checks whether the positive-integer triple $(5, 12, 13)$ is a Baudhāyana triple.

Which two claims correctly classify it?

options.A: Call the answer the legs $5$ and $12$ alone, and stop.
options.B: The largest entry is $13$, and $5^2+12^2=25+144=169=13^2$, so the triple satisfies $a^2+b^2=c^2$.
options.C: Because $a^2+b^2=c^2$ holds with largest entry $c=13$, $(5, 12, 13)$ is a Baudhāyana triple.
options.D: Decide only because $13$ is the largest printed number in the triple, with no square check.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Smita knows that $(5, 12, 13)$ is a Baudhāyana triple. She multiplies every entry by $3$ to get $(15, 36, 39)$.

parts.text: Is $(15, 36, 39)$ also a Baudhāyana triple?

options.text: Yes
No

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anaya knows that $(3,4,5)$ is a Baudhāyana triple. She multiplies every entry by $2$ to get $(6,8,10)$.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: $(6,8,10)$ is a Baudhāyana triple only if the factor $2$ is renamed hypotenuse.
options.B: $(6,8,10)$ satisfies $6^{2}+8^{2}=10^{2}$, so it is still a Baudhāyana triple.
options.C: Multiplying every entry of a Baudhāyana triple by the same positive integer preserves the triple relation.
options.D: $(6,8,10)$ looks larger in print than $(3,4,5)$, so it cannot stay a Baudhāyana triple.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kunal knows that $(3, 4, 5)$ and $(6, 8, 10)$ both satisfy $a^{2} + b^{2} = c^{2}$.

Which two claims correctly distinguish a primitive Baudhāyana triple from a scaled triple?

options.A: The answer for $(6, 8, 10)$ is the label non-primitive triple, with no common-factor check.
options.B: $(3, 4, 5)$ is primitive because $3$, $4$, and $5$ have no common factor greater than $1$.
options.C: $(6, 8, 10)$ is not primitive because $2$ divides $6$, $8$, and $10$.
options.D: $(6, 8, 10)$ must be primitive because scaling $(3, 4, 5)$ by $2$ still gives $a^{2} + b^{2} = c^{2}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Farhan knows that $(5, 12, 13)$ and $(10, 24, 26)$ both satisfy $a^{2} + b^{2} = c^{2}$.

parts.text: Which claim correctly distinguishes the triples?

options.text: $(5, 12, 13)$ is primitive because $\gcd(5,12,13)=1$; $(10, 24, 26)$ is a scale of that triple by $2$.
Call $(10, 24, 26)$ a non-primitive triple label only, with no common-factor check.
Scaling every entry by $2$ is what creates the primitive triple $(5, 12, 13)$ from $(10, 24, 26)$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Megha uses the identity $(n-1)^{2}+(2n-1)=n^{2}$. She takes the case $2n-1=25=5^{2}$.

parts.text: Which Baudhāyana triple does this case give?
Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Adil uses the odd-number square identity $(n-1)^{2}+(2n-1)=n^{2}$. When $2n-1$ is itself a square $m^{2}$, the triple $(m,\,n-1,\,n)$ is a Baudh\={a}yana triple. Here $2n-1=9$.

parts.text: Which triple does that value give?
Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Heena compares $x^{2}+y^{2}=z^{2}$ with $x^{n}+y^{n}=z^{n}$ for integers $n>2$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Both equations are Baudhāyana triples under one shared name.
options.B: Solutions for $n>2$ are what produce the square-power triples, rather than the square case being the one with triples.
options.C: Positive natural-number solutions exist for the square case, but not when $n>2$.
options.D: The equations match because both print a plus sign between powers.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Avni compares $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$ with $a^{n}+b^{n}=c^{n}$ for integers $n>2$.

parts.text: Which claim is correct?

options.text: Positive natural-number solutions exist for the square case, but not when $n>2$.
Both equations are Baudhāyana triples under one shared name.
Solutions for $n>2$ are what produce the square-power triples.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Uma compares the two-term ratios 2:5 and 4:10.

Which decision is correct?

options.A: They are proportional because both ratios mention corresponding terms.
options.B: They are proportional even if the second ratio is read as 10:4.
options.C: They are proportional because $2 \times 10 = 5 \times 4$.
options.D: They are proportional only when every ingredient of a full mixture matches, not just these two terms.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Adil compares the two-term ratios 3 : 7 and 6 : 14.

parts.text: Which decision is correct?

options.text: They are proportional because $3 \times 14 = 7 \times 6$.
They are proportional even if the second ratio is read as 14 : 6.
They are proportional because both ratios mention corresponding terms.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Karan compares the two-term ratios $2:3$ and $8:12$.

parts.text: Which claim correctly decides whether the ratios are proportional?

options.text: Yes: $2\times 12=3\times 8$, so the ratios are proportional.
No: $8$ is larger than $2$, so the ratios cannot be proportional.
Yes: both ratios use only even numbers.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

subject: maths
stem:
Bharat reads a map with representative fraction 1 : 50,000. The measured map distance between two towns is 4 cm.

What is the actual ground distance?

options.A: 4 cm, because that is the map distance he measured.
options.B: The ground distance produces the representative fraction, so he divides 4 by 50,000.
options.C: 2 km, because 4 cm on the map stands for 4 × 50,000 cm = 200,000 cm = 2 km.
options.D: 50,000 km, because 50,000 is the largest number printed on the map key.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kavya reads a map with representative fraction $1 : 50{,}000$. The measured map distance between two towns is $3\,\mathrm{cm}$.

Which two claims correctly convert that map distance into ground distance?

options.A: Call the answer the measured map distance $3\,\mathrm{cm}$, and stop there.
options.B: Ground distance $= 3 \times 50{,}000 = 1{,}50{,}000\,\mathrm{cm}$, which is $1.5\,\mathrm{km}$.
options.C: The representative fraction links $1\,\mathrm{cm}$ on the map to $50{,}000\,\mathrm{cm}$ on the ground, so multiply the map length by $50{,}000$.
options.D: Divide $50{,}000$ by $3$ to undo the representative fraction.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Indira reads a map with representative fraction $1 : 40{,}000$. The measured map distance between two temples is $5\,\mathrm{cm}$.

parts.text: What is the actual ground distance?

options.text: $2\,\mathrm{km}$
$5\,\mathrm{km}$
$40\,\mathrm{km}$

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

subject: maths
stem:
Rina shares prize money in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5. The first share is ₹20.

Which statement correctly gives all three shares?

options.A: The answer is "corresponding terms", without finding the rupee amounts.
options.B: The shares ₹20, ₹30, ₹50 are what create the ratio 2 : 3 : 5, so she works backwards without a common factor.
options.C: Multiply every term by 10: the shares are ₹20, ₹30 and ₹50.
options.D: Give ₹5 to someone, because 5 is the largest number printed in the ratio.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Diya shares prize money in the ratio $2 : 3 : 5$. The first share is ₹40.

parts.text: Which claim correctly gives all three shares?

options.text: Multiply every term by 20: the shares are ₹40, ₹60 and ₹100.
The shares ₹40, ₹60, ₹100 are what create the ratio $2 : 3 : 5$, so she works backwards without a common factor.
Give ₹5 to someone, because 5 is the largest number printed in the ratio.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Indira shares prize money in the ratio $3 : 4 : 5$. The first share is ₹$30$.

parts.text: Which statement correctly gives all three shares?

options.text: The shares are ₹$30$, ₹$40$, ₹$50$, each term scaled by the same factor $10$.
Scale only the first term to ₹$30$ and leave the other terms as ₹$4$ and ₹$5$.
The shares are ₹$30$, ₹$30$, ₹$30$, because ₹$30$ is the printed first share.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

subject: maths
stem:
Jatin must divide ₹$60$ among three friends in the ratio $2 : 3 : 5$.

How should he find the three shares?

options.A: Answer "ratio terms", naming that phrase instead of computing rupee amounts.
options.B: Treat the problem as two people sharing a work job, and add work rates instead of splitting ₹$60$.
options.C: Add the terms $2+3+5=10$, then give $\frac{2}{10}\times 60$, $\frac{3}{10}\times 60$, and $\frac{5}{10}\times 60$, so ₹$12$, ₹$18$, and ₹$30$.
options.D: Divide $60$ by each of $2$, $3$, and $5$ separately, getting $30$, $20$, and $12$, instead of multiplying each term by $60/10$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Tara must divide ₹$84$ among three friends in the ratio $2 : 3 : 7$.

parts.text: How should she find the three shares?

options.text: Answer "ratio terms", naming that phrase instead of computing rupee amounts.
Treat the problem as two people sharing a work job, and add work rates instead of splitting ₹$84$.
Add the terms $2+3+7=12$, then give $\frac{2}{12}\times 84$, $\frac{3}{12}\times 84$, and $\frac{7}{12}\times 84$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Esha must divide ₹$90$ among three friends in the ratio $1 : 2 : 3$.

parts.text: How should she find the three shares?

options.text: The answer is the phrase "ratio terms", with no rupee amounts computed.
Treat the problem as two people sharing a work job, and add work rates instead of splitting ₹$90$.
Add the terms $1+2+3=6$, then give $\frac{1}{6}\times 90$, $\frac{2}{6}\times 90$, and $\frac{3}{6}\times 90$, so ₹$15$, ₹$30$, and ₹$45$.
Divide $90$ by each of $1$, $2$, and $3$ separately, getting $90$, $45$, and $30$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nalini draws a pie chart for three categories with counts $10$, $20$, and $30$.

How many degrees should the $20$ category occupy?

options.A: Report the category count $20$ itself as the number of degrees on the pie chart.
options.B: Compute $\dfrac{20}{360}\times 100$ degrees, as if the three counts need not form one complete whole.
options.C: The whole is $10+20+30=60$, so the slice is $\dfrac{20}{60}\times 360^{\circ}=120^{\circ}$.
options.D: Choose $30^{\circ}$ only because $30$ is the largest printed count among $10$, $20$, and $30$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Diya draws the pie chart in the diagram for class votes: cricket $8$, football $12$, kabaddi $4$.

How many degrees should the football category occupy?

options.A: Report $12^{\circ}$, taking the football count itself as the degree measure.
options.B: Treat $360$ as the category total and compute $\dfrac{12}{360}\times 24$ degrees.
options.C: The whole is $8+12+4=24$, so football occupies $\dfrac{12}{24}\times 360^{\circ}=180^{\circ}$.

stem: Esha draws a pie chart for library loans in three categories: fiction $15$, science $25$, and comics $10$.

parts.text: How many degrees should the science category occupy?
Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Asha drives a fixed distance. She asks how travel time changes when her speed doubles.

Which claim is correct before finding the new time?

options.A: Call the answer inverse proportion, without deciding how speed and time are related for the fixed distance.
options.B: Treat it as direct proportion even though speed and time do not increase together on a fixed distance.
options.C: Treat it as inverse proportion: for fixed distance, speed $\times$ time stays constant, so doubling speed halves the time.
options.D: Say that the inverse relationship is what creates the fixed distance.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anaya compares two situations before calculating a missing value.
Situation 1: more identical taps fill a tank in less time.
Situation 2: more notebooks at the same price cost more money.

Which two claims correctly classify the relationships?

options.A: Call Situation 1 inverse proportion as a label and Situation 2 the same label.
options.B: Situation 1 is inverse proportion, because taps and time move in opposite directions.
options.C: Situation 2 is direct proportion, because notebooks and cost increase together.
options.D: Inverse proportion is what creates more taps finishing the tank sooner.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Hemant has a fixed wall to paint. He asks how the number of days changes when the number of identical workers doubles.

Which claim is correct before finding the new number of days?

options.A: Call the situation direct proportion, because the word double appears.
options.B: Treat days and workers as rising together, even though the wall size is fixed.
options.C: Treat days and workers as inverse proportion: more workers mean fewer days for the same wall.
options.D: Workers produce the wall size, so reverse and ignore how days change.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tanya knows $x$ and $y$ are inversely proportional. When $x=4$, $y=15$. She needs $y$ when $x=6$.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Call the answer inverse proportion only, without keeping the product $x\times y$ constant.
options.B: Use $4\times15=60$, but then find the new $y$ without setting $6\times y=60$.
options.C: Keep the product constant: $4\times15=6\times y$, so $y=60/6=10$.
options.D: Choose $y=15$ again only because $15$ is the largest printed number among $4$, $15$, and $6$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ira's pump empties a fixed tank. With 6 workers the job takes 10 hours. The work rate is inversely proportional to the time, and the tank size stays fixed.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: The needed idea is only the phrase constant product, so the inverse link between workers and hours can be ignored.
options.B: Keep the product of workers and hours constant: $6\times10=60$.
options.C: With 4 workers the time is $60/4=15$ hours.
options.D: The same 60 also settles a changing tank size mid-job.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Hemant knows the number of taps and the time to fill a fixed tank are inversely proportional. With $5$ taps the job takes $12$ hours. He needs the time when $8$ taps work on the same tank.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Keep the product constant: $5\times12=8\times t$, so $t=\dfrac{60}{8}=7.5$ hours.
options.B: The constant product is only a label, so ignore the fixed tank and pick any time.
options.C: Scale time the same way as taps: $t=12\times\dfrac{8}{5}=19.2$ hours, as if the tank size need not stay fixed.
options.D: The answer is $12$ hours because $12$ is the only time printed in the stem.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tushar paints $\dfrac{1}{6}$ of a wall in one hour. Pallavi paints $\dfrac{1}{3}$ of the same wall in one hour. They work together on that wall.

Which claim correctly combines their work?

options.A: Keep only one individual rate as the answer, without combining the two hourly amounts.
options.B: The finishing time is what produces each painter's individual rate.
options.C: Add the hourly amounts: $\dfrac{1}{6}+\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{1}{2}$ of the wall per hour, so together they finish in $2$ hours.
options.D: Multiply $\dfrac{1}{6}$ by $\dfrac{1}{3}$ as if inverse proportion alone settled the shared task.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Krish fills $\dfrac{1}{8}$ of a tank in one hour. Anvi fills $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of the same tank in one hour. They work together.

Which two claims correctly combine their work?

options.A: The combined answer is Krish's individual rate $\dfrac{1}{8}$ alone.
options.B: In one hour they fill $\dfrac{1}{8}+\dfrac{1}{4}=\dfrac{3}{8}$ of the tank.
options.C: Their combined rate is the sum of the fractions of the tank each fills in one hour.
options.D: Treat the times as inversely proportional constants and solve $8\times4=k$ for the joint time.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nitin studies a fern leaf in which each leaflet looks like a smaller copy of the whole leaf. He also looks at a plain rectangle with no smaller copies inside it.

Which claim about the fern leaf is correct?

options.A: It is a fractal, because the same pattern repeats at smaller scales.
options.B: It is a fractal, because any leaf counts as a fractal.
options.C: It is not a fractal, because only computer drawings can be fractals.
options.D: It is not a fractal, because the plain rectangle is the true fractal pattern.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kavya studies a branching-tree drawing in which each small branch looks like a smaller copy of the whole tree. She also looks at a plain oval with no smaller copies inside it.

Which two claims are correct?

options.A: The plain oval is a fractal, because any closed curve counts as a fractal.
options.B: The branching tree is a fractal, because the same structure repeats at smaller scales.
options.C: The plain oval is not a fractal, because it has no self-similar smaller copies.
options.D: Only computer drawings can be fractals, so the branching tree is not one.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows pattern $P$ that Inaya drew: a large Y with a smaller Y on each tip, and a still smaller Y on each of those tips.

Which claim correctly decides whether pattern $P$ is a fractal?

options.A: Pattern $P$ is a fractal because it repeats a similar Y shape at smaller scales.
options.B: Pattern $P$ is not a fractal because the branches get shorter.
options.C: Pattern $P$ is a fractal because it is drawn with straight line segments.
options.D: Pattern $P$ is not a fractal because a Y is not a closed polygon.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Farhan builds a Sierpinski Carpet starting from 1 square at step 0. At each next step, every remaining square is replaced by 8 smaller remaining squares, so R_{n+1} = 8 R_n with R_0 = 1.

How many remaining squares are there at step 2?
author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Farhan builds a Sierpinski Carpet. The diagram shows step $1$, where the starting square is divided into $9$ equal squares and the centre square is removed, leaving $8$ remaining squares. Each later step replaces every remaining square by $8$ smaller remaining squares, so $R_{n+1} = 8 R_n$ with $R_0 = 1$.

How many remaining squares are there at step $3$?

options.A: $24$, adding $8$ three times from the step-$1$ count.
options.B: $9^{3} = 729$, squaring-style growth on the $9$-way split.
options.D: $8^{2} = 64$, stopping at the formula for a different removal count.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Javed builds a Sierpinski Carpet with $R_{0} = 1$. At each next step every remaining square becomes $8$ smaller remaining squares, so $R_{n+1} = 8 R_{n}$.

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

statements.text: At step $2$ there are $64$ remaining squares.
At step $3$ there are $24$ remaining squares.
The count of remaining squares follows $R_{n} = 8^{n}$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Wasim builds a Sierpinski Carpet. After step 1 he has H₁ = 1 hole and R₁ = 8 remaining squares. At the next step every remaining square gains one new centre hole, and old holes stay.

How many holes are there at step 2?

options.A: 8, counting the remaining squares as if they were the holes.
options.B: 8, adding only the new holes and forgetting the 1 old hole.
options.C: 9, because H₂ = H₁ + R₁ = 1 + 8.
options.D: 17, by also counting the 8 filled remaining squares as holes.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows a Sierpinski Carpet after step 1: $H_{1}=1$ hole and $R_{1}=8$ remaining squares. Ishaan moves to step 2, where every remaining square gains one new hole and all old holes remain.

How many holes are there at step 2?

options.B: $8$, counting the remaining squares as if they were the holes.
options.C: $8$, adding only the new holes and forgetting the $1$ old hole.
options.D: $17$, by also counting the $8$ filled remaining squares as holes.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Javed builds a Sierpinski Carpet. After step $2$ he has $H_{2} = 9$ holes and $R_{2} = 64$ remaining squares. At the next step every remaining square gains one new centre hole, and old holes stay, so $H_{n+1} = H_{n} + R_{n}$.

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

statements.text: At step $3$ there are $64$ holes.
At step $3$ there are $73$ holes, because $H_{3} = H_{2} + R_{2} = 9 + 64$.
Old holes remain when the new centre holes are added.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nitin builds a Sierpinski Triangle. He starts with one filled equilateral triangle. At each step he joins the midpoints of every remaining filled triangle and removes the open middle triangle.

After step $1$, how many filled triangles remain?

options.A: $1$, keeping the original triangle without removing the open middle.
options.B: Say that removing the middle is what creates the midpoints, so he skips joining midpoints first.
options.C: $3$, because joining the midpoints makes four congruent small triangles and the open middle is removed.
options.D: Count holes with the Sierpinski Carpet square-hole rule instead of midpoint removal on triangles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Imran builds a Sierpinski Triangle as in the diagram. He starts with one filled equilateral triangle. At each step he joins the midpoints of every remaining filled triangle and removes the open middle triangle.

After step $1$, how many filled triangles remain?

options.A: $1$, keeping the original triangle together with the middle piece.
options.B: Removing the middle is what creates the midpoints on the sides.
options.C: $3$, because joining the midpoints makes four congruent small triangles and the open middle is removed.
options.D: Count holes with the Sierpinski Carpet square-hole rule instead of midpoint removal on triangles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Alok builds a Sierpinski Triangle. He starts with one filled equilateral triangle. At each step he joins the midpoints of every remaining filled triangle and removes the open middle triangle.

Which statements are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

statements.text: After step $1$, $3$ filled triangles remain.
After step $2$, $9$ filled triangles remain.
After step $1$, $4$ filled triangles remain because the middle triangle is kept.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Farhan has finished Koch Snowflake step $0$: one equilateral triangle. He applies the side-replacement rule once to get step $1$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the answer "equilateral triangle", without applying the side-replacement rule.
options.B: Update only one side, skipping that every current side gets the same replacement.
options.C: Replace every current side: divide into $3$ equal parts, raise an equilateral bump on the middle third and remove that middle segment, so all $3$ sides are updated.
options.D: Say the jagged snowflake boundary is what produces the replacement rule.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows a Koch Snowflake at step $0$ (one equilateral triangle) and at step $1$ after the side-replacement rule. Rohan predicts step $2$ from step $1$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Replace every current side of the step-$1$ boundary with the same bump-shaped structure.
options.B: Call the next figure an equilateral triangle and treat that starting label as step $2$.
options.C: Update only the original three sides from step $0$, leaving the new bump edges unchanged.
options.D: A more jagged snowflake boundary is what produces the choice to bump every current side.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Alok has a Koch Snowflake at step $1$. He predicts step $2$ by the side-replacement rule.

Which statements are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

statements.text: Every current side of the step-$1$ boundary is replaced by the same bump-shaped structure.
Only the original three sides from step $0$ are updated; new bump edges stay unchanged.
After one replacement, each former side becomes four segments along the new boundary.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Hassan views a cube from the front and sees a square profile. He asks whether only a cube can show that square from a chosen viewpoint.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Conclude that only the cube works, skipping that the same square profile can come from more than one solid or viewpoint.
options.B: Say that the square profile is what creates the front viewpoint on the cube, instead of the viewpoint choosing the visible profile.
options.C: A cube can show a square from the front, but more than one solid can fit that same square profile from some viewpoint.
options.D: Use the same profile question to compute the cube's volume, beyond identifying possible profiles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows Adil's cube and the square profile seen from the front view.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: A cube can show that square from the front, and more than one solid can fit the same square profile from some viewpoint.
options.B: Only the cube works for that square, because the viewpoint may be ignored when naming the profile.
options.C: The square front profile is what creates the front viewpoint on the cube.
options.D: Use the same square-profile question to compute the cube's volume.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Esha views a cylinder from the side and sees a rectangular profile. She asks whether only a cylinder can show that rectangle from a chosen viewpoint.

parts.text: Which claim is correct?

options.text: A rectangular side profile can come from more than one solid, not only from a cylinder.
Any solid shows a rectangle from the side, so the viewpoint need not be checked.
The rectangular outline is what chooses the viewpoint, rather than the viewpoint shaping the profile.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Xavier has a solid with two parallel pentagon faces joined by five rectangular faces. He wants its type and its face, edge, and vertex counts.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the solid an "edge" count only, without classifying it from its faces.
options.B: Say that listing $15$ edges is what creates the two pentagon bases, instead of reading the face arrangement first.
options.C: It is a pentagonal prism: $n=5$ gives $n+2=7$ faces, $3n=15$ edges, and $2n=10$ vertices.
options.D: Switch to dropping perpendiculars from points to a plane, and treat that projection method as this face-edge-vertex count.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows a solid with two parallel hexagon faces joined by six rectangular faces.

Which claim correctly names the solid and counts its faces, edges, and vertices?

options.A: It is a hexagonal prism with $8$ faces, $18$ edges, and $12$ vertices.
options.B: Count edges as the solid's faces, so the face total is $18$.
options.C: The face-edge-vertex counts produce the hexagon base shape.
options.D: Treat it as a hexagonal pyramid, which also has two parallel hexagon faces.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem: Esha has a solid with two parallel triangle faces joined by three rectangular faces. She wants its type and its face, edge, and vertex counts.

parts.text: Which claim correctly names the solid and counts its faces, edges, and vertices?

options.text: It is a triangular prism with $5$ faces, $9$ edges, and $6$ vertices.
The solid is named from its edges alone, so call it a $9$-edge solid and skip the face count.
The face–edge–vertex counts produce the triangle bases, so start from $5$, $9$, and $6$ without reading the faces.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Naveen checks flat card cut-outs meant as nets for a cube.

Which arrangements are valid mathematical nets for a cube? Two options are correct.

options.A: Six squares in a straight row.
options.B: A cross of five squares with one more square joined to a side of the centre strip.
options.C: Four squares in a row, with one square joined above the second and one joined below the third.
options.D: Six face squares plus thin joining flaps treated as extra faces.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Aarav looks at the diagram: a flat arrangement of six rectangles labelled $A$–$F$.

Which claim correctly decides whether this arrangement is a valid net for a cuboid?

options.A: It is a valid net: the six faces fold into a cuboid with no overlaps, and joining flaps are not counted as extra faces.
options.B: Call it a net even when the faces cannot meet edge-to-edge when folded from paper or cardboard.
options.C: Accept it as a net only because it has six regions, even if some faces would overlap when folded.
options.D: Call it a net only because the word net is the most obvious printed label near the diagram.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows a net of a cuboid with edges 6 cm, 4 cm and 3 cm. An ant crawls on the surface from corner $A$ to corner $G$.

Which claim correctly identifies a shortest surface path?

options.A: On the net that joins a 6-by-4 face to a 6-by-3 face, the straight $A$-to-$G$ segment has length $\sqrt{6^{2}+7^{2}}=\sqrt{85}$ cm and is shortest among the three face-pair unfolds.
options.B: The shortest surface path is $\sqrt{6^{2}+4^{2}+3^{2}}$ cm, the interior space diagonal.
options.C: Adding $6+4+3$ gives the shortest surface path.
options.D: The unfold with length $\sqrt{109}$ cm is shortest because that net covers more area.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows a net of a cuboid with edges $5$ cm, $4$ cm and $3$ cm. An ant crawls on the surface from corner $A$ to opposite corner $G$.

Which claim correctly identifies a shortest surface path?

options.A: On the net that joins a $5$-by-$4$ face to a $5$-by-$3$ face into a $5$-by-$7$ rectangle, the straight $A$-to-$G$ segment has length $\sqrt{5^{2}+7^{2}}=\sqrt{74}$ cm, shortest among the three standard unfolds.
options.B: The shortest surface path is $\sqrt{5^{2}+4^{2}+3^{2}}$ cm, the interior space diagonal.
options.C: Adding $5+4+3$ gives the shortest surface path.
options.D: The unfold of length $\sqrt{3^{2}+9^{2}}=\sqrt{90}$ cm is shortest because that net covers more area.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows point $P$, line $L$, and points $F$ and $Q$ on $L$. Segment $PF$ meets $L$ at right angles. Segment $PQ$ is drawn dashed.

Which claim about the perpendicular projection of $P$ onto $L$ is correct?

options.A: Point $F$ is the perpendicular projection of $P$ onto $L$, and $PF$ is the shortest segment from $P$ to $L$.
options.B: Segment $PQ$ is the perpendicular projection of $P$ onto $L$.
options.C: Every segment from $P$ to a point on $L$ is a perpendicular projection onto $L$.
options.D: Point $F$ is the projection of $P$ onto $L$ only because $F$ is labelled on $L$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows point $P$, line $L$, and points $F$ and $Q$ on $L$. Segment $PF$ meets $L$ at right angles. Segment $PQ$ is slanted.

Which two claims correctly describe the perpendicular projection of $P$ onto $L$?

options.A: The foot $F$ is the perpendicular projection of $P$ onto $L$.
options.B: Call the answer plane only, with no choice between $F$ and $Q$.
options.C: $PF$ is shorter than $PQ$ because the perpendicular segment is the shortest path from $P$ to $L$.
options.D: Point $Q$ is the projection because $Q$ is the rightmost labelled point on $L$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows the front, top, and side views of a solid.

Which claim correctly tells how to identify the solid?

options.A: Use the front, top, and side views together, because a single projection does not fix a unique solid.
options.B: The front view alone names the solid.
options.C: Naming the solid is what creates the front, top, and side views.
options.D: Any one of the three views is enough for every solid in this topic.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Meher looks at the diagram. It shows the front, top, and side views of one solid.

Which claim correctly decides how to identify the solid from those views?

options.A: Use the front, top, and side views together; one projection alone is not enough.
options.B: Match the solid from the front view alone.
options.C: Having named the solid is what creates the three views.
options.D: Also treat any single corner sketch as enough under the same three-view rule.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows a $2$ by $1$ by $1$ solid of unit cubes on an isometric grid. Komal wants to read its length, depth, and height from the grid.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Count $2$ units along length, $1$ along depth, and $1$ along height using the three isometric grid directions.
options.B: Count the solid on a square grid only; the three isometric directions are not needed.
options.C: The three isometric grid directions are produced by the $2$ by $1$ by $1$ solid.
options.D: The same three isometric directions also serve for every flat square-grid drawing of a rectangle.

subject: maths
stem:
The diagram shows a $3$ by $1$ by $1$ solid of unit cubes on an isometric grid. Sameer wants to read its length, depth, and height from the grid.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Count $3$ units along length, $1$ along depth, and $1$ along height using the three isometric grid directions.
options.B: Count only on a square grid; the three isometric directions are not needed.
options.C: The three isometric grid directions are produced by the $3$ by $1$ by $1$ solid.
options.D: Add $3+1+1$ on one axis to get the solid's size.
